terms.apa_reference: Cohen, M. D., March, J. G., & Olsen, J. P. (1972). A garbage can model of organizational choice. Administrative Science Quarterly, 17(1), 1–25. https://doi.org/10.2307/2392088

terms.vietnamese: Mô hình phương sai thay đổi có điều kiện tự hồi quy tổng quát
vietnamese_variants: Mô hình biến động tài chính GARCH
terms.core_definition: Mô hình GARCH (Bollerslev, 1986) là mô hình kinh tế lượng tài chính chuẩn mực mở rộng từ mô hình ARCH của Engle (1982), dùng để mô hình hóa và dự báo phương sai có điều kiện (biến động - volatility) của chuỗi thời gian tài chính. GARCH nắm bắt xuất sắc hiện tượng cụm biến động (volatility clustering: các dao động lớn có xu hướng đi liền với các dao động lớn) và đặc tính phân phối đuôi dày (fat tails/leptokurtosis).
terms.seminal_citation: Bollerslev (1986); Engle (1982)
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #1091; LaTeX thô; nguồn ghi ngưỡng
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of GARCH according to Tổng các hệ số ARCH và GARCH (α + β) phải nhỏ hơn 1 để đảm bảo tính dừng của phương sai có điều kiện..
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Phương trình giá trị trung bình: y_t = mu + e_t với e_t = σ_t · z_t, z_t ~ i.i.d(0, 1). 2. Phương trình phương sai có điều kiện GARCH(1,1): σ_t² = ω + α · e_{t-1}² + β · sigma_{t-1}², trong đó ω > 0, α ≥ 0, β ≥ 0. 3. alpha đo lường mức độ phản ứng tức thời trước các cú sốc mới (ARCH effect); beta đo lường mức độ dai dẳng của biến động trong quá khứ (GARCH effect).
terms.benchmarks: Điều kiện dừng hiệp phương sai (Covariance Stationarity): Tổng α + β < 1. Độ dai dẳng của biến động (Persistence): (α + beta) thường dao động trong khoảng 0.90 đến 0.99 trong dữ liệu tài chính hàng ngày. Ước lượng thông qua Hợp lý cực đại chuẩn tắc (Quasi-Maximum Likelihood - QMLE) với sai số chuẩn vững Bollerslev-Wooldridge.
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: (1) Mô hình GARCH chuẩn là mô hình đối xứng, không thể nắm bắt được hiệu ứng đòn bẩy (Leverage effect: tin xấu làm tăng biến động mạnh hơn tin tốt cùng độ lớn); khi đó bắt buộc phải chuyển sang các mô hình phi đối xứng như EGARCH (Nelson 1991) hoặc GJR-GARCH (Glosten et al. 1993); (2) Tổng α + β ≥ 1 vi phạm điều kiện dừng (chuyển sang IGARCH).
terms.apa_reference: Bollerslev, T. (1986). Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity. Journal of Econometrics, 31(3), 307–327. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4076(86)90063-1

terms.vietnamese: Mô hình GARCH (Tự hồi quy có điều kiện phương sai thay đổi tổng quát)
vietnamese_variants: Phương sai có điều kiện ARCH tổng quát
Mô hình biến động tài chính GARCH
terms.core_definition: GARCH (Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity), introduced by Tim Bollerslev (1986) as an extension of Robert Engle's ARCH model (1982), is an econometric modeling framework designed to estimate and forecast time-varying volatility in high-frequency financial and economic time series. GARCH models the conditional variance of the error term as a linear function of both past squared innovations (lagged shocks / ARCH terms) and past conditional variances (lagged volatility / GARCH terms). This autoregressive structure enables GARCH to capture volatility clustering (large changes tend to be followed by large changes of either sign), leptokurtosis (fat tails), and mean reversion in volatility with substantially greater parsimony than higher-order ARCH models.
terms.seminal_citation: Bollerslev, T. (1986). Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity. Journal of Econometrics, 31(3), 307-327.
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #1090
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of GARCH (Generalized ARCH) according to Bollerslev (1986).
terms.operational_mechanism: In a standard GARCH(p, q) model, the return process is specified as y_t = mu_t + epsilon_t, where epsilon_t = sigma_t * z_t with z_t ~ i.i.d. N(0, 1) or Student's t. The conditional variance equation for the canonical GARCH(1,1) is: sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha_1 * epsilon_{t-1}^2 + beta_1 * sigma_{t-1}^2, subject to constraints: omega > 0, alpha_1 >= 0, beta_1 >= 0, and persistence condition alpha_1 + beta_1 < 1 to ensure covariance stationarity. The model is estimated via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) or Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation (QMLE) under robust Bollerslev-Wooldridge standard errors.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: In a standard GARCH(p, q) model, the return process is specified as y_t = mu_t + epsilon_t, where epsilon_t = sigma_t * z_t with z_t ~ i.i.d. N(0, 1) or Student's t. The conditional variance equation for the canonical GARCH(1,1) is: sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha_1 * epsilon_{t-1}^2 + beta_1 * sigma_{t-1}^2, subject to constraints: omega > 0, alpha_1 >= 0, beta_1 >= 0, and persistence condition alpha_1 + beta_1 < 1 to ensure covariance stationarity. The model is estimated via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) or Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation (QMLE) under robust Bollerslev-Wooldridge standard errors.
terms.benchmarks: In empirical finance and macroeconomics: (1) In a standard daily financial return GARCH(1,1), alpha_1 typically ranges between 0.05 and 0.15 (reaction to immediate shock), while beta_1 ranges between 0.80 and 0.90 (volatility persistence); (2) Covariance stationarity requires alpha_1 + beta_1 < 1.0 (if alpha + beta = 1.0, an Integrated GARCH / IGARCH model is indicated); (3) Standardized residuals e_t = epsilon_t / sigma_t must pass the ARCH-LM test (p > 0.05) and Ljung-Box Q-test on squared residuals to confirm that conditional heteroskedasticity has been successfully modeled.
terms.pitfalls: Common econometric errors include: (1) Estimating GARCH under assumption of Gaussian errors when financial returns exhibit extreme kurtosis, failing to specify Student-t or Generalized Error Distributions (GED); (2) Ignoring leverage effects (where negative shocks generate greater volatility than positive shocks of equal magnitude), failing to consider asymmetric extensions like EGARCH (Nelson, 1991) or GJR-GARCH (Glosten et al., 1993); and (3) Violating the stationarity constraint (alpha + beta >= 1) without transitioning to non-stationary cointegrated or fractionally integrated volatility models.
terms.apa_reference: Bollerslev, T. (1986). Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity. Journal of Econometrics, 31(3), 307–327. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4076(86)90063-1

terms.vietnamese: Người gác cổng (Kiểm soát tiếp cận tổ chức)
vietnamese_variants: Nhân vật kiểm duyệt tiếp cận hiện trường
terms.core_definition: In qualitative research methodology, ethnography, and sociology, a Gatekeeper is an individual, executive, or governing entity possessing formal authority or informal socio-structural power to grant, condition, restrict, or deny a researcher physical, institutional, or informational access to a research site, organizational members, or target participant populations. First conceptualized sociologically by Kurt Lewin (1947) and developed in fieldwork methodology by Hammersley and Atkinson, gatekeepers act as boundary-spanning filters who assess the perceived legitimacy, institutional risks, operational disruption, and socio-political implications of permitting external investigative inquiry.
terms.seminal_citation: Hammersley, M., & Atkinson, P. (2007). Ethnography: Principles in practice (3rd ed.). Routledge.
terms.expert_notes: Đã được biên tập và chuẩn hóa định nghĩa học thuật theo giáo trình kinh điển.
terms.core_definition_en: Rigorous scholarly definition of Gatekeeper according to established research methodology literature.
terms.operational_mechanism: Navigating gatekeepers follows a strategic diplomatic protocol: (1) Stakeholder mapping: Identifying formal gatekeepers (CEOs, school principals, ethics review boards, prison wardens) and informal cultural gatekeepers (respected elders, executive assistants, union representatives); (2) Value proposition and risk mitigation: Crafting research briefing notes emphasizing participant confidentiality, anonymization protocols, non-evaluative stances, and reciprocal insights; (3) Iterative negotiation: Securing formal sponsorship agreements or Memoranda of Understanding (MoU) defining parameters of observation and non-disclosure; and (4) Managing boundary spanners: Maintaining transparent communication while safeguarding research independence against gatekeeper censorship or co-optation.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Navigating gatekeepers follows a strategic diplomatic protocol: (1) Stakeholder mapping: Identifying formal gatekeepers (CEOs, school principals, ethics review boards, prison wardens) and informal cultural gatekeepers (respected elders, executive assistants, union representatives); (2) Value proposition and risk mitigation: Crafting research briefing notes emphasizing participant confidentiality, anonymization protocols, non-evaluative stances, and reciprocal insights; (3) Iterative negotiation: Securing formal sponsorship agreements or Memoranda of Understanding (MoU) defining parameters of observation and non-disclosure; and (4) Managing boundary spanners: Maintaining transparent communication while safeguarding research independence against gatekeeper censorship or co-optation.
terms.benchmarks: Methodological credibility indicators: (1) Full transparency in reporting the gatekeeper pathway, documenting who granted access, what conditions were negotiated, and whether access was monitored; (2) Evidence of independent sampling, demonstrating that participants were not exclusively hand-picked by management to present an institutional whitewash; (3) Explicit documentation of researcher reflexivity regarding potential biases introduced by gatekeeper affiliation in institutional ethnographies.
terms.pitfalls: Critical qualitative pitfalls: (1) Over-identification with the gatekeeper ('going native' with executive leadership), leading subordinates to view the researcher as an management spy, causing response bias; (2) Allowing gatekeepers to veto critical or unflattering findings, compromising academic integrity; and (3) Failing to cultivate informal gatekeepers, relying solely on executive top-down directives which often generates passive participant resistance.
terms.apa_reference: Hammersley, M., & Atkinson, P. (2007). Ethnography: Principles in practice (3rd ed.). Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203944769

terms.vietnamese: Các đối tượng gác cổng trong tiếp cận hiện trường
vietnamese_variants: Các tầng lớp gác cổng hiện trường
Tác nhân kiểm soát thâm nhập nghiên cứu
terms.core_definition: Gatekeepers in Field Access refers to the multifaceted network of actors, institutional committees, administrative gatekeepers, and community leaders who collectively regulate entry into empirical settings, vulnerable populations, or closed cultural groups. In sociological and anthropological field methods, gaining access is not a single discrete event but an ongoing, negotiated socio-political process across multiple levels of hierarchy. Researchers must successfully navigate both formal gatekeepers (authorized signatories, legal departments, institutional review boards) and informal gatekeepers (opinion leaders, group matriarchs, team leads) to establish sustained trust and genuine rapport.
terms.seminal_citation: Burgess, R. G. (1984). In the field: An introduction to field research. Routledge.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gatekeepers according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism: Field access management operates across four distinct phases: (1) Preliminary scouting and identification: Distinguishing institutional gatekeepers from de facto cultural gatekeepers within the community; (2) Multi-level credentialing: Securing formal institutional approval while simultaneously presenting culturally attuned explanations to community gatekeepers; (3) Relational diplomacy and boundary setting: Defining mutual expectations, negotiating observational boundaries, and assuring non-interference in daily operations; and (4) Continuous relational maintenance: Continually renegotiating access as field dynamics shift, key gatekeepers exit, or sensitive organizational conflicts emerge.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Field access management operates across four distinct phases: (1) Preliminary scouting and identification: Distinguishing institutional gatekeepers from de facto cultural gatekeepers within the community; (2) Multi-level credentialing: Securing formal institutional approval while simultaneously presenting culturally attuned explanations to community gatekeepers; (3) Relational diplomacy and boundary setting: Defining mutual expectations, negotiating observational boundaries, and assuring non-interference in daily operations; and (4) Continuous relational maintenance: Continually renegotiating access as field dynamics shift, key gatekeepers exit, or sensitive organizational conflicts emerge.
terms.benchmarks: Evaluation criteria for methodological rigor: (1) Detailed audit trail of access negotiations including initial refusals, renegotiated scopes, and ethical clearances; (2) Verification of voluntary consent free from gatekeeper coercion (ensuring employees or students do not feel compelled to participate because a senior supervisor signed off); (3) Demonstrable diversification of access channels to prevent structural distortion of sample demographics.
terms.pitfalls: Frequent fieldwork pitfalls: (1) Assuming institutional executive sign-off guarantees participant cooperation; (2) Compromising ethical confidentiality by sharing preliminary field observations or participant identities with curious gatekeepers; (3) Structural sample bias where gatekeepers direct the ethnographer exclusively to 'exemplary' or compliant subjects; and (4) Neglecting to plan for gatekeeper turnover, leaving the research project vulnerable to sudden termination when a supportive sponsor departs.
terms.apa_reference: Burgess, R. G. (1984). In the field: An introduction to field research. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203418161

terms.vietnamese: Định lý Gauss-Markov
vietnamese_variants: Định lý Gauss-Markov về ước lượng BLUE
Định lý ước lượng tuyến tính không chệch tốt nhất
terms.core_definition: The Gauss-Markov Theorem is a central mathematical foundation of classical linear regression analysis. It states that under a set of standard classical assumptions (linearity in parameters, strict exogeneity, absence of perfect multicollinearity, and spherical error disturbances characterized by homoscedasticity and zero autocorrelation), the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimator is BLUE—Best Linear Unbiased Estimator. 'Best' signifies that the OLS estimator possesses the minimum variance among all possible unbiased linear estimators of the regression coefficients, establishing its mathematical optimality without requiring the assumption of normally distributed error terms.
terms.seminal_citation: Greene, W. H. (2018). Econometric analysis (8th ed.). Pearson.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gauss-Markov Theorem according to Greene (2018).
terms.operational_mechanism: For the linear model Y = X * beta + epsilon, the Gauss-Markov conditions require: (1) E[epsilon | X] = 0 (strict exogeneity); (2) rank(X) = k (full column rank / no perfect collinearity); (3) Var(epsilon_i | X) = sigma^2 (homoscedasticity); and (4) Cov(epsilon_i, epsilon_j | X) = 0 for all i != j (no serial correlation). Under these conditions, the OLS estimator is hat{beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'Y. For any other linear unbiased estimator tilde{beta} = CY, the difference in covariance matrices Var(tilde{beta}) - Var(hat{beta}) is a positive semi-definite matrix, proving that OLS minimizes estimation variance.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: For the linear model Y = X * beta + epsilon, the Gauss-Markov conditions require: (1) E[epsilon | X] = 0 (strict exogeneity); (2) rank(X) = k (full column rank / no perfect collinearity); (3) Var(epsilon_i | X) = sigma^2 (homoscedasticity); and (4) Cov(epsilon_i, epsilon_j | X) = 0 for all i != j (no serial correlation). Under these conditions, the OLS estimator is hat{beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'Y. For any other linear unbiased estimator tilde{beta} = CY, the difference in covariance matrices Var(tilde{beta}) - Var(hat{beta}) is a positive semi-definite matrix, proving that OLS minimizes estimation variance.
terms.benchmarks: When all Gauss-Markov assumptions hold, OLS is universally optimal within the class of linear unbiased estimators. When homoscedasticity fails (Var(epsilon_i | X) != sigma^2) or errors are serially correlated, OLS remains unbiased and consistent, but ceases to be 'Best' (efficient), and standard standard error formulas yield biased t- and F-statistics. In such cases, Generalized Least Squares (GLS) becomes BLUE, or Huber-White / Newey-West heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors must be applied.
terms.pitfalls: Common misconceptions: (1) Believing that the Gauss-Markov theorem requires normality of errors (normality is required for finite-sample exact t- and F-distributions, but NOT for the BLUE property); (2) Assuming that violation of homoscedasticity causes bias in coefficient estimates (it causes inefficiency and standard error distortion, not bias); and (3) Conflating BLUE with Minimum Mean Squared Error (MSE), overlooking that biased estimators (such as Ridge or Lasso regression) can achieve lower total MSE than OLS by trading a small amount of bias for a large reduction in variance.
terms.apa_reference: Greene, W. H. (2018). Econometric analysis (8th ed.). Pearson.

terms.vietnamese: Thống kê C của Geary
vietnamese_variants: Chỉ số tự tương quan không gian Geary's C
terms.core_definition: Geary's C Statistic (also known as Geary's Contiguity Ratio), formulated by Roy C. Geary (1954), is a classical measure of global spatial autocorrelation in continuous geographic or spatial lattice data. While Moran's I measures spatial association based on cross-products of deviations from the global mean (functioning analogously to a spatial Pearson correlation coefficient), Geary's C is calculated from the squared differences between attribute values of neighboring spatial units, functioning similarly to an empirical variogram. It is especially sensitive to local, fine-scale spatial discrepancies and abrupt boundaries between adjacent geographic units.
terms.seminal_citation: Geary, R. C. (1954). The contiguity ratio and statistical mapping. The Incorporated Statistician, 5(3), 115-146.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Geary's C Statistic according to Geary (1954).
terms.operational_mechanism: Geary's C is computed as: C = [(N - 1) / (2 * S_0)] * [sum_{i=1}^N sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij} * (y_i - y_j)^2] / [sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - bar{y})^2], where N is the number of spatial units, w_{ij} is the spatial weight between units i and j, S_0 = sum_i sum_j w_{ij} is the sum of all spatial weights, and bar{y} is the attribute mean. Statistical significance is tested under normality or randomization assumptions against the null hypothesis of spatial randomness (no spatial autocorrelation).
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Geary's C is computed as: C = [(N - 1) / (2 * S_0)] * [sum_{i=1}^N sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij} * (y_i - y_j)^2] / [sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - bar{y})^2], where N is the number of spatial units, w_{ij} is the spatial weight between units i and j, S_0 = sum_i sum_j w_{ij} is the sum of all spatial weights, and bar{y} is the attribute mean. Statistical significance is tested under normality or randomization assumptions against the null hypothesis of spatial randomness (no spatial autocorrelation).
terms.benchmarks: Interpretation scale: The theoretical expected value under the null hypothesis of no spatial autocorrelation is E[C] = 1.0. (1) C < 1.0 indicates positive spatial autocorrelation (neighboring units have similar values, clustering of like values); (2) C > 1.0 indicates negative spatial autocorrelation (neighboring units have highly dissimilar values, spatial dispersion / checkerboard pattern); (3) C = 1.0 indicates complete spatial randomness. Values generally range from 0 to 2, though extreme negative autocorrelation can exceed 2.
terms.pitfalls: Common analytical pitfalls: (1) Inverting the interpretation by erroneously assuming C > 1 means positive correlation (unlike Moran's I where positive values indicate positive autocorrelation, in Geary's C values below 1 indicate positive autocorrelation); (2) Sensitivity to extreme outliers due to squaring neighbor differences (y_i - y_j)^2; and (3) Relying exclusively on Geary's C without testing Moran's I or Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA), missing macro-level clustering trends across larger geographic distances.
terms.apa_reference: Geary, R. C. (1954). The contiguity ratio and statistical mapping. The Incorporated Statistician, 5(3), 115–146. https://doi.org/10.2307/2986645

terms.vietnamese: Chẩn đoán Gelman-Rubin (Chỉ số R-hat)
vietnamese_variants: Chỉ số thu hẹp phương sai tiềm tàng
terms.core_definition: The Gelman-Rubin Diagnostic (commonly denoted as R-hat or Potential Scale Reduction Factor, PSRF), developed by Andrew Gelman and Donald Rubin (1992), is the primary convergence diagnostic metric in Bayesian estimation using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations. It assesses whether multiple independent Markov chains initialized from overdispersed starting values have converged to the target stationary posterior distribution. R-hat compares the variance between the means of different chains to the average variance within individual chains, determining whether additional sampling could substantially reduce the estimated posterior uncertainty.
terms.seminal_citation: Gelman, A., & Rubin, D. B. (1992). Inference from iterative simulation using multiple sequences. Statistical Science, 7(4), 457-472.
terms.expert_notes: ngưỡng R-hat hiện khuyến nghị < 1.01 (Vehtari et al. 2021), 1.05/1.1 là chuẩn cũ
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gelman-Rubin Diagnostic (R-hat) according to Gelman & Rubin (1992).
terms.operational_mechanism: Given M chains each of length N (after discarding the warm-up/burn-in iterations): (1) Calculate the between-chain variance B/N = [1 / (M - 1)] * sum_{m=1}^M (bar{theta}_m - bar{theta}_{..})^2; (2) Calculate the within-chain variance W = (1 / M) * sum_{m=1}^M s_m^2; (3) Estimate the marginal posterior variance of the parameter as widehat{Var}^{+}(theta | y) = [(N - 1) / N] * W + (1 / N) * B; (4) Compute R-hat = sqrt(widehat{Var}^{+}(theta | y) / W). As N -> infinity, if all chains mix thoroughly and sample from the same stationary distribution, B/N -> 0 and R-hat -> 1.0.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Given M chains each of length N (after discarding the warm-up/burn-in iterations): (1) Calculate the between-chain variance B/N = [1 / (M - 1)] * sum_{m=1}^M (bar{theta}_m - bar{theta}_{..})^2; (2) Calculate the within-chain variance W = (1 / M) * sum_{m=1}^M s_m^2; (3) Estimate the marginal posterior variance of the parameter as widehat{Var}^{+}(theta | y) = [(N - 1) / N] * W + (1 / N) * B; (4) Compute R-hat = sqrt(widehat{Var}^{+}(theta | y) / W). As N -> infinity, if all chains mix thoroughly and sample from the same stationary distribution, B/N -> 0 and R-hat -> 1.0.
terms.benchmarks: Modern methodological standards (Vehtari, Gelman, Simpson, Carpenter, & Bürkner, 2021 rank-normalized folded R-hat): (1) Strict convergence threshold: R-hat < 1.01 (or at most < 1.05 in older literature) across all monitored parameters, latent variables, and transformed quantities; (2) Values of R-hat >= 1.05 or >= 1.10 indicate severe non-convergence, multimodal posterior surfaces, or inadequate chain length; (3) Must be paired with Bulk Effective Sample Size (Bulk-ESS > 400) and Tail Effective Sample Size (Tail-ESS > 400) to ensure reliable posterior inference and accurate credible intervals.
terms.pitfalls: Critical Bayesian traps: (1) Running only a single MCMC chain and attempting to assess convergence (R-hat fundamentally requires M >= 3 or 4 independent chains with dispersed starting values); (2) Reporting parameter estimates when R-hat > 1.05, which renders posterior point estimates and 95% highest density intervals statistically invalid; (3) Relying on standard R-hat for heavy-tailed distributions without rank-transformation, which modern Stan and ArviZ diagnostics resolve through rank-normalized split-R-hat; and (4) Confusing MCMC convergence (R-hat approx 1.0) with model correctness or goodness of fit.
terms.apa_reference: Gelman, A., & Rubin, D. B. (1992). Inference from iterative simulation using multiple sequences. Statistical Science, 7(4), 457–472. https://doi.org/10.1214/ss/1177011136

terms.vietnamese: Phương pháp Ước lượng Mô-men Tổng quát (Ước lượng GMM Hansen)
terms.core_definition: Khung phương pháp luận ước lượng kinh tế lượng đoạt giải Nobel do Lars Peter Hansen (1982) sáng lập, bao trùm hầu hết các phương pháp ước lượng cổ điển như OLS, 2SLS, và Cực đại Hợp lý (MLE). GMM không đòi hỏi nhà nghiên cứu phải giả định phân phối xác suất cụ thể của số hạng sai số (phương pháp phi tham số), mà chỉ dựa trên các điều kiện trực giao lý thuyết giữa các hàm sai số và tập biến công cụ (Moment Conditions: E[z_i ε_i] = 0). GMM tìm kiếm vectơ tham số tối thiểu hóa một hàm toàn phương có trọng số của các mô-men mẫu.
terms.seminal_citation: Hansen, L. P. (1982). Large sample properties of generalized method of moments estimators. Econometrica, 50(4), 1029–1054. https://doi.org/10.2307/1912775
terms.expert_notes: tên đúng là "Generalized Method of Moments" (Hansen 1982); Arellano–Bond là ứng dụng cho bảng động, không phải nguồn gốc
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of General Method of Moments (GMM) according to Arellano & Bond (1991).
terms.benchmarks: Ma trận trọng số tối ưu (Optimal Weighting Matrix): Sử dụng ước lượng GMM hai bước (Two-step GMM) kết hợp hiệu chỉnh sai số chuẩn mẫu nhỏ Windmeijer (2005) để tránh sai số chuẩn bị thu hẹp giả tạo. Khi số điều kiện mô-men lớn hơn số tham số (m > k), bắt buộc chạy Kiểm định Quá nhận diện Hansen J-test với p > 0.05.
terms.pitfalls: Sử dụng Two-step GMM mà không dùng hiệu chỉnh Windmeijer correction, khiến sai số chuẩn bị chệch xuống thấp nghiêm trọng và các giá trị t-statistic bị thổi phồng độ tin cậy; lạm dụng quá nhiều điều kiện mô-men làm suy giảm phẩm chất mẫu hữu hạn của ước lượng.
terms.apa_reference: Hansen, L. P. (1982). Large sample properties of generalized method of moments estimators. Econometrica, 50(4), 1029–1054.

terms.core_definition: The General Social Survey (GSS) is a nationally representative, repeated cross-sectional (and recently panel) sociological survey conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago since 1972. Widely recognized as one of the most authoritative data sources in the social sciences, the GSS monitors long-term societal trends, attitudes, behaviors, and institutional trust among non-institutionalized English- and Spanish-speaking adults in the United States. It utilizes rigorous multistage probability sampling and standardized questionnaire modules, serving as an international benchmark for survey research methodology, public opinion tracking, and cross-national harmonization (such as the International Social Survey Programme, ISSP).
terms.seminal_citation: Smith, T. W., Marsden, P. V., Hout, M., & Kim, J. (2018). General Social Surveys, 1972-2018: Cumulative codebook. National Opinion Research Center (NORC).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of General Social Survey (GSS) according to NORC (1972-present).
terms.operational_mechanism: GSS methodology involves: (1) Multistage area probability sampling designed to give every household an equal probability of selection, incorporating primary sampling units (PSUs), segments, and housing units; (2) Data collection primarily through face-to-face computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI) with average duration of 90 minutes, augmented by mixed-mode web-push protocols in recent rounds; (3) Split-ballot design and modular questionnaire structures balancing permanent core demographic/attitudinal items with rotating topical modules (e.g., religion, social networks, work orientations); and (4) Provision of post-stratification sampling weights (WTSSALL, WTSSNR) to adjust for household size selection probabilities and non-response bias.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: GSS methodology involves: (1) Multistage area probability sampling designed to give every household an equal probability of selection, incorporating primary sampling units (PSUs), segments, and housing units; (2) Data collection primarily through face-to-face computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI) with average duration of 90 minutes, augmented by mixed-mode web-push protocols in recent rounds; (3) Split-ballot design and modular questionnaire structures balancing permanent core demographic/attitudinal items with rotating topical modules (e.g., religion, social networks, work orientations); and (4) Provision of post-stratification sampling weights (WTSSALL, WTSSNR) to adjust for household size selection probabilities and non-response bias.
terms.benchmarks: Analytical standards for GSS data utilization: (1) Application of survey design weights (WTSSALL) is mandatory in all statistical and econometric analyses to prevent biased point estimates; (2) Use of complex survey design standard errors (Taylor series linearization or jackknife replicate weights) to account for clustering within PSUs and stratification; (3) Item non-response imputation or documentation adhering to AAPOR (American Association for Public Opinion Research) standards.
terms.pitfalls: Common methodological errors in published literature: (1) Analyzing raw GSS data with standard unweighted OLS or logistic regression without adjusting for complex survey design (clustering and stratification), which artificially deflates standard errors and yields spurious statistical significance; (2) Confusing repeated cross-sectional cohorts with true longitudinal panel data when making dynamic within-individual causal claims; and (3) Overlooking historical question wording shifts or changes from paper-and-pencil to CAPI / mixed-mode administration across longitudinal wave comparisons.
terms.apa_reference: Smith, T. W., Marsden, P. V., Hout, M., & Kim, J. (2018). General Social Surveys, 1972–2018: Cumulative codebook. National Opinion Research Center (NORC).

terms.core_definition: Generalizability Theory (G-Theory), formulated by Lee Cronbach, Goldine Gleser, Harinder Nanda, and Nageswari Rajaratnam (1972), is an advanced psychometric framework that extends Classical Test Theory (CTT) by applying analysis of variance (ANOVA) variance-component decomposition to measurement error. While CTT collapses all measurement error into a single undifferentiated random residual term (E), G-Theory explicitly disentangles, estimates, and differentiates multiple facets of measurement error (e.g., items, raters, test occasions, test forms, and their complex interactions) simultaneously in a single statistical model.
terms.seminal_citation: Cronbach, L. J., Gleser, G. C., Nanda, H., & Rajaratnam, N. (1972). The dependability of behavioral measurements: Theory of generalizability for scores and profiles. John Wiley & Sons.
terms.expert_notes: Đã chuẩn hóa từ bảng trích xuất sang định dạng từ điển chuẩn.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Generalizability theory (G-theory) according to DeVellis (2016).
terms.operational_mechanism: G-Theory proceeds in two distinct empirical phases: (1) Generalizability Study (G-Study): Estimates variance components associated with the object of measurement (e.g., persons p) and multiple error facets (e.g., raters r, items i) using a factorial or nested ANOVA design: sigma_X^2 = sigma_p^2 + sigma_r^2 + sigma_i^2 + sigma_pr^2 + sigma_pi^2 + sigma_ri^2 + sigma_pri,e^2; (2) Decision Study (D-Study): Uses the variance components obtained from the G-Study to design optimal future measurement protocols, calculating two distinct reliability-like coefficients: Generalizability Coefficient Erho^2 (for relative/norm-referenced decisions, evaluating rank-order consistency) and Dependability Coefficient Phi (for absolute/criterion-referenced decisions, evaluating performance against a fixed cut-score).
terms.operational_mechanism_en: G-Theory proceeds in two distinct empirical phases: (1) Generalizability Study (G-Study): Estimates variance components associated with the object of measurement (e.g., persons p) and multiple error facets (e.g., raters r, items i) using a factorial or nested ANOVA design: sigma_X^2 = sigma_p^2 + sigma_r^2 + sigma_i^2 + sigma_pr^2 + sigma_pi^2 + sigma_ri^2 + sigma_pri,e^2; (2) Decision Study (D-Study): Uses the variance components obtained from the G-Study to design optimal future measurement protocols, calculating two distinct reliability-like coefficients: Generalizability Coefficient Erho^2 (for relative/norm-referenced decisions, evaluating rank-order consistency) and Dependability Coefficient Phi (for absolute/criterion-referenced decisions, evaluating performance against a fixed cut-score).
terms.benchmarks: Threshold standards: (1) Generalizability coefficient Erho^2 >= 0.80 for low-stakes research decisions; Erho^2 >= 0.90 for high-stakes individual evaluations (e.g., medical licensing, academic tenure); (2) Dependability coefficient Phi >= 0.80 for criterion-referenced certification; (3) In the D-study optimization, researchers simulate the number of raters (n_r) and items (n_i) needed to achieve Erho^2 >= 0.85 with minimal operational cost.
terms.pitfalls: Common research mistakes: (1) Using Classical Test Theory (Cronbach's alpha) when measurement involves multi-facet evaluations (e.g., multiple raters grading multiple essays across occasions), which confounds rater variance with item variance; (2) Conflating relative decisions (using Erho^2) with absolute decisions (requiring Phi), leading to overly optimistic reliability claims in criterion-referenced testing; and (3) Failing to distinguish between crossed designs (p x r x i) and nested designs (r:p), which leads to misspecification of variance components.
terms.apa_reference: Cronbach, L. J., Gleser, G. C., Nanda, H., & Rajaratnam, N. (1972). The dependability of behavioral measurements: Theory of generalizability for scores and profiles. John Wiley & Sons.

terms.vietnamese: Quá trình tự hồi quy có điều kiện phương sai thay đổi tổng quát

terms.core_definition: The Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) process is an econometric time series process developed by Tim Bollerslev (1986) to model time-varying, clustered volatility in financial asset returns and macroeconomic series. Unlike Engle's ARCH(q) process which requires an impractical number of lagged squared residuals to capture long memory in volatility, a GARCH(p, q) process incorporates autoregressive terms of conditional variance itself. This allows for an infinite-order ARCH representation through an ARMA-like parameterization, capturing persistent volatility clustering, leptokurtic distribution tails, and mean reversion in risk dynamics.
terms.seminal_citation: Bollerslev, T. (1986). Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity. Journal of Econometrics, 31(3), 307-327.
terms.expert_notes: LaTeX thô; nguồn ghi ngưỡng
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity according to Tổng các hệ số ARCH và GARCH (α + β) phải nhỏ hơn 1 để đảm bảo tính dừng của phương sai có điều kiện..
terms.operational_mechanism: A GARCH(p, q) process specifies the error term epsilon_t = sigma_t * z_t, where z_t is an independent and identically distributed innovation with E[z_t] = 0 and Var(z_t) = 1. The conditional variance evolves according to: sigma_t^2 = omega + sum_{i=1}^q alpha_i * epsilon_{t-i}^2 + sum_{j=1}^p beta_j * sigma_{t-j}^2. For the standard GARCH(1,1), stationarity is maintained when omega > 0, alpha_1 >= 0, beta_1 >= 0, and the persistence parameter lambda = alpha_1 + beta_1 < 1. Estimation is carried out via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) with numerical optimization using the Berndt-Hall-Hall-Hausman (BHHH) algorithm.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: A GARCH(p, q) process specifies the error term epsilon_t = sigma_t * z_t, where z_t is an independent and identically distributed innovation with E[z_t] = 0 and Var(z_t) = 1. The conditional variance evolves according to: sigma_t^2 = omega + sum_{i=1}^q alpha_i * epsilon_{t-i}^2 + sum_{j=1}^p beta_j * sigma_{t-j}^2. For the standard GARCH(1,1), stationarity is maintained when omega > 0, alpha_1 >= 0, beta_1 >= 0, and the persistence parameter lambda = alpha_1 + beta_1 < 1. Estimation is carried out via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) with numerical optimization using the Berndt-Hall-Hall-Hausman (BHHH) algorithm.
terms.benchmarks: Empirical parameter behavior in daily financial returns: (1) alpha_1 approx 0.05 to 0.12 (short-term shock response); (2) beta_1 approx 0.85 to 0.93 (persistence of variance); (3) Total persistence alpha_1 + beta_1 is typically between 0.95 and 0.99 in high-frequency equity and foreign exchange data, implying a half-life of volatility shocks of ln(0.5) / ln(alpha_1 + beta_1) trading days; (4) Standardized residuals z_t = epsilon_t / sigma_t should exhibit no remaining serial correlation or ARCH effects in Ljung-Box Q and Engle's LM tests.
terms.pitfalls: Key empirical errors: (1) Failing to test whether alpha_1 + beta_1 >= 1.0, which indicates a non-stationary Integrated GARCH (IGARCH) process where volatility shocks persist indefinitely; (2) Assuming standard normal distributions for errors when return innovations exhibit fat tails (requiring Student-t or skewed Student-t distributions); and (3) Ignoring volatility asymmetry, where negative asset price shocks generate larger volatility increases than positive shocks, necessitating asymmetric GARCH variants (e.g., GJR-GARCH, EGARCH).
terms.apa_reference: Bollerslev, T. (1986). Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity. Journal of Econometrics, 31(3), 307–327. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4076(86)90063-1

terms.vietnamese: Phương pháp bình phương bé nhất tổng quát
vietnamese_variants: Hồi quy bình phương tối thiểu tổng quát
terms.core_definition: Generalized Least Squares (GLS) is an estimation technique formulated by Alexander Aitken (1936) that extends Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) to linear regression models where the classical Gauss-Markov assumption of spherical errors is violated. When the disturbance vector epsilon has a non-scalar, known covariance matrix Omega = sigma^2 * V (exhibiting heteroscedasticity, cross-sectional correlation, or serial autocorrelation), OLS remains unbiased but loses efficiency and produces invalid standard errors. GLS transforms the regression system by multiplying it by V^{-1/2}, converting non-spherical disturbances into homoscedastic, uncorrelated spherical errors where OLS becomes the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE).
terms.seminal_citation: Aitken, A. C. (1936). IV.—On least squares and linear combinations of observations. Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, 55, 42-48.
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Generalized Least Squares according to Hiệu quả hơn OLS thông thường; được hiện thực hóa qua Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS) khi ma trận hiệp phương sai sai số chưa biết..
terms.benchmarks: Optimality properties: Aitken's Theorem guarantees that hat{beta}_{GLS} is BLUE, achieving the Cramer-Rao lower bound for linear unbiased estimators when Omega is known. In empirical research where V is unknown, Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS) estimates hat{V} from first-stage OLS residuals, which is asymptotically efficient as N -> infinity, provided N is substantially larger than the number of estimated covariance parameters.
terms.operational_mechanism: In the model Y = X * beta + epsilon with E[epsilon | X] = 0 and Var(epsilon | X) = sigma^2 * V (where V is a positive-definite symmetric n x n matrix): (1) Cholesky decomposition or spectral decomposition is applied to factorize V^{-1} = P'P; (2) The model is transformed into Y* = X* * beta + epsilon*, where Y* = PY, X* = PX, and epsilon* = P * epsilon; (3) The transformed disturbance has spherical covariance: Var(epsilon*) = P * Var(epsilon) * P' = sigma^2 * P * V * P' = sigma^2 * I_n; (4) The resulting GLS estimator is hat{beta}_{GLS} = (X' V^{-1} X)^{-1} X' V^{-1} Y, with covariance Var(hat{beta}_{GLS}) = sigma^2 (X' V^{-1} X)^{-1}.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: In the model Y = X * beta + epsilon with E[epsilon | X] = 0 and Var(epsilon | X) = sigma^2 * V (where V is a positive-definite symmetric n x n matrix): (1) Cholesky decomposition or spectral decomposition is applied to factorize V^{-1} = P'P; (2) The model is transformed into Y* = X* * beta + epsilon*, where Y* = PY, X* = PX, and epsilon* = P * epsilon; (3) The transformed disturbance has spherical covariance: Var(epsilon*) = P * Var(epsilon) * P' = sigma^2 * P * V * P' = sigma^2 * I_n; (4) The resulting GLS estimator is hat{beta}_{GLS} = (X' V^{-1} X)^{-1} X' V^{-1} Y, with covariance Var(hat{beta}_{GLS}) = sigma^2 (X' V^{-1} X)^{-1}.
terms.pitfalls: Common research traps: (1) Applying standard GLS when the error covariance matrix V is unknown without recognizing that FGLS introduces finite-sample bias and instability; (2) Using FGLS in small samples (small N or short panel T), where sampling error in estimating hat{V} can make FGLS less efficient than OLS with robust Huber-White cluster standard errors; and (3) Failing to test for endogeneity—if E[X' epsilon] != 0, GLS is inconsistent just like OLS.
terms.apa_reference: Aitken, A. C. (1936). IV.—On least squares and linear combinations of observations. Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, 55, 42–48. https://doi.org/10.1017/S037016460001443X

terms.term: Generalized Least Squares (GLS Estimation in Linear Models)
terms.vietnamese: Ước lượng bình phương bé nhất tổng quát trong mô hình tuyến tính
terms.core_definition: Generalized Least Squares (GLS) estimation in linear models refers to the operational implementation of Aitken's generalized regression framework to obtain optimal parameter estimates in the presence of structured heteroscedasticity and autoregressive error processes. When disturbance terms violate spherical assumptions (Var(epsilon) = Omega != sigma^2 * I_n), the standard OLS formula yields inefficient point estimates and severely biased variance-covariance matrices. GLS explicitly incorporates the weighting matrix Omega^{-1} to downweight high-variance or serially correlated observations, restoring minimum variance and valid hypothesis testing.
terms.seminal_citation: Wooldridge, J. M. (2010). Econometric analysis of cross section and panel data (2nd ed.). MIT Press.
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #1102
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Generalized Least Squares (GLS) according to Aitken (1935).
terms.operational_mechanism: Operational execution involves: (1) Diagnosing the structure of non-spherical disturbances (e.g., Breusch-Pagan test for heteroscedasticity, Durbin-Watson or Wooldridge test for serial correlation); (2) Specifying the parametric form of Omega (e.g., panel groupwise heteroscedasticity Omega = diag(sigma_1^2 * I_T, ..., sigma_N^2 * I_T) or AR(1) autocorrelation Omega_{t,s} = sigma^2 * rho^{|t-s|}); (3) Computing the closed-form GLS solution hat{beta}_{GLS} = (X' Omega^{-1} X)^{-1} X' Omega^{-1} Y; and (4) Conducting Wald, t-, and F-tests using the true asymptotic covariance matrix (X' Omega^{-1} X)^{-1}.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Operational execution involves: (1) Diagnosing the structure of non-spherical disturbances (e.g., Breusch-Pagan test for heteroscedasticity, Durbin-Watson or Wooldridge test for serial correlation); (2) Specifying the parametric form of Omega (e.g., panel groupwise heteroscedasticity Omega = diag(sigma_1^2 * I_T, ..., sigma_N^2 * I_T) or AR(1) autocorrelation Omega_{t,s} = sigma^2 * rho^{|t-s|}); (3) Computing the closed-form GLS solution hat{beta}_{GLS} = (X' Omega^{-1} X)^{-1} X' Omega^{-1} Y; and (4) Conducting Wald, t-, and F-tests using the true asymptotic covariance matrix (X' Omega^{-1} X)^{-1}.
terms.benchmarks: Comparative benchmark: (1) Under perfect spherical errors, GLS reduces algebraically to OLS; (2) In heteroscedastic settings, Weighted Least Squares (WLS)—a special diagonal case of GLS—achieves substantial efficiency gains (variance reduction of 20% to 50% compared to OLS); (3) In large sample econometrics, researchers frequently benchmark FGLS results against OLS with Driscoll-Kraay or clustered standard errors to ensure robust inference against potential misspecification of Omega.
terms.pitfalls: Reviewer rejection traps: (1) Misinterpreting FGLS in panel models with large N and small T, where estimating N(N+1)/2 covariance elements leads to severe incidental parameter bias; (2) Claiming GLS corrects for omitted variable bias or endogeneity (GLS only corrects variance structures; strict exogeneity E[epsilon | X] = 0 is still required); and (3) Neglecting to report whether Prais-Winsten or Cochrane-Orcutt transformations were employed in time-series GLS.
terms.apa_reference: Wooldridge, J. M. (2010). Econometric analysis of cross section and panel data (2nd ed.). MIT Press.

terms.vietnamese: Phân tích thành phần cấu trúc tổng quát (GSCA)
vietnamese_variants: Phân tích thành phần cấu trúc tổng quát hóa
terms.core_definition: Generalized Structured Component Analysis (GSCA), developed by Heungsun Hwang and Yoshio Takane (2004), is a component-based structural equation modeling approach designed to overcome a primary theoretical limitation of Partial Least Squares (PLS-SEM): the absence of a global optimization criterion. While PLS-SEM relies on iterative alternating least squares across localized sub-models, GSCA optimizes a single, well-defined global least-squares criterion function that simultaneously minimizes the discrepancy between observed variables and model-implied components across measurement, structural, and formative relations.
terms.seminal_citation: Hwang, H., & Takane, Y. (2004). Generalized structured component analysis. Psychometrika, 69(1), 81-99.
terms.expert_notes: Lộ tên file nội bộ
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Generalized Structured Component Analysis (GSCA) according to Henseler et al. (2015); Henseler et al. (2015).
terms.operational_mechanism: GSCA specifies an integrated matrix formulation: Gamma = [Z; f], where Z is the J x N matrix of observed indicators and f is the T x N matrix of latent components. The system minimizes the global objective function: phi(W, B) = || Gamma - W * Gamma - B * Gamma ||^2, subject to identification constraints, via the Alternating Least Squares (ALS) algorithm. This global criterion enables GSCA to compute authentic overall model fit indices (FIT, AFIT, GFI, SRMR) and permits extensions to generalized structured component models with non-linear relationships, multi-group comparisons, and mixed-mode indicators.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: GSCA specifies an integrated matrix formulation: Gamma = [Z; f], where Z is the J x N matrix of observed indicators and f is the T x N matrix of latent components. The system minimizes the global objective function: phi(W, B) = || Gamma - W * Gamma - B * Gamma ||^2, subject to identification constraints, via the Alternating Least Squares (ALS) algorithm. This global criterion enables GSCA to compute authentic overall model fit indices (FIT, AFIT, GFI, SRMR) and permits extensions to generalized structured component models with non-linear relationships, multi-group comparisons, and mixed-mode indicators.
terms.benchmarks: Goodness of fit thresholds in GSCA: (1) FIT: Measures the proportion of total variance explained by the specified model (values > 0.50 are acceptable, > 0.60 indicate strong fit); (2) AFIT (Adjusted FIT): Penalizes model complexity analogous to adjusted R^2; (3) GFI (Goodness-of-Fit Index) >= 0.90; (4) SRMR (Standardized Root Mean Square Residual) <= 0.08 indicates good fit. Bootstrap standard errors (5,000 resamples) evaluate component weight and path significance.
terms.pitfalls: Common research pitfalls: (1) Confusing GSCA with covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM), overlooking that GSCA remains a component proxy method subject to composite scores rather than error-free latent variables; (2) Neglecting sample size requirements when testing complex non-linear specifications; and (3) Relying on legacy software implementations without verifying recent developments such as fuzzy GSCA or regularized GSCA.
terms.apa_reference: Hwang, H., & Takane, Y. (2004). Generalized structured component analysis. Psychometrika, 69(1), 81–99. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02295841

terms.vietnamese: Phương pháp đối chứng tổng hợp tổng quát (GSynth)
vietnamese_variants: Kiểm soát tổng hợp tổng quát hóa
Mô hình GSynth nhân tố tương tác
Synthetic control có nhân tố tương tác
terms.core_definition: Generalized Synthetic Control (GSynth), developed by Yiqing Xu (2017), is an advanced causal inference estimator that merges the Synthetic Control Method (Abadie et al.) with Interactive Fixed Effects (IFE) models (Bai, 2009). Traditional synthetic control requires a single treated unit and non-negative convex weights, while standard Difference-in-Differences (DiD) relies on the restrictive parallel trends assumption. GSynth generalizes both approaches by allowing multiple treated units, staggered treatment adoption timings, and high-dimensional unobserved time-varying confounders modeled via latent factor structures (lambda_i' * f_t).
terms.seminal_citation: Xu, Y. (2017). Generalized synthetic control method: Causal inference with interactive fixed effects models. Political Analysis, 25(1), 57-76.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Generalized Synthetic Control (GSynth) according to Xu (2017).
terms.operational_mechanism: The model specification is Y_{it} = D_{it} * delta_{it} + X_{it}' * beta + lambda_i' * f_t + epsilon_{it}, where D_{it} is the binary treatment indicator, delta_{it} is the heterogeneous treatment effect, X_{it} are time-varying covariates, lambda_i are unit factor loadings, and f_t are latent time-varying common factors. The estimation follows three steps: (1) Fit an interactive fixed effects model on untreated units and pre-treatment periods of treated units to estimate beta, f_t, and control factor loadings; (2) Predict counterfactual outcomes hat{Y}_{it}(0) for treated units in post-treatment periods using estimated factor loadings hat{lambda}_i and factors hat{f}_t; (3) Compute average treatment effects on the treated (ATT) as ATT_t = (1 / N_{tr,t}) * sum_{i in Tr} (Y_{it} - hat{Y}_{it}(0)), with uncertainty quantified via parametric or non-parametric block bootstrapping.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: The model specification is Y_{it} = D_{it} * delta_{it} + X_{it}' * beta + lambda_i' * f_t + epsilon_{it}, where D_{it} is the binary treatment indicator, delta_{it} is the heterogeneous treatment effect, X_{it} are time-varying covariates, lambda_i are unit factor loadings, and f_t are latent time-varying common factors. The estimation follows three steps: (1) Fit an interactive fixed effects model on untreated units and pre-treatment periods of treated units to estimate beta, f_t, and control factor loadings; (2) Predict counterfactual outcomes hat{Y}_{it}(0) for treated units in post-treatment periods using estimated factor loadings hat{lambda}_i and factors hat{f}_t; (3) Compute average treatment effects on the treated (ATT) as ATT_t = (1 / N_{tr,t}) * sum_{i in Tr} (Y_{it} - hat{Y}_{it}(0)), with uncertainty quantified via parametric or non-parametric block bootstrapping.
terms.benchmarks: Empirical validation benchmarks: (1) Cross-validation (CV) error to select the optimal number of latent factors r (minimizing mean squared prediction error on pre-treatment validation periods); (2) Pre-treatment Mean Squared Prediction Error (MSPE): Treated units must show tight counterfactual fit before treatment (pre-treatment ATT estimates statistically indistinguishable from zero across all t < T0); (3) Dynamic ATT trajectory plots with 95% confidence bands illustrating treatment timing and persistence.
terms.pitfalls: Methodological pitfalls in top journals: (1) Setting the number of latent factors r arbitrarily rather than using data-driven cross-validation, leading to either under-fitting (omitted time-varying confounders) or over-fitting (noise fitting); (2) Applying GSynth when the pre-treatment period is very short (T0 < 10), which prevents stable estimation of latent factor loadings; and (3) Violating the absence of cross-unit spillovers (SUTVA violations among control units).
terms.apa_reference: Xu, Y. (2017). Generalized synthetic control method: Causal inference with interactive fixed effects models. Political Analysis, 25(1), 57–76. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2016.2

terms.term: Genre Analysis (Communicative Genres in Sociology of Knowledge)
terms.vietnamese: Phân tích thể loại giao tiếp (Theo Thomas Luckmann)
vietnamese_variants: Phân tích thể loại giao tiếp xã hội
Xã hội học thể loại giao tiếp
terms.core_definition: Genre Analysis in the sociological tradition of Thomas Luckmann (developed alongside Jörg Bergmann and Hubert Knoblauch) examines 'communicative genres'—historically stabilized, socially routinized, and culturally institutionalized patterns of communication that social actors employ to solve recurrent communicative problems. Rooted in Berger and Luckmann's social construction of reality and Schütz's phenomenological sociology, communicative genres (such as gossiping, condolences, organizational dispute settlement, or medical consultations) function as pre-patterned social institutions that structure subjective consciousness and coordinate intersubjective interaction.
terms.seminal_citation: Luckmann, T. (1986). Grundformen der gesellschaftlichen Vermittlung des Wissens: Kommunikative Gattungen. Kölner Zeitschrift für Soziologie und Sozialpsychologie, 27, 191-211.
terms.expert_notes: Rác Markdown/bảng; mảnh trích
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Genre Analysis (Thomas Luckmann) according to Flick et al. (2004).
terms.operational_mechanism: Luckmann's genre analysis examines communicative interactions across three structural levels: (1) Internal structure (interne Struktur): Linguistic and prosodic components, formulaic phrases, lexical choices, rhetoric, and conversational turn-taking structures; (2) Situational structure (situative Struktur): The interactive face-to-face or mediated ecology, participation framework (Goffman), physical setting, body posture, and non-verbal gestures; and (3) External structure (externe Struktur): The societal institutions, social roles, cultural norms, and communicative budget (communicative distribution of knowledge) within which the genre is anchored and enacted.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Luckmann's genre analysis examines communicative interactions across three structural levels: (1) Internal structure (interne Struktur): Linguistic and prosodic components, formulaic phrases, lexical choices, rhetoric, and conversational turn-taking structures; (2) Situational structure (situative Struktur): The interactive face-to-face or mediated ecology, participation framework (Goffman), physical setting, body posture, and non-verbal gestures; and (3) External structure (externe Struktur): The societal institutions, social roles, cultural norms, and communicative budget (communicative distribution of knowledge) within which the genre is anchored and enacted.
terms.benchmarks: Rigor criteria in communicative genre studies: (1) Naturalistic data capture: Use of high-fidelity audio/video recordings of naturally occurring communicative events (rather than post-hoc interviews); (2) Multi-level transcription standards (e.g., Jeffersonian or GAT-2 transcription system capturing prosody, pauses, intonation); (3) Demonstrable evidence of institutional sediment: Proof that actors orient to deviations from the communicative template through repair mechanisms.
terms.pitfalls: Common research flaws: (1) Conflating Luckmann's communicative genres with literary or linguistic genre analysis (e.g., Swales), overlooking the deep phenomenological and sociological focus on institutional action; (2) Treating communicative genres as rigid deterministic scripts rather than flexible, interactionally negotiated frameworks; and (3) Analyzing spoken text in isolation from situational bodily gestures and broader macro-societal power structures.
terms.apa_reference: Luckmann, T. (1986). Grundformen der gesellschaftlichen Vermittlung des Wissens: Kommunikative Gattungen. Kölner Zeitschrift für Soziologie und Sozialpsychologie, 27, 191–211.

terms.vietnamese: Hồi quy trọng số địa lý
vietnamese_variants: Hồi quy không gian không đồng nhất
terms.core_definition: Hồi quy trọng số địa lý (GWR - Brunsdon, Fotheringham, & Charlton, 1996) là kỹ thuật phân tích không gian cục bộ (spatial econometrics) cho phép các hệ số hồi quy biến thiên liên tục theo tọa độ không gian địa lý. GWR giải quyết triệt để hiện tượng không đồng nhất không gian (spatial non-stationarity) — tình trạng mà mối quan hệ kinh tế/xã hội thay đổi bản chất tùy theo từng vùng lãnh thổ.
terms.seminal_citation: Brunsdon, Fotheringham, & Charlton (1996); Fotheringham, Brunsdon, & Charlton (2002)
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) according to Brunsdon, Fotheringham & Charlton (1996).
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Phương trình mô hình: y_i = β_0(u_i, v_i) + sum_k [β_k(u_i, v_i) · x_ik] + ε_i, trong đó (u_i, v_i) là tọa độ địa lý của quan sát i. 2. Ước lượng hệ số cục bộ tại vị trí i bằng phương pháp OLS có trọng số: β_hat(u_i, v_i) = (X' * W(u_i, v_i) · X)⁻¹ * X' * W(u_i, v_i) · y. 3. Ma trận trọng số không gian W được tính bằng hàm nhân (kernel function: Gaussian hoặc Bisquare) dựa trên khoảng cách địa lý d_ij.
terms.benchmarks: Lựa chọn độ rộng băng thông tối ưu (Optimal Bandwidth) thông qua tiêu chuẩn AICc hiệu chỉnh hoặc Cross-Validation (CV). Băng thông có thể là cố định (fixed bandwidth) hoặc thích ứng theo mật độ điểm (adaptive bandwidth). Mô hình GWR được xem là vượt trội so với OLS toàn cục khi AICc của GWR nhỏ hơn AICc của OLS ít nhất 3 đơn vị (Delta AICc > 3).
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: (1) Hiện tượng đa cộng tuyến cục bộ (local multicollinearity) giữa các biến độc lập trong một số vùng địa lý hẹp làm dấu hệ số bị đảo lộn bất thường; (2) Lựa chọn băng thông quá nhỏ dẫn đến hiện tượng quá khớp dữ liệu (overfitting) và mất bậc tự do nghiêm trọng.
terms.apa_reference: Brunsdon, C., Fotheringham, A. S., & Charlton, M. E. (1996). Geographically weighted regression: A method for exploring spatial nonstationarity. Geographical Analysis, 28(4), 281–298. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1538-4632.1996.tb00936.x

terms.vietnamese: Phân tích điểm nóng Getis-Ord Gi*
vietnamese_variants: Phân tích cụm không gian Gi*
terms.core_definition: The Getis-Ord Gi* statistic, developed by Arthur Getis and J.K. Ord (1992, 1995), is a local spatial statistical method that identifies statistically significant spatial clusters of high values ('hotspots') and low values ('coldspots'). Unlike global spatial autocorrelation indices (such as Moran's I or Geary's C) which provide a single summary metric for an entire map, Gi* calculates a local z-score and corresponding p-value for each individual spatial unit by comparing the local sum of an attribute within a specified spatial neighborhood (including the target feature itself) to the proportional global sum across all units.
terms.seminal_citation: Getis, A., & Ord, J. K. (1992). The analysis of spatial association by use of distance statistics. Geographical Analysis, 24(3), 189-206.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Getis-Ord Gi · Hotspot Analysis according to Getis & Ord (1992).
terms.operational_mechanism: For each spatial location i, the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic is formulated as: G_i* = [sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij} * x_j - bar{X} * sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij}] / [ S * sqrt( [N * sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij}^2 - (sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij})^2] / (N - 1) ) ], where x_j is the attribute value for feature j, w_{ij} is the spatial weight between i and j (with w_{ii} > 0), bar{X} is the global mean, S is the global standard deviation, and N is the total number of features. Because Gi* is a standard z-score under the null hypothesis of spatial randomness, statistical significance is interpreted via standard normal critical values.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: For each spatial location i, the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic is formulated as: G_i* = [sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij} * x_j - bar{X} * sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij}] / [ S * sqrt( [N * sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij}^2 - (sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij})^2] / (N - 1) ) ], where x_j is the attribute value for feature j, w_{ij} is the spatial weight between i and j (with w_{ii} > 0), bar{X} is the global mean, S is the global standard deviation, and N is the total number of features. Because Gi* is a standard z-score under the null hypothesis of spatial randomness, statistical significance is interpreted via standard normal critical values.
terms.benchmarks: Interpretation standards for local clusters: (1) Hotspot: Z(Gi*) > +1.96 (p < 0.05, 95% confidence) or Z(Gi*) > +2.58 (p < 0.01, 99% confidence), representing a statistically significant spatial cluster of high attribute values surrounded by high values; (2) Coldspot: Z(Gi*) < -1.96 (p < 0.05) or Z(Gi*) < -2.58 (p < 0.01), representing a statistically significant cluster of low attribute values surrounded by low values; (3) Non-significant: -1.96 <= Z(Gi*) <= +1.96 indicates spatial randomness.
terms.pitfalls: Common methodological pitfalls: (1) Failing to apply multiple comparison adjustments (such as the False Discovery Rate / FDR correction or Bonferroni adjustment), which generates substantial false-positive hotspots across large spatial grids; (2) Arbitrary selection of the spatial conceptualization or distance band without testing spatial scale sensitivity; and (3) Confusing a single high-value outlier with a hotspot (a high value surrounded by low values is a spatial outlier, not a hotspot, and will not yield a significant Gi*).
terms.apa_reference: Getis, A., & Ord, J. K. (1992). The analysis of spatial association by use of distance statistics. Geographical Analysis, 24(3), 189–206. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1538-4632.1992.tb00261.x

terms.vietnamese: Tác giả bóng ma (Đứng tên ẩn danh)
vietnamese_variants: Ẩn danh tác giả bất chính
terms.core_definition: Ghost Authorship is a severe form of academic publication malpractice wherein an individual who has made substantial intellectual, analytical, or drafting contributions to a scholarly manuscript is intentionally omitted from the list of named authors and acknowledgments. Frequently documented in industry-sponsored biomedical and pharmaceutical trials, ghost authorship often involves commercial medical writers, corporate statisticians, or junior researchers preparing manuscripts that are subsequently attributed exclusively to prominent academic 'guest' or 'honorary' authors (key opinion leaders) to mask commercial conflicts of interest and impart unwarranted academic credibility.
terms.seminal_citation: International Committee of Medical Journal Editors. (2023). Recommendations for the conduct, reporting, editing, and publication of scholarly work in medical journals (ICMJE Recommendations). ICMJE.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Ghost Authorship according to ICMJE (2019).
terms.operational_mechanism: Ghost authorship manifests through structured concealment mechanisms: (1) Commercial preparation: An undisclosed corporate sponsor or commercial communications agency drafts the study protocol, conducts analyses, and writes the manuscript; (2) Recruitment of academic figureheads: Prominent independent scholars are invited to append their names to the byline with minimal editorial involvement; (3) Erasure of intellectual origin: Substantive writing and funding sources are concealed or buried in vague acknowledgments; (4) Violation of international publication standards, particularly the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) criteria and Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) guidelines.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Ghost authorship manifests through structured concealment mechanisms: (1) Commercial preparation: An undisclosed corporate sponsor or commercial communications agency drafts the study protocol, conducts analyses, and writes the manuscript; (2) Recruitment of academic figureheads: Prominent independent scholars are invited to append their names to the byline with minimal editorial involvement; (3) Erasure of intellectual origin: Substantive writing and funding sources are concealed or buried in vague acknowledgments; (4) Violation of international publication standards, particularly the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) criteria and Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) guidelines.
terms.benchmarks: ICMJE authorship criteria (all 4 must be satisfied for authorship; failure to name anyone meeting all 4 constitutes ghost authorship): (1) Substantial contributions to the conception or design, or acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data; (2) Drafting the work or revising it critically for important intellectual content; (3) Final approval of the version to be published; and (4) Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work. Any non-author technical/writing contributor must be explicitly recognized in the Acknowledgments section with declared corporate affiliations.
terms.pitfalls: Consequences and red flags: (1) Retraction of manuscript and formal institutional misconduct investigation by ethics committees; (2) Disqualification from national grant funding bodies (e.g., NIH, ERC); (3) Disguising substantial statistical or drafting contributions as 'editorial assistance' without disclosing commercial sponsorship; and (4) Exploitation of doctoral students and research assistants whose intellectual work is published solely under senior faculty names.
terms.apa_reference: International Committee of Medical Journal Editors. (2023). Recommendations for the conduct, reporting, editing, and publication of scholarly work in medical journals. ICMJE. http://www.icmje.org/recommendations/

terms.vietnamese: Lấy mẫu Gibbs (Thuật toán MCMC)
vietnamese_variants: Lấy mẫu Markov Chain Monte Carlo Gibbs
terms.core_definition: Lấy mẫu Gibbs (Geman & Geman, 1984; Gelfand & Smith, 1990) là thuật toán Chuỗi Markov Monte Carlo (MCMC) nền tảng trong thống kê Bayes hiện đại. Thuật toán cho phép trích xuất các mẫu ngẫu nhiên từ một phân phối xác suất đồng thời đa biến phức tạp (joint posterior distribution P(θ_1, ..., θ_p | Y)) bằng cách lấy mẫu tuần tự lần lượt từng tham số từ các phân phối có điều kiện đầy đủ (full conditional distributions) của chính nó khi cố định tất cả các tham số còn lại.
terms.seminal_citation: Geman & Geman (1984); Gelfand & Smith (1990)
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gibbs Sampling according to Geman & Geman (1984).
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Khởi tạo vector tham số ban đầu θ^(0). 2. Tại mỗi vòng lặp t: (A) Lấy mẫu θ_1^(t) từ P(θ_1 | θ_2^(t-1), ..., θ_p^(t-1), Y); (B) Lấy mẫu θ_2^(t) từ P(θ_2 | θ_1^(t), θ_3^(t-1), ..., θ_p^(t-1), Y); ... (C) Lấy mẫu θ_p^(t) từ P(θ_p | θ_1^(t), ..., θ_(p-1)^(t), Y). 3. Lặp lại hàng ngàn chu kỳ để chuỗi Markov đạt trạng thái dừng (Stationary distribution). 4. Bỏ qua giai đoạn làm nóng (Burn-in period) và tính toán ước lượng hậu nghiệm (Posterior Mean, Credible Intervals).
terms.benchmarks: Được tích hợp trong các phần mềm Bayes kinh điển như BUGS, JAGS. Thẩm định sự hội tụ của chuỗi MCMC bắt buộc phải thông qua Chỉ số R-hat Gelman-Rubin (R_hat < 1.05, lý tưởng < 1.01) và Quy mô mẫu hiệu dụng (Effective Sample Size - ESS > 400-1000).
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: Hiện tượng tương quan chuỗi cao (High autocorrelation) khi các tham số hậu nghiệm có mối tương quan mạnh với nhau. Khi đó, thuật toán Gibbs di chuyển cực kỳ chậm chạp trong không gian tham số (hiện tượng kẹt bước đi ngẫu nhiên random-walk trap), đòi hỏi phải chuyển sang thuật toán Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC).
terms.apa_reference: Gelfand, A. E., & Smith, A. F. (1990). Sampling-based approaches to calculating marginal densities. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 85(410), 398–409. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1990.10476213

terms.vietnamese: Hệ số bất bình đẳng Gini
vietnamese_variants: Chỉ số bất bình đẳng Gini
terms.core_definition: The Gini Coefficient, formulated by Italian statistician Corrado Gini (1912), is the premier quantitative metric used globally to measure economic inequality, income dispersion, and wealth concentration within a population. Geometrically derived from the Lorenz curve (which plots the cumulative percentage of total national income earned against the cumulative percentage of the population), the Gini coefficient represents the ratio of the area between the line of perfect equality (the 45-degree diagonal) and the empirical Lorenz curve to the total area under the line of perfect equality.
terms.seminal_citation: Gini, C. (1912). Variabilità e mutabilità: Contributo allo studio delle distribuzioni e delle relazioni statistiche. Tipografia di Paolo Cuppini.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gini Coefficient of Inequality according to Gini (1912).
terms.operational_mechanism: Let the Lorenz curve be L(p), where p is the cumulative population share (0 <= p <= 1). The Gini coefficient G is defined mathematically as: G = 1 - 2 * integral_0^1 L(p) dp = A / (A + B), where A is the area between the 45-degree line and the Lorenz curve, and B is the area under the Lorenz curve. For discrete, ordered individual or household income observations y_1 <= y_2 <= ... <= y_n: G = [1 / (2 * n^2 * bar{y})] * sum_{i=1}^n sum_{j=1}^n |y_i - y_j| = [2 * sum_{i=1}^n i * y_i] / [n * sum_{i=1}^n y_i] - (n + 1) / n.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Let the Lorenz curve be L(p), where p is the cumulative population share (0 <= p <= 1). The Gini coefficient G is defined mathematically as: G = 1 - 2 * integral_0^1 L(p) dp = A / (A + B), where A is the area between the 45-degree line and the Lorenz curve, and B is the area under the Lorenz curve. For discrete, ordered individual or household income observations y_1 <= y_2 <= ... <= y_n: G = [1 / (2 * n^2 * bar{y})] * sum_{i=1}^n sum_{j=1}^n |y_i - y_j| = [2 * sum_{i=1}^n i * y_i] / [n * sum_{i=1}^n y_i] - (n + 1) / n.
terms.benchmarks: Empirical socioeconomic thresholds: (1) G = 0 represents perfect equality (everyone has identical income); (2) G = 1 (or 100 on the Gini index) represents absolute inequality (one single entity possesses all income); (3) G < 0.30 indicates low inequality (typical of Nordic social-democratic economies); (4) 0.30 <= G < 0.40 indicates moderate inequality; (5) 0.40 <= G < 0.50 denotes high inequality (UN/World Bank warning threshold for social instability); (6) G >= 0.50 signifies severe, destabilizing structural inequality.
terms.pitfalls: Methodological traps: (1) Conflating income Gini with wealth Gini (wealth Gini coefficients are systematically higher, routinely exceeding 0.75 even in low-income-inequality countries); (2) Comparing pre-tax market income Gini directly with post-tax/post-transfer disposable income Gini, obscuring the redistributive impact of welfare policy; and (3) Overlooking that distinct Lorenz curves with different shapes (e.g., severe poverty at the bottom vs. extreme concentration at the top) can generate identical Gini coefficients, necessitating complementary decile ratios (e.g., Palma ratio, 90/10 ratio).
terms.apa_reference: Gini, C. (1912). Variabilità e mutabilità: Contributo allo studio delle distribuzioni e delle relazioni statistiche. Tipografia di Paolo Cuppini.

terms.vietnamese: Các chiều kích tổng hợp trong phương pháp Gioia
domain_tags: Qualitative Data Analysis & Inductive Grounded Theory
terms.core_definition: In the Gioia methodology for inductive, qualitative theory building (Dennis A. Gioia, Kevin G. Corley, & Aimee L. Hamilton, 2013), Aggregate Dimensions represent the highest, most abstract tier of the qualitative data structure. They are overarching theoretical constructs synthesized by grouping related second-order themes. While 1st-order concepts capture informant-centric raw meanings and 2nd-order themes articulate researcher-centric conceptual mechanisms, Aggregate Dimensions elevate the analysis to formal theoretical abstraction, providing the structural building blocks for constructing a novel conceptual framework or dynamic theoretical model.
terms.seminal_citation: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15-31.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gioia Aggregate Dimensions according to Gioia, Corley & Hamilton (2013).
terms.category: Qualitative Data Analysis & Inductive Grounded Theory
terms.operational_mechanism: The synthesis of aggregate dimensions follows a systematic analytical progression: (1) Assembling 2nd-order themes: The researcher clusters theoretically related 2nd-order themes that explain different facets of the same overarching organizational phenomenon; (2) Elevating theoretical abstraction: Identifying latent meta-constructs that transcend the immediate empirical context; (3) Establishing boundary conditions: Defining the conceptual boundaries and nomological relations between aggregate dimensions; and (4) Theoretical modeling: Transforming the static Gioia data structure into a dynamic, process-oriented conceptual model that depicts how the aggregate dimensions interact over time to drive organizational outcomes.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: The synthesis of aggregate dimensions follows a systematic analytical progression: (1) Assembling 2nd-order themes: The researcher clusters theoretically related 2nd-order themes that explain different facets of the same overarching organizational phenomenon; (2) Elevating theoretical abstraction: Identifying latent meta-constructs that transcend the immediate empirical context; (3) Establishing boundary conditions: Defining the conceptual boundaries and nomological relations between aggregate dimensions; and (4) Theoretical modeling: Transforming the static Gioia data structure into a dynamic, process-oriented conceptual model that depicts how the aggregate dimensions interact over time to drive organizational outcomes.
terms.benchmarks: Exemplary rigor standards in top management journals (AMJ, ASQ, OrgSci): (1) Parsimony: A typical Gioia data structure contains between 2 and 5 aggregate dimensions, avoiding conceptual clutter; (2) Exhaustive grounding: Every aggregate dimension must trace transparently back through 2nd-order themes to rich, informant-centric 1st-order concepts; (3) Theoretical novelty: Dimensions must offer fresh theoretical terminology or distinct reconfigurations of established constructs rather than merely reproducing familiar textbook labels.
terms.pitfalls: Common reviewer rejection traps: (1) Leaping directly from raw interview quotes (1st-order) to aggregate dimensions without developing rigorous, empirically distinguished 2nd-order themes; (2) Formulating aggregate dimensions that are overly descriptive or industry-specific rather than theoretically portable; and (3) Leaving aggregate dimensions disconnected in a static table without illustrating their dynamic interrelationships in a formal process model.
terms.apa_reference: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15–31. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428112452151

terms.vietnamese: Cấu trúc dữ liệu Gioia
vietnamese_variants: Sơ đồ cấu trúc dữ liệu Gioia
Khung phân tích dữ liệu Gioia
domain_tags: Qualitative Data Analysis & Inductive Grounded Theory
terms.core_definition: The Gioia Data Structure is the central visual, analytical, and methodological artifact of the Gioia approach to inductive qualitative research (Gioia et al., 2013). It provides a transparent, graphic audit trail that visually demonstrates the rigorous transition from raw, participant-driven qualitative field evidence to formal theoretical abstraction. Structured across three interconnected hierarchical columns—1st-Order Concepts (informant-centric codes using participants' own language), 2nd-Order Themes (researcher-centric theoretical codes answering 'what is going on here theoretically?'), and Aggregate Dimensions (overarching conceptual pillars)—it serves as the definitive standard of qualitative rigor in administrative science.
terms.seminal_citation: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15-31.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gioia Data Structure according to Gioia, Corley & Hamilton (2013).
terms.category: Qualitative Data Analysis & Inductive Grounded Theory
terms.operational_mechanism: Construction of a Gioia data structure proceeds through four steps: (1) Open coding of raw transcripts to produce an extensive initial inventory of 1st-order in-vivo and descriptive codes; (2) Constant comparison to eliminate redundancies and group 1st-order codes into cohesive thematic categories; (3) Theorizing 2nd-order themes: Elevating the analysis into theoretical domain language, asking whether existing literature explains the categories or if new concepts are emerging; and (4) Synthesizing aggregate dimensions: Clustering 2nd-order themes into overarching dimensions, visually rendering the complete structure as a three-column tree diagram or hierarchical table.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Construction of a Gioia data structure proceeds through four steps: (1) Open coding of raw transcripts to produce an extensive initial inventory of 1st-order in-vivo and descriptive codes; (2) Constant comparison to eliminate redundancies and group 1st-order codes into cohesive thematic categories; (3) Theorizing 2nd-order themes: Elevating the analysis into theoretical domain language, asking whether existing literature explains the categories or if new concepts are emerging; and (4) Synthesizing aggregate dimensions: Clustering 2nd-order themes into overarching dimensions, visually rendering the complete structure as a three-column tree diagram or hierarchical table.
terms.benchmarks: Evaluation benchmarks for publication in elite journals (AMJ, ASQ, SMJ): (1) Audit trail completeness: Complete visibility showing how raw interview quotes flow directly into aggregate theoretical dimensions; (2) Balance: Typically 15-30 representative 1st-order concepts mapped into 6-12 2nd-order themes, consolidated into 2-5 aggregate dimensions; (3) Paired quote tables: Accompanied in the manuscript by an exhaustive evidence table displaying multiple supporting quotes per 2nd-order theme.
