terms.pitfalls: Methodological flaws: (1) Presenting a 'fake' Gioia structure where 1st-order concepts are already contaminated with theoretical academic jargon rather than honoring informants' voice; (2) Treating the data structure as the final product of research rather than the foundational stepping stone to building a dynamic process model; and (3) Forcing data mechanically into pre-existing theoretical templates, violating the inductive spirit of the methodology.
terms.apa_reference: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15–31. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428112452151

terms.vietnamese: Các khái niệm bậc một trong phương pháp Gioia
vietnamese_variants: Khái niệm người cung cấp thông tin
domain_tags: Qualitative Data Analysis & Inductive Grounded Theory
terms.core_definition: In the Gioia methodology for qualitative research (Gioia et al., 2013), 1st-Order Concepts are the initial, informant-centric codes generated during the earliest stages of inductive analysis. Adhering strictly to the epistemological premise that organizational participants are 'knowledgeable agents' who can explain their thoughts, intentions, and actions, 1st-order analysis adheres closely to informant terms, metaphors, and narratives. The researcher intentionally refrains from imposing scholarly jargon or prior theoretical frameworks, creating an open coding space that prioritizes the lived reality and subjective meanings of organizational actors.
terms.seminal_citation: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15-31.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gioia Methodology 1st-Order Concepts according to Gioia, Corley & Hamilton (2013).
terms.category: Qualitative Data Analysis & Inductive Grounded Theory
terms.operational_mechanism: Developing 1st-order concepts involves: (1) Micro-analysis of raw interview transcripts, meeting recordings, and field notes; (2) Open coding generating hundreds of informant-near phrases, verbatim in-vivo quotes, and descriptive summaries; (3) Comparative reduction: Systematically cross-comparing initial codes across informants to identify recurring patterns, overlaps, and similarities; and (4) Consolidation into a manageable inventory of well-defined, informant-grounded 1st-order concepts that preserve the authentic voice and phenomenological nuances of the participants.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Developing 1st-order concepts involves: (1) Micro-analysis of raw interview transcripts, meeting recordings, and field notes; (2) Open coding generating hundreds of informant-near phrases, verbatim in-vivo quotes, and descriptive summaries; (3) Comparative reduction: Systematically cross-comparing initial codes across informants to identify recurring patterns, overlaps, and similarities; and (4) Consolidation into a manageable inventory of well-defined, informant-grounded 1st-order concepts that preserve the authentic voice and phenomenological nuances of the participants.
terms.benchmarks: Rigor criteria: (1) Authentic informant voice: Codes must be expressed in language familiar to participants (e.g., 'feeling blindsided by executive decisions' rather than 'perceived organizational injustice'); (2) Data saturation: Concepts must be corroborated across multiple participants or data sources (triangulation); (3) Traceability: Each 1st-order concept must be supported by extensive raw textual citations in qualitative evidence tables.
terms.pitfalls: Common errors: (1) Theoretical contamination: Prematurely labeling 1st-order codes with academic constructs (e.g., labeling an informant's comment as 'cognitive dissonance' rather than 'internal conflict over company policy'); (2) Over-aggregation: Reducing raw codes too quickly into vague generalities, losing vital empirical context; and (3) Ignoring dissenting or negative cases that challenge dominant informant narratives.
terms.apa_reference: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15–31. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428112452151

terms.vietnamese: Các chủ đề bậc hai trong phương pháp Gioia
vietnamese_variants: Khái niệm lý thuyết bậc hai Gioia
domain_tags: Qualitative Data Analysis & Inductive Grounded Theory
terms.core_definition: In the Gioia methodology for qualitative research (Gioia et al., 2013), 2nd-Order Themes represent the crucial theoretical pivot where the researcher transitions from informant-centric empirical accounts (1st-order concepts) to researcher-centric conceptual abstraction. Asking 'what is going on here theoretically?', the researcher interrogates whether emerging patterns can be explained by existing organizational and social science concepts, or whether the phenomena demand the formulation of novel, nascent theoretical concepts that enrich or challenge extant theory.
terms.seminal_citation: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15-31.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gioia Methodology 2nd-Order Themes according to Gioia, Corley & Hamilton (2013).
terms.category: Qualitative Data Analysis & Inductive Grounded Theory
terms.operational_mechanism: Constructing 2nd-order themes involves: (1) Systematically reviewing the complete array of 1st-order concepts; (2) Identifying underlying latent theoretical commonalities across disparate informant descriptions; (3) Engaging in abductive reasoning—iterating continuously between emerging empirical patterns and relevant literature; (4) Naming 2nd-order themes using theoretical concepts that describe psychological mechanisms, organizational routines, relational practices, or cognitive frames; and (5) Preparing a structured quotes table that provides transparent empirical evidence for each theme.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Constructing 2nd-order themes involves: (1) Systematically reviewing the complete array of 1st-order concepts; (2) Identifying underlying latent theoretical commonalities across disparate informant descriptions; (3) Engaging in abductive reasoning—iterating continuously between emerging empirical patterns and relevant literature; (4) Naming 2nd-order themes using theoretical concepts that describe psychological mechanisms, organizational routines, relational practices, or cognitive frames; and (5) Preparing a structured quotes table that provides transparent empirical evidence for each theme.
terms.benchmarks: Publication standards in top-tier qualitative journals: (1) Theoretical elevation: Themes must be clearly differentiated from mere descriptive summaries of events, expressing theoretical mechanisms or organizational processes; (2) Grounded justification: Each 2nd-order theme should cluster 2 to 5 distinct 1st-order concepts; (3) Evidentiary depth: Backed by at least 3 to 6 distinct informant quotes from varied organizational echelons or data modalities in supplementary tables.
terms.pitfalls: Common analytical traps: (1) Naming 2nd-order themes with generic procedural terms (e.g., 'communication', 'training') that convey zero theoretical insight; (2) Forcing data to conform to pre-existing textbook concepts rather than allowing novel theoretical themes to emerge; and (3) Inadequate conceptual differentiation where two 2nd-order themes heavily overlap in meaning.
terms.apa_reference: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. (2013). Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15–31. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428112452151

terms.vietnamese: Phương pháp GLS (Bình phương bé nhất tổng quát)
vietnamese_variants: Kỹ thuật bình phương tối thiểu tổng quát
terms.core_definition: GLS (Generalized Least Squares) is a foundational econometric estimation technique designed to estimate parameters in a linear regression model when the error terms exhibit non-spherical variance-covariance structures—namely, heteroscedasticity (differing error variances across observations) or serial/spatial autocorrelation (correlated disturbances). Under such violations, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) point estimates remain unbiased and consistent but forfeit statistical efficiency, yielding standard errors that produce invalid t- and F-tests. GLS reweights the data using the inverse of the error covariance matrix, restoring minimum variance and valid statistical inference.
terms.seminal_citation: Greene, W. H. (2018). Econometric analysis (8th ed.). Pearson.
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of GLS according to Hiệu quả hơn OLS thông thường; được hiện thực hóa qua Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS) khi ma trận hiệp phương sai sai số chưa biết..
terms.benchmarks: Econometric efficiency benchmarks: (1) Asymptotic equivalence: Under valid specification of Omega, FGLS is asymptotically equivalent to true GLS and achieves the Gauss-Markov efficiency bound; (2) In panel models with N > T, cluster-robust standard errors or Driscoll-Kraay standard errors are often reported alongside FGLS to ensure robustness against potential misspecification of the error covariance structure.
terms.operational_mechanism: Given the linear regression model Y = X * beta + epsilon where E[epsilon | X] = 0 and Var(epsilon | X) = Omega: (1) When Omega is known, the Aitken GLS estimator is hat{beta}_{GLS} = (X' Omega^{-1} X)^{-1} X' Omega^{-1} Y; (2) When Omega is unknown, Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS) is employed: First, estimate the model via OLS to obtain residuals hat{epsilon}; second, use residuals to model and estimate hat{Omega}; third, replace Omega with hat{Omega} to compute hat{beta}_{FGLS} = (X' hat{Omega}^{-1} X)^{-1} X' hat{Omega}^{-1} Y; (3) In panel models, random effects GLS weights cross-sectional and time-series variation by theta = 1 - sqrt(sigma_e^2 / (T * sigma_u^2 + sigma_e^2)).
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Given the linear regression model Y = X * beta + epsilon where E[epsilon | X] = 0 and Var(epsilon | X) = Omega: (1) When Omega is known, the Aitken GLS estimator is hat{beta}_{GLS} = (X' Omega^{-1} X)^{-1} X' Omega^{-1} Y; (2) When Omega is unknown, Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS) is employed: First, estimate the model via OLS to obtain residuals hat{epsilon}; second, use residuals to model and estimate hat{Omega}; third, replace Omega with hat{Omega} to compute hat{beta}_{FGLS} = (X' hat{Omega}^{-1} X)^{-1} X' hat{Omega}^{-1} Y; (3) In panel models, random effects GLS weights cross-sectional and time-series variation by theta = 1 - sqrt(sigma_e^2 / (T * sigma_u^2 + sigma_e^2)).
terms.pitfalls: Common econometric errors: (1) Applying FGLS in small samples (small N or short T), where estimation noise in hat{Omega} causes severe downward bias in standard errors and inflated Type I error rates; (2) Believing that GLS fixes endogeneity caused by omitted variables or simultaneity (GLS requires strict exogeneity E[epsilon | X] = 0; if violated, Instrumental Variables / 2SLS must be used); and (3) Failing to test whether the Random Effects GLS assumption of zero correlation between individual effects and regressors holds via the Hausman test.
terms.apa_reference: Greene, W. H. (2018). Econometric analysis (8th ed.). Pearson.

terms.vietnamese: Độ phù hợp toàn cục (GoF trong mô hình PLS-SEM)
vietnamese_variants: Độ phù hợp mô hình PLS-SEM
terms.core_definition: Goodness of Fit (GoF) in Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), proposed by Michel Tenenhaus et al. (2005), is a composite metric formulated to assess the overall quality and global explanatory power of a PLS path model across both the measurement (outer) and structural (inner) models. Defined as the geometric mean of the average communality (or average variance extracted, AVE) and the average coefficient of determination (average R^2) of endogenous constructs, GoF was intended to provide a single holistic fit index analogous to global fit statistics in Covariance-Based SEM (CB-SEM).
terms.seminal_citation: Tenenhaus, M., Vinzi, V. E., Chatelin, Y. M., & Lauro, C. (2005). PLS path modeling. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 48(1), 159-205.
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of GoF according to Trong CB-SEM: kết hợp chi-square, RMSEA, CFI, TLI, SRMR. Trong PLS-SEM: Tenenhaus GoF = √(AVE_tb · R²_tb)..
terms.benchmarks: Empirical cutoffs (Wetzels et al., 2009): (1) GoF_small = sqrt(0.50 * 0.02) = 0.10; (2) GoF_medium = sqrt(0.50 * 0.13) = 0.25; (3) GoF_large = sqrt(0.50 * 0.26) = 0.36. Modern PLS-SEM guidance (Henseler et al., 2016; Hair et al., 2022): While GoF was historically popular, contemporary PLS-SEM methodologists recommend using Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR <= 0.08) and exact fit criteria (d_ULS, d_G via bootstrapping) rather than Tenenhaus GoF.
terms.operational_mechanism: The formula for the Tenenhaus GoF is: GoF = sqrt( bar{AVE} * bar{R}^2 ), where bar{AVE} is the arithmetic mean of the Average Variance Extracted across all reflective latent constructs, and bar{R}^2 is the arithmetic mean of the R^2 values of all endogenous latent constructs in the structural model. Wetzels et al. (2009) established baseline effect-size benchmarks by combining Cohen's f^2 criteria for R^2 (small = 0.02, medium = 0.13, large = 0.26) with the minimum acceptable AVE threshold of 0.50.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: The formula for the Tenenhaus GoF is: GoF = sqrt( bar{AVE} * bar{R}^2 ), where bar{AVE} is the arithmetic mean of the Average Variance Extracted across all reflective latent constructs, and bar{R}^2 is the arithmetic mean of the R^2 values of all endogenous latent constructs in the structural model. Wetzels et al. (2009) established baseline effect-size benchmarks by combining Cohen's f^2 criteria for R^2 (small = 0.02, medium = 0.13, large = 0.26) with the minimum acceptable AVE threshold of 0.50.
terms.pitfalls: Critical reviewer pitfalls: (1) Using GoF for models containing formative constructs (AVE is mathematically undefined for formative indicators, rendering GoF invalid); (2) Treating GoF as a statistical hypothesis test (GoF cannot distinguish between valid models and misspecified models, as demonstrated by Henseler & Sarstedt, 2013); and (3) Reporting GoF as the primary validation criterion in top Q1 journals without evaluating out-of-sample predictive power via PLSpredict.
terms.apa_reference: Tenenhaus, M., Vinzi, V. E., Chatelin, Y. M., & Lauro, C. (2005). PLS path modeling. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 48(1), 159–205. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2004.03.005

terms.vietnamese: Kiểm định phương sai thay đổi Goldfeld-Quandt
terms.core_definition: Kiểm định Goldfeld-Quandt (Goldfeld & Quandt, 1965) là phép kiểm định tham số kinh tế lượng cổ điển dùng để phát hiện hiện tượng phương sai sai số thay đổi (heteroskedasticity) khi phương sai được giả định tỷ lệ đơn điệu thuận hoặc nghịch với một biến giải thích cụ thể.
terms.seminal_citation: Goldfeld & Quandt (1965)
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Goldfeld-Quandt Test according to Goldfeld & Quandt (1965).
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Sắp xếp toàn bộ N quan sát theo thứ tự tăng dần của biến giải thích X bị nghi ngờ gây ra phương sai thay đổi. 2. Loại bỏ c quan sát ở giữa (thường chọn c xấp xỉ N/5 đến N/4) để tối đa hóa sự phân tách giữa hai nhóm. 3. Ước lượng OLS riêng biệt cho hai nhóm quan sát còn lại: Nhóm 1 (n_1 quan sát nhỏ nhất) thu được SSR_1; Nhóm 2 (n_2 quan sát lớn nhất) thu được SSR_2. 4. Thống kê kiểm định F = (SSR_2 / df_2) / (SSR_1 / df_1) tuân theo phân phối F(df_2, df_1).
terms.benchmarks: Giả thuyết H0: Phương sai sai số đồng nhất (Homoscedasticity, σ_1² = σ_2²). Nếu p-value < 0.05 (F-stat > F_critical): Bác bỏ H0, khẳng định tồn tại phương sai thay đổi. Kiểm định có sức mạnh kiểm định rất cao khi biết chính xác biến gây ra phương sai thay đổi đơn điệu.
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: Không áp dụng được khi phương sai thay đổi có dạng phi đơn điệu (non-monotonic) hoặc do tổ hợp đa biến phức tạp gây ra. Trong trường hợp tổng quát, kiểm định White (1980) hoặc Breusch-Pagan/Koenker (1979) linh hoạt và được ưu tiên hơn trong các nghiên cứu kinh tế lượng hiện đại.
terms.apa_reference: Goldfeld, S. M., & Quandt, R. E. (1965). Some tests for homoskedasticity. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 60(310), 539–547. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1965.10480811

terms.vietnamese: Phân rã Goodman-Bacon trong mô hình DiD
vietnamese_variants: Phân rã trọng số DiD so le
terms.core_definition: The Goodman-Bacon Decomposition, formulated by Andrew Goodman-Bacon (2021), is an econometric diagnostic theorem demonstrating that the canonical Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) Difference-in-Differences (DiD) estimator with staggered treatment timing is a weighted average of all potential 2x2 DiD sub-comparisons. Crucially, it reveals that when treatment effects are heterogeneous over time, TWFE DiD assigns substantial and sometimes negative weights to 'forbidden comparisons'—specifically comparisons where already-treated units act as controls for later-treated units. This can introduce severe bias, including reversing the sign of estimated treatment effects.
terms.seminal_citation: Goodman-Bacon, A. (2021). Difference-in-differences with variation in treatment timing. Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 254-277.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Goodman-Bacon Decomposition according to Goodman-Bacon (2021).
terms.operational_mechanism: Goodman-Bacon shows that in a balanced panel with variation in treatment timing, the TWFE coefficient hat{beta}^{TWFE} decomposes as: hat{beta}^{TWFE} = sum_{k != l} s_{kl} * hat{beta}_{kl}^{2x2} + sum_k s_{kU} * hat{beta}_{kU}^{2x2}, where comparisons fall into three categories: (1) Earlier treated vs. Later treated (using later units as controls before they receive treatment); (2) Treated vs. Never-treated / Untreated (clean comparisons); and (3) Later treated vs. Already-treated (using already-treated units as controls). In the third comparison, changes in treatment effects over time in the already-treated group are subtracted from the later-treated group's gains, which can generate negative weights and distort treatment effect estimates.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Goodman-Bacon shows that in a balanced panel with variation in treatment timing, the TWFE coefficient hat{beta}^{TWFE} decomposes as: hat{beta}^{TWFE} = sum_{k != l} s_{kl} * hat{beta}_{kl}^{2x2} + sum_k s_{kU} * hat{beta}_{kU}^{2x2}, where comparisons fall into three categories: (1) Earlier treated vs. Later treated (using later units as controls before they receive treatment); (2) Treated vs. Never-treated / Untreated (clean comparisons); and (3) Later treated vs. Already-treated (using already-treated units as controls). In the third comparison, changes in treatment effects over time in the already-treated group are subtracted from the later-treated group's gains, which can generate negative weights and distort treatment effect estimates.
terms.benchmarks: Diagnostic standards in modern empirical papers: (1) Compute and report the Goodman-Bacon decomposition table showing the proportion of total weight assigned to clean comparisons (treated vs. untreated) versus problematic comparisons (later vs. already-treated); (2) If already-treated units receive a substantial share of total weight (> 15% to 20%) and treatment effects are dynamic, TWFE is considered compromised; (3) Authors must adopt robust staggered DiD estimators: Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021), Sun & Abraham (2021), de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille (2020), or Borusyak, Jaravel & Spiess (2024).
terms.pitfalls: Common econometric errors: (1) Publishing a staggered DiD design without conducting a Goodman-Bacon decomposition or modern robust event-study estimator, which is an immediate rejection trigger in top economics and finance journals; (2) Erroneously assuming that dynamic two-way fixed effects event-study leads/lags resolve the weighting issue (Sun & Abraham show event studies also suffer from contaminated weights); and (3) Failing to evaluate whether negative weights occur in the empirical setting.
terms.apa_reference: Goodman-Bacon, A. (2021). Difference-in-differences with variation in treatment timing. Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 254–277. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2021.03.014

terms.vietnamese: Độ phù hợp của mô hình
vietnamese_variants: Độ thích hợp mô hình thống kê
Chỉ số tương thích mô hình
terms.core_definition: Goodness of Fit is an overarching statistical concept and operational evaluation framework assessing how well an empirical model or theoretical probability distribution conforms to observed sample data. Across statistical paradigms—from Pearson's chi-square test in categorical analysis and R^2 in linear regression to likelihood ratio tests in Generalized Linear Models and multi-index fit batteries in Structural Equation Modeling—goodness of fit quantifies the discrepancy between observed values and the values predicted or implied by the hypothesized model.
terms.seminal_citation: Kline, R. B. (2023). Principles and practice of structural equation modeling (5th ed.). Guilford Press.
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Goodness of Fit according to Trong CB-SEM: kết hợp chi-square, RMSEA, CFI, TLI, SRMR. Trong PLS-SEM: Tenenhaus GoF = √(AVE_tb · R²_tb)..
terms.benchmarks: Standard fit benchmarks: (1) Pearson/Deviance goodness of fit: p > 0.05 indicates the model does not significantly deviate from observed data; (2) SEM global fit: RMSEA <= 0.06 (upper 90% CI < 0.08), CFI >= 0.95, TLI >= 0.95, SRMR <= 0.08; (3) Model selection: Differences in Bayesian Information Criterion Delta BIC > 10 provide decisive evidence favoring the model with the lower BIC.
terms.operational_mechanism: Goodness of fit evaluation follows model-specific mathematical metrics: (1) Categorical distribution: Pearson's Chi-square statistic chi^2 = sum (O_i - E_i)^2 / E_i, tested against chi^2 distribution with (k - 1) degrees of freedom; (2) Linear regression: Coefficient of determination R^2 = 1 - (SS_{res} / SS_{tot}) and Adjusted R^2; (3) Maximum Likelihood & GLM: Deviance D = 2 * (ln L_{sat} - ln L_{model}), alongside information criteria (AIC, BIC); and (4) Covariance structures (SEM): Assessing discrepancy between sample covariance matrix S and model-implied covariance matrix Sigma(theta) via chi^2, RMSEA, CFI, TLI, and SRMR.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Goodness of fit evaluation follows model-specific mathematical metrics: (1) Categorical distribution: Pearson's Chi-square statistic chi^2 = sum (O_i - E_i)^2 / E_i, tested against chi^2 distribution with (k - 1) degrees of freedom; (2) Linear regression: Coefficient of determination R^2 = 1 - (SS_{res} / SS_{tot}) and Adjusted R^2; (3) Maximum Likelihood & GLM: Deviance D = 2 * (ln L_{sat} - ln L_{model}), alongside information criteria (AIC, BIC); and (4) Covariance structures (SEM): Assessing discrepancy between sample covariance matrix S and model-implied covariance matrix Sigma(theta) via chi^2, RMSEA, CFI, TLI, and SRMR.
terms.pitfalls: Critical methodological traps: (1) Equating high goodness of fit with causal validity (a severely misspecified model with omitted confounders or reverse causality can exhibit near-perfect fit); (2) Overfitting—maximizing in-sample fit by adding superfluous parameters, which undermines out-of-sample predictive validity; and (3) Relying exclusively on chi-square significance in large samples (N > 500) where trivial discrepancies trigger statistical rejection.
terms.apa_reference: Kline, R. B. (2023). Principles and practice of structural equation modeling (5th ed.). Guilford Press.

terms.term: Goodness of Fit Index (GFI in SEM)
terms.vietnamese: Chỉ số độ phù hợp GFI
terms.core_definition: The Goodness of Fit Index (GFI), developed by Karl Jöreskog and Dag Sörbom (1981) for the LISREL framework, is an absolute fit index assessing the proportion of variance and covariance in the sample covariance matrix S explained by the model-implied covariance matrix Sigma(hat{theta}). Analogous to R^2 in multiple regression, GFI measures fit without referencing a baseline null model, while its adjusted counterpart, AGFI (Adjusted Goodness of Fit Index), introduces a penalty term for model complexity based on degrees of freedom relative to the number of observed variables.
terms.seminal_citation: Jöreskog, K. G., & Sörbom, D. (1981). LISREL V: Analysis of linear structural relationships by maximum likelihood and ordinary least squares methods. International Educational Services.
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Goodness of Fit Index according to Giá trị GFI ≥ 0.90 (hoặc khắt khe ≥ 0.95) biểu thị mô hình phù hợp tốt với dữ liệu thực tế..
terms.benchmarks: Historical vs. Modern Standards: Historically, GFI >= 0.90 and AGFI >= 0.85 were accepted as benchmarks for adequate model fit. However, extensive Monte Carlo simulation studies by Marsh, Balla, and McDonald (1988) and Hu and Bentler (1998, 1999) demonstrated that GFI and AGFI are heavily biased by sample size (inflated in large samples, depressed in small samples) and sensitive to model complexity. Consequently, modern Q1 journal guidelines recommend reporting RMSEA, CFI, TLI, and SRMR instead of relying on GFI/AGFI.
terms.operational_mechanism: Under Maximum Likelihood estimation in CB-SEM, GFI is computed as: GFI = 1 - [tr((Sigma^{-1} S - I)^2) / tr((Sigma^{-1} S)^2)]. The Adjusted GFI is defined as: AGFI = 1 - [(p(p + 1) / (2 * df)) * (1 - GFI)], where p is the number of observed indicators and df is model degrees of freedom. Values range between 0 and 1, where 1.0 represents a perfect fit of the model to the sample covariance matrix.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Under Maximum Likelihood estimation in CB-SEM, GFI is computed as: GFI = 1 - [tr((Sigma^{-1} S - I)^2) / tr((Sigma^{-1} S)^2)]. The Adjusted GFI is defined as: AGFI = 1 - [(p(p + 1) / (2 * df)) * (1 - GFI)], where p is the number of observed indicators and df is model degrees of freedom. Values range between 0 and 1, where 1.0 represents a perfect fit of the model to the sample covariance matrix.
terms.pitfalls: Common reporting pitfalls: (1) Relying on GFI >= 0.90 to justify model adequacy when modern indices (CFI, RMSEA) indicate poor fit; (2) Reporting GFI without reporting RMSEA and SRMR, which reviewers routinely flag as selective reporting; and (3) Using GFI to compare non-nested models (GFI does not account for parsimony as effectively as AIC or BIC).
terms.apa_reference: Jöreskog, K. G., & Sörbom, D. (1981). LISREL V: Analysis of linear structural relationships by maximum likelihood and ordinary least squares methods. International Educational Services.

terms.vietnamese: Khung đánh giá GRADE
vietnamese_variants: Đánh giá chất lượng bằng chứng GRADE
terms.core_definition: The GRADE Framework (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation), formulated by the international GRADE Working Group (Guyatt et al., 2008), is the universally endorsed methodological standard for grading the certainty (or quality) of scientific evidence and determining the strength of practical/clinical recommendations in systematic reviews, health policy, and evidence-based practice. Moving beyond simplistic hierarchies that equate study design directly with evidence quality, GRADE systematically appraises evidence across specific patient-important outcomes through explicit, transparent, and reproducible criteria.
terms.seminal_citation: Guyatt, G. H., Oxman, A. D., Vist, G. E., Kunz, R., Falck-Ytter, Y., Alonso-Coello, P., & Schünemann, H. J. (2008). GRADE: An emerging consensus on rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations. BMJ, 336(7650), 924-926.
terms.expert_notes: Từ vựng học thuật chuẩn Academic Word List (AWL - Averil Coxhead, 2000).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic Word List headword (Averil Coxhead). Essential lexical item frequently occurring in peer-reviewed scientific publications.
terms.academic_example: This study systematically investigates how grade operates within the proposed conceptual framework.
terms.operational_mechanism: Evidence evaluation under GRADE follows a standardized four-tier rating: High, Moderate, Low, or Very Low certainty. Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) begin at High certainty, whereas observational studies begin at Low certainty. Ratings are modified based on eight explicit domains: (1) Five downgrading factors: Risk of bias (study limitations), Inconsistency (unexplained heterogeneity, I^2), Indirectness (population, intervention, or outcome differences), Imprecision (wide confidence intervals crossing clinical decision thresholds), and Publication bias; (2) Three upgrading factors (applicable primarily to observational studies): Large magnitude of effect (RR > 2 or > 5), Dose-response gradient, and Plausible confounding working against the observed effect.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Evidence evaluation under GRADE follows a standardized four-tier rating: High, Moderate, Low, or Very Low certainty. Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) begin at High certainty, whereas observational studies begin at Low certainty. Ratings are modified based on eight explicit domains: (1) Five downgrading factors: Risk of bias (study limitations), Inconsistency (unexplained heterogeneity, I^2), Indirectness (population, intervention, or outcome differences), Imprecision (wide confidence intervals crossing clinical decision thresholds), and Publication bias; (2) Three upgrading factors (applicable primarily to observational studies): Large magnitude of effect (RR > 2 or > 5), Dose-response gradient, and Plausible confounding working against the observed effect.
terms.benchmarks: Evidence certainty tiers: (1) High: Very confident that true effect lies close to the estimate; (2) Moderate: Moderately confident, true effect likely close, but possibility of substantial difference exists; (3) Low: Limited confidence, true effect may be substantially different; (4) Very Low: Very little confidence in the effect estimate. Recommendations are categorized as either 'Strong' (almost all informed individuals would choose the recommended course) or 'Weak/Conditional' (most would choose, but substantial variation in values exists).
terms.pitfalls: Critical review traps: (1) Evaluating certainty at the overall study level rather than separately for each specific outcome; (2) Downgrading repeatedly across multiple domains for the same underlying methodological flaw (double-penalization); (3) Equating a 'weak recommendation' with weak scientific evidence (a weak recommendation can be based on high-certainty evidence if risks and benefits are closely balanced); and (4) Omitting a formal 'Summary of Findings' (SoF) table in the published review.
terms.apa_reference: Guyatt, G. H., Oxman, A. D., Vist, G. E., Kunz, R., Falck-Ytter, Y., Alonso-Coello, P., & Schünemann, H. J. (2008). GRADE: An emerging consensus on rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations. BMJ, 336(7650), 924–926. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.39489.470347.AD

terms.vietnamese: Cách tiếp cận GRADE trong đánh giá độ tin cậy của bằng chứng
vietnamese_variants: Quy trình đánh giá độ chắc chắn GRADE
Tiếp cận GRADE đánh giá bằng chứng
Độ tin cậy bằng chứng GRADE
terms.core_definition: The GRADE Approach for Certainty of Evidence Assessment is the operationalized protocol developed by the GRADE Working Group to judge the extent to which researchers and decision-makers can be confident that an effect estimate reflects the true causal effect. In meta-analyses and evidence syntheses, certainty is assessed independently for each predefined primary and secondary outcome, ensuring that synthesized conclusions explicitly reflect the vulnerability of the evidence base to systematic bias, random error, and contextual misalignment.
terms.seminal_citation: Balshem, H., Helfand, M., Schünemann, H. J., Oxman, A. D., Kunz, R., Brozek, J., Vist, G. E., Falck-Ytter, Y., Meerpohl, J., Norris, S., & Guyatt, G. H. (2011). GRADE guidelines: 3. Rating the quality of evidence. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 64(4), 401-406.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of GRADE Approach (Certainty of Evidence) according to Guyatt et al. (2008).
terms.operational_mechanism: Assessment is structured across five specific downgrading domains: (1) Risk of Bias: Evaluated using validated tools (e.g., Cochrane RoB 2, ROBINS-I); (2) Inconsistency: Assessed via point estimate overlap, statistical heterogeneity tests (p < 0.10 for Chi^2, I^2 > 50%), and consistency of effect directions across studies; (3) Indirectness: Evaluates whether the study populations, interventions, comparisons, or surrogate outcomes differ from the primary research question; (4) Imprecision: Assessed by determining whether 95% confidence intervals cross critical clinical importance thresholds or if the optimal information size (OIS) is not achieved; and (5) Publication Bias: Investigated via funnel plot asymmetry, Egger's regression test, and clinical trial registries.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Assessment is structured across five specific downgrading domains: (1) Risk of Bias: Evaluated using validated tools (e.g., Cochrane RoB 2, ROBINS-I); (2) Inconsistency: Assessed via point estimate overlap, statistical heterogeneity tests (p < 0.10 for Chi^2, I^2 > 50%), and consistency of effect directions across studies; (3) Indirectness: Evaluates whether the study populations, interventions, comparisons, or surrogate outcomes differ from the primary research question; (4) Imprecision: Assessed by determining whether 95% confidence intervals cross critical clinical importance thresholds or if the optimal information size (OIS) is not achieved; and (5) Publication Bias: Investigated via funnel plot asymmetry, Egger's regression test, and clinical trial registries.
terms.benchmarks: Rating levels: (1) Downgrading is calibrated in integer steps (-1 for serious concerns, -2 for very serious concerns per domain); (2) High Certainty: 0 downgrades across all 5 domains; (3) Moderate Certainty: -1 downgrade; (4) Low Certainty: -2 downgrades; (5) Very Low Certainty: -3 or more downgrades. Results must be summarized in a GRADE Evidence Profile or Summary of Findings (SoF) table containing absolute effect estimates (risk differences per 1,000 participants).
terms.pitfalls: Common research mistakes: (1) Downgrading for imprecision solely based on sample size without checking whether the 95% confidence interval excludes both null effect and clinical decision thresholds; (2) Ignoring trial registries when searching for unpublished negative trials, overlooking publication bias; and (3) Inadequately explaining the rationale for downgrading decisions in table footnotes.
terms.apa_reference: Balshem, H., Helfand, M., Schünemann, H. J., Oxman, A. D., Kunz, R., Brozek, J., Vist, G. E., Falck-Ytter, Y., Meerpohl, J., Norris, S., & Guyatt, G. H. (2011). GRADE guidelines: 3. Rating the quality of evidence. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 64(4), 401–406. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2010.07.015

terms.vietnamese: Mô hình phản hồi theo cấp độ (Mô hình GRM)
vietnamese_variants: Mô hình phản hồi từng bậc
Mô hình IRT cho thang đo Likert
terms.core_definition: The Graded Response Model (GRM), formulated by Fumiko Samejima (1969), is an item response theory (IRT) mathematical model designed for polytomous items with ordered categorical response options, such as Likert-type scales (e.g., 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree') or partial credit scoring rubrics. In contrast to binary IRT models, the GRM models the cumulative probability that an individual with latent trait level theta will endorse a response category at or above a specific threshold, accounting for varying item discrimination parameters across individual items.
terms.seminal_citation: Samejima, F. (1969). Estimation of latent ability using a response pattern of graded scores. Psychometrika Monograph Supplement, 34(4, Pt. 2), 1-100.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Graded Response Model (GRM) according to Samejima (1969).
terms.operational_mechanism: For an item i with K ordered categories (k = 0, 1, ..., K-1): (1) Cumulative category response functions P_{ik}^*(theta) calculate the probability of responding in category k or higher: P_{ik}^*(theta) = 1 / [1 + exp(-a_i * (theta - b_{ik}))], where a_i is the item discrimination parameter and b_{ik} is the threshold/difficulty parameter between category k-1 and category k (with b_{i1} < b_{i2} < ... < b_{i,K-1}); (2) Boundary conditions specify P_{i0}^*(theta) = 1 and P_{iK}^*(theta) = 0; (3) The category probability of selecting category k is computed by subtraction: P_{ik}(theta) = P_{ik}^*(theta) - P_{i,k+1}^*(theta); (4) Parameters are estimated via Marginal Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MMLE) using the EM algorithm.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: For an item i with K ordered categories (k = 0, 1, ..., K-1): (1) Cumulative category response functions P_{ik}^*(theta) calculate the probability of responding in category k or higher: P_{ik}^*(theta) = 1 / [1 + exp(-a_i * (theta - b_{ik}))], where a_i is the item discrimination parameter and b_{ik} is the threshold/difficulty parameter between category k-1 and category k (with b_{i1} < b_{i2} < ... < b_{i,K-1}); (2) Boundary conditions specify P_{i0}^*(theta) = 1 and P_{iK}^*(theta) = 0; (3) The category probability of selecting category k is computed by subtraction: P_{ik}(theta) = P_{ik}^*(theta) - P_{i,k+1}^*(theta); (4) Parameters are estimated via Marginal Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MMLE) using the EM algorithm.
terms.benchmarks: Parameter interpretation guidelines: (1) Discrimination parameter a_i: < 0.65 (very low), 0.65-1.34 (moderate), 1.35-1.69 (high), >= 1.70 (very high); (2) Threshold parameters b_{ik}: Should span across a broad range of the latent continuum (e.g., from -2.5 to +2.5) with strictly ordered spacing (b_{ik} < b_{i,k+1}); (3) Item Information Functions (IIF): Highest information is achieved in regions where category thresholds are clustered.
terms.pitfalls: Common psychometric errors: (1) Applying GRM to unordered nominal categorical data (where Bock's Nominal Response Model is appropriate); (2) Confusing GRM with the Partial Credit Model (PCM) or Rating Scale Model (RSM)—GRM is a difference model based on cumulative logits, whereas PCM/RSM are divide-by-total adjacent-category models; and (3) Retaining items with disordered empirical thresholds or negative discrimination parameters, which indicates flawed response scale wording.
terms.apa_reference: Samejima, F. (1969). Estimation of latent ability using a response pattern of graded scores. Psychometrika Monograph Supplement, 34(4, Pt. 2), 1–100. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03372160

terms.term: Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE System)
terms.vietnamese: Hệ thống phân hạng đánh giá, xây dựng và thẩm định khuyến nghị (GRADE)
vietnamese_variants: Hệ thống thẩm định khuyến nghị GRADE
terms.core_definition: The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE System) is a comprehensive, transparent framework used by the World Health Organization (WHO), Cochrane Collaboration, and over 110 international health and scientific organizations to transition systematically from synthesized empirical evidence to actionable policy recommendations and clinical practice guidelines. The GRADE system explicitly separates the process of judging the certainty of scientific evidence from the subsequent, distinct process of determining the direction and strength of clinical or managerial recommendations.
terms.seminal_citation: Andrews, J. C., Schünemann, H. J., Oxman, A. D., Pottie, K., Meerpohl, J. J., Alonso-Coello, P., Rind, D., Montori, V. M., Brito, J. P., Norris, S., El-Jardali, F., & Guyatt, G. H. (2013). GRADE guidelines: 15. Going from evidence to recommendation—determinants of a recommendation's direction and strength. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 66(7), 726-735.
terms.expert_notes: Nguồn ghi ngưỡng
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation according to Hạ bậc chất lượng bằng chứng khi phát hiện: Risk of Bias, Inconsistency, Indirectness, Imprecision, hoặc Publication Bias..
terms.operational_mechanism: The GRADE decision framework transitions from evidence to recommendations via the Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework, which evaluates four key criteria: (1) Balance of desirable and undesirable consequences: Assessing whether the anticipated benefits clearly outweigh the harms; (2) Certainty of evidence: Derived from the outcome-specific GRADE evidence profile; (3) Values and preferences: Considering the relative importance that patients and stakeholders assign to specific outcomes and potential variability in preferences; and (4) Resource implications, feasibility, and equity: Evaluating cost-effectiveness, implementation barriers, and impact on socioeconomic health disparities.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: The GRADE decision framework transitions from evidence to recommendations via the Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework, which evaluates four key criteria: (1) Balance of desirable and undesirable consequences: Assessing whether the anticipated benefits clearly outweigh the harms; (2) Certainty of evidence: Derived from the outcome-specific GRADE evidence profile; (3) Values and preferences: Considering the relative importance that patients and stakeholders assign to specific outcomes and potential variability in preferences; and (4) Resource implications, feasibility, and equity: Evaluating cost-effectiveness, implementation barriers, and impact on socioeconomic health disparities.
terms.benchmarks: Recommendation classifications: (1) Strong recommendation: Panel is confident that the desirable effects of adherence outweigh undesirable effects (worded as 'We recommend...'); (2) Weak/Conditional recommendation: Desirable effects probably outweigh undesirable effects, but significant uncertainty remains regarding values, costs, or baseline evidence (worded as 'We suggest...'); (3) High certainty of evidence does not automatically produce a strong recommendation if trade-offs are sensitive to individual stakeholder preferences.
terms.pitfalls: Common institutional errors: (1) Merging evidence quality with recommendation strength into a single composite score, obscuring value judgments; (2) Making strong recommendations supported only by very low certainty evidence without meeting one of GRADE's formal paradigmatic exceptions (e.g., life-saving interventions in catastrophic emergencies); and (3) Neglecting to document the stakeholder consensus process and voting distributions in Guideline development reports.
terms.apa_reference: Andrews, J. C., Schünemann, H. J., Oxman, A. D., Pottie, K., Meerpohl, J. J., Alonso-Coello, P., Rind, D., Montori, V. M., Brito, J. P., Norris, S., El-Jardali, F., & Guyatt, G. H. (2013). GRADE guidelines: 15. Going from evidence to recommendation—determinants of a recommendation's direction and strength. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 66(7), 726–735. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2013.02.003

terms.vietnamese: Định tâm theo trung bình tổng thể và định tâm theo trung bình nhóm
vietnamese_variants: Centering trong mô hình đa cấp HLM
Định tâm biến độc lập đa tầng
terms.core_definition: Grand-Mean Centering vs. Group-Mean Centering represents the critical methodological choice of how to rescale Level-1 predictors in Multilevel Modeling (MLM) and Hierarchical Linear Modeling (HLM). In Grand-Mean Centering (CGM), the overall sample mean across all clusters is subtracted from each raw score (x_{ij} - bar{x}_{..}), adjusting for between-cluster differences and facilitating the interpretation of the intercept as the expected outcome for an individual with an average score across the entire population. In Group-Mean Centering (CWC, Centering Within Cluster), the cluster-specific mean is subtracted from each raw score (x_{ij} - bar{x}_{.j}), mathematically removing all between-cluster variance from the predictor and isolating the pure, unconfounded within-cluster effect.
terms.seminal_citation: Enders, C. K., & Tofighi, D. (2007). Centering predictor variables in cross-sectional multilevel models: A new look at an old issue. Psychological Methods, 12(2), 121-138.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Grand-Mean Centering vs. Group-Mean Centering according to Enders & Tofighi (2007).
terms.operational_mechanism: Mathematical formulation and behavioral divergence: (1) Grand-Mean Centering: x_{ij}^{CGM} = x_{ij} - bar{x}_{..}. In random intercept models, the Level-1 slope reflects a composite blend of within-group and between-group regression relationships; (2) Group-Mean Centering: x_{ij}^{CWC} = x_{ij} - bar{x}_{.j}. The Level-1 slope estimates the pure within-cluster relationship (beta_W). To capture the between-cluster effect, the cluster mean bar{x}_{.j} (often grand-mean centered) must be explicitly reintroduced as a Level-2 predictor: y_{ij} = gamma_{00} + gamma_{10}(x_{ij} - bar{x}_{.j}) + gamma_{01}(bar{x}_{.j} - bar{x}_{..}) + u_{0j} + e_{ij}. The contextual effect is then estimated as gamma_{01} - gamma_{10}.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Mathematical formulation and behavioral divergence: (1) Grand-Mean Centering: x_{ij}^{CGM} = x_{ij} - bar{x}_{..}. In random intercept models, the Level-1 slope reflects a composite blend of within-group and between-group regression relationships; (2) Group-Mean Centering: x_{ij}^{CWC} = x_{ij} - bar{x}_{.j}. The Level-1 slope estimates the pure within-cluster relationship (beta_W). To capture the between-cluster effect, the cluster mean bar{x}_{.j} (often grand-mean centered) must be explicitly reintroduced as a Level-2 predictor: y_{ij} = gamma_{00} + gamma_{10}(x_{ij} - bar{x}_{.j}) + gamma_{01}(bar{x}_{.j} - bar{x}_{..}) + u_{0j} + e_{ij}. The contextual effect is then estimated as gamma_{01} - gamma_{10}.
terms.benchmarks: Decision framework (Enders & Tofighi, 2007): (1) Use Group-Mean Centering (CWC) when the primary research question focuses on Level-1 individual-level processes unconfounded by cluster-level variation, when testing cross-level interactions (Level-2 moderating Level-1 slope), or when estimating contextual effects; (2) Use Grand-Mean Centering (CGM) when the primary research focus is on predicting Level-2 outcomes or when Level-1 predictors are primarily control variables where cluster-level separation is not theoretically meaningful.
terms.pitfalls: Major analytical errors in management and psychology journals: (1) Leaving Level-1 predictors uncentered, which causes the intercept to represent an uninterpretable extrapolation where x = 0; (2) Using Grand-Mean Centering when testing cross-level interactions, which conflates within- and between-level variance and introduces severe bias into cross-level moderation estimates; and (3) Failing to explicitly declare the centering strategy used in the methodology section, preventing replication.
terms.apa_reference: Enders, C. K., & Tofighi, D. (2007). Centering predictor variables in cross-sectional multilevel models: A new look at an old issue. Psychological Methods, 12(2), 121–138. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.12.2.121

terms.vietnamese: Kiểm định quan hệ nhân quả Granger
terms.core_definition: Kiểm định nhân quả Granger (Granger, 1969) là khái niệm thống kê định lượng dựa trên nguyên lý tiên đoán thời gian (temporal precedence): Một biến X được gọi là 'Granger-gây ra' biến Y nếu các giá trị quá khứ của X chứa đựng thông tin giúp dự báo Y tốt hơn so với việc chỉ sử dụng các giá trị quá khứ của chính Y.
terms.seminal_citation: Granger (1969); Toda & Yamamoto (1995)
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Granger Causality according to Granger (1969).
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Ước lượng mô hình tự hồi quy vectơ (VAR): Y_t = c_1 + ∑ [α_i · Y_{t-i}] + ∑ [β_j · X_{t-j}] + u_1t. 2. Giả thuyết H0: β_1 = β_2 = ... = β_p = 0 (X không Granger-gây ra Y). 3. Sử dụng kiểm định Wald F-test hoặc Chi-bình phương để kiểm tra các ràng buộc bằng 0 đồng thời trên các hệ số trễ của X. 4. Kiểm tra chiều ngược lại (Y có Granger-gây ra X hay không) để xác định tính tương hỗ (bidirectional causality).
terms.benchmarks: Nếu p-value < 0.05: Bác bỏ H0, kết luận X Granger-gây ra Y ở mức ý nghĩa 5%. Để kết quả kiểm định hợp lệ, tất cả các chuỗi thời gian bắt buộc phải dừng (stationary). Nếu các chuỗi là không dừng I(1) và có đồng liên kết, phải dùng mô hình VECM hoặc phương pháp tiếp cận Toda & Yamamoto (1995) tăng bậc trễ (augmented lag VAR) để tránh phân phối F suy biến.
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện kinh điển: Đồng nhất nhân quả Granger với quan hệ nhân quả thực sự (true philosophical / structural causality). Nhân quả Granger về bản chất thuần túy là khả năng tiên đoán có tính trước-sau về mặt thời gian (predictive precedence); hai biến cùng bị chi phối bởi một biến thứ ba (omitted common cause) vẫn có thể cho kết quả nhân quả Granger mạnh.
terms.apa_reference: Granger, C. W. J. (1969). Investigating causal relations by econometric models and cross-spectral methods. Econometrica, 37(3), 424–438. https://doi.org/10.2307/1912791

terms.vietnamese: Kiểm định Quan hệ Nhân quả Granger
domain_tags: Kinh tế lượng Chuỗi thời gian
Quan hệ Dự báo Thời gian
terms.core_definition: Phép kiểm định thống kê kinh điển đoạt giải Nobel do Clive Granger (1969) phát triển để đánh giá xem các giá trị trong quá khứ của một biến X có chứa đựng thông tin hữu ích giúp dự báo biến Y tốt hơn so với việc chỉ sử dụng riêng các thông tin trong quá khứ của chính Y hay không. Bản chất của 'Nhân quả Granger' là TÍNH ƯU TRỘI VỀ DỰ BÁO TRONG THỜI GIAN (Predictive priority), dựa trên tiên đề triết học: 'Quá khứ và hiện tại có thể gây ra tương lai, nhưng tương lai không thể gây ra quá khứ'.
terms.seminal_citation: Granger, C. W. J. (1969). Investigating causal relations by econometric models and cross-spectral methods. Econometrica, 37(3), 424–438. https://doi.org/10.2307/1912791
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Granger Causality Test according to Granger (1969).
terms.benchmarks: Đánh giá qua kiểm định F-test (hoặc Wald test) trên các hệ số trễ của biến X trong phương trình giải thích Y: Giả thuyết vô hiệu H0: β_1 = β_2 = ... = β_p = 0 (X không gây ra Y theo nghĩa Granger). Bác bỏ H0 khi p < 0.05 và kết luận X có quan hệ nhân quả Granger đối với Y. Phân loại 4 kết cục: (1) X tác động một chiều lên Y; (2) Y tác động một chiều lên X; (3) Nhân quả hai chiều (Feedback loop / Bidirectional causality); (4) Độc lập thống kê.
terms.pitfalls: Ngụy biện 'Hậu quả do tiền lệ' (Post hoc ergo propter hoc): Đồng nhất Nhân quả Granger với Nhân quả Triết học/Cấu trúc thực sự. Một biến X có thể dẫn trước Y đơn thuần vì cả hai cùng chịu ảnh hưởng bởi một biến ẩn thứ ba Z hoặc do phản ánh kỳ vọng duy lý của thị trường; thực hiện kiểm định trên các chuỗi không dừng mà không sai phân hóa làm kết quả F-test bị sai lệch tiệm cận.
terms.apa_reference: Granger, C. W. J. (1969). Investigating causal relations by econometric models and cross-spectral methods. Econometrica, 37(3), 424–438.

terms.vietnamese: Mô hình trọng lực trong thương mại quốc tế
vietnamese_variants: Mô hình hấp dẫn thương mại
terms.core_definition: Mô hình trọng lực thương mại quốc tế (Tinbergen, 1962; Anderson & van Wincoop, 2003) là mô hình kinh tế lượng chuẩn mực lý giải kim ngạch thương mại song phương giữa hai quốc gia. Bắt nguồn từ định luật vạn vật hấp dẫn của Newton và được hoàn thiện với nền tảng kinh tế học vi mô chặt chẽ, mô hình chỉ ra rằng quy mô thương mại tỷ lệ thuận với quy mô kinh tế của hai nước (GDP) và tỷ lệ nghịch với khoảng cách địa lý cùng các chi phí thương mại cản trở.
terms.seminal_citation: Tinbergen (1962); Anderson & van Wincoop (2003); Santos Silva & Tenreyro (2006)
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gravity Model of International Trade according to Tinbergen (1962), Anderson & van Wincoop (2003).
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Phương trình cấu trúc (Structural Gravity): X_ij = (Y_i · E_j / Y_w) · (t_ij / (P_i · P_j))^(1 - σ), trong đó P_i và P_j là các chỉ số kháng trở thương mại đa phương (Multilateral Resistance Terms - MRT). 2. Ước lượng chuẩn mực hiện đại (Silva & Tenreyro, 2006): Sử dụng mô hình Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood (PPML) với biến phụ thuộc dạng mức X_ij (xử lý triệt để giá trị thương mại bằng 0 và hiện tượng phương sai thay đổi trong hàm mũ) kết hợp hiệu ứng cố định nước xuất khẩu - thời gian và nước nhập khẩu - thời gian.
terms.benchmarks: Hệ số co giãn theo khoảng cách thông thường xấp xỉ -0.7 đến -1.1 (giảm ~1% kim ngạch trên mỗi 1% tăng khoảng cách). Hệ số co giãn theo quy mô kinh tế (GDP) xấp xỉ +0.8 đến +1.0. Ước lượng PPML là yêu cầu bắt buộc trên các tạp chí kinh tế quốc tế Q1 (AER, JIE) để thay thế hoàn toàn OLS log-tuyến tính truyền thống.
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: 'The Gold Standard Violations' (Baldwin & Taglioni, 2006): (1) Sai sót huy chương bạc: Bỏ qua biến kháng trở đa phương MRT (khắc phục bằng cặp Fixed Effects xuất khẩu/nhập khẩu); (2) Sai sót huy chương đồng: Loại bỏ các cặp quốc gia có kim ngạch bằng 0 do lấy logarit (khắc phục bằng PPML); (3) Đưa trực tiếp GDP vào mô hình khi đã có fixed effects xuất khẩu/nhập khẩu theo thời gian dẫn đến cộng tuyến hoàn hảo.
terms.apa_reference: Santos Silva, J. M. C., & Tenreyro, S. (2006). The log of gravity. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 88(4), 641–658. https://doi.org/10.1162/rest.88.4.641

terms.vietnamese: Hiệu chỉnh Epsilon Greenhouse-Geisser
terms.core_definition: The Greenhouse-Geisser Epsilon Correction, developed by Samuel Greenhouse and Jerome Geisser (1959), is an adjustment procedure for the degrees of freedom in Repeated Measures Analysis of Variance (RM-ANOVA) when the assumption of sphericity is violated. Sphericity requires that the variances of the differences between all possible pairs of repeated measures conditions are equal. When sphericity is violated, standard F-tests exhibit severely inflated Type I error rates. The Greenhouse-Geisser correction estimates an epsilon factor (hat{epsilon} <= 1) from the sample variance-covariance matrix and multiplies both numerator and denominator degrees of freedom by hat{epsilon}, adjusting critical values to maintain nominal alpha levels.
terms.seminal_citation: Greenhouse, S. W., & Geisser, S. (1959). On methods in the analysis of profile data. Psychometrika, 24(2), 95-112.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Greenhouse-Geisser Epsilon Correction according to Greenhouse & Geisser (1959).
terms.operational_mechanism: Given a sample covariance matrix S among k repeated measures: (1) Sphericity is assessed using Mauchly's test of sphericity; (2) If Mauchly's test is significant (p < 0.05), the Greenhouse-Geisser epsilon is computed as: hat{epsilon}_{GG} = [k^2 * (bar{s}_{ii} - bar{s}_{..})^2] / [ (k - 1) * (sum sum s_{ij}^2 - 2k sum bar{s}_{i.}^2 + k^2 bar{s}_{..}^2) ]; (3) The original degrees of freedom df_1 = k - 1 and df_2 = (k - 1)(N - 1) are adjusted to df_1^* = hat{epsilon} * df_1 and df_2^* = hat{epsilon} * df_2; (4) The F-ratio remains unchanged, but the p-value is recalculated using the lower adjusted degrees of freedom.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Given a sample covariance matrix S among k repeated measures: (1) Sphericity is assessed using Mauchly's test of sphericity; (2) If Mauchly's test is significant (p < 0.05), the Greenhouse-Geisser epsilon is computed as: hat{epsilon}_{GG} = [k^2 * (bar{s}_{ii} - bar{s}_{..})^2] / [ (k - 1) * (sum sum s_{ij}^2 - 2k sum bar{s}_{i.}^2 + k^2 bar{s}_{..}^2) ]; (3) The original degrees of freedom df_1 = k - 1 and df_2 = (k - 1)(N - 1) are adjusted to df_1^* = hat{epsilon} * df_1 and df_2^* = hat{epsilon} * df_2; (4) The F-ratio remains unchanged, but the p-value is recalculated using the lower adjusted degrees of freedom.
terms.benchmarks: Correction selection criteria: (1) Theoretical range of epsilon: 1 / (k - 1) <= hat{epsilon} <= 1.0 (where 1.0 represents perfect sphericity); (2) If hat{epsilon} > 0.75, Greenhouse-Geisser can be slightly conservative; Girden (1992) and Howell (2013) recommend using the Huynh-Feldt correction when hat{epsilon} > 0.75; (3) If hat{epsilon} < 0.75 or if Mauchly's test is significant with severe departure from sphericity, Greenhouse-Geisser is the mandatory standard.
terms.pitfalls: Common reporting errors: (1) Reporting uncorrected degrees of freedom and p-values after Mauchly's test has rejected sphericity (p < 0.05); (2) Applying the Huynh-Feldt correction when epsilon < 0.75, which fails to adequately protect against Type I error inflation; and (3) Failing to report the estimated epsilon value alongside adjusted degrees of freedom in APA format: F(df_1^*, df_2^*) = F_val, p = p_val, epsilon = hat{epsilon}_{GG}.
terms.apa_reference: Greenhouse, S. W., & Geisser, S. (1959). On methods in the analysis of profile data. Psychometrika, 24(2), 95–112. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02289823

terms.vietnamese: Sự bền bỉ: Đam mê và kiên trì
vietnamese_variants: Đam mê và nỗ lực trường kỳ
terms.core_definition: Grit is a non-cognitive psychological trait formulated by Angela Duckworth and colleagues (2007), defined as passion and perseverance for long-term, distal goals. Operating as a higher-order compound personality construct distinct from general cognitive ability (IQ) and talent, Grit entails working strenuously toward challenges, maintaining sustained effort and intense interest over years despite failure, adversity, plateaus in progress, and shifting environmental temptations. In empirical organizational behavior and educational psychology, it is measured as a two-dimensional construct comprising Consistency of Interest and Perseverance of Effort.
terms.seminal_citation: Duckworth, A. L., Peterson, C., Matthews, M. D., & Kelly, D. R. (2007). Grit: Perseverance and passion for long-term goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 92(6), 1087-1101.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Grit: Passion and Perseverance (Duckworth) according to Duckworth et al. (2007).
terms.operational_mechanism: Grit is quantitatively assessed using the Grit-O (12 items) or Short Grit Scale (Grit-S, 8 items) across two correlated first-order factors: (1) Consistency of Interest (e.g., 'I often set a goal but later choose to pursue a different one' - reverse coded), capturing long-term goal focus; and (2) Perseverance of Effort (e.g., 'Setbacks don't discourage me; I don't give up easily'), capturing resilience and stamina. Items are evaluated on a 5-point Likert scale. Psychometric validation involves second-order confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) or bifactor modeling to evaluate the general grit factor versus specific facet variance, alongside hierarchical regressions predicting achievement outcomes while controlling for Big Five Conscientiousness.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Grit is quantitatively assessed using the Grit-O (12 items) or Short Grit Scale (Grit-S, 8 items) across two correlated first-order factors: (1) Consistency of Interest (e.g., 'I often set a goal but later choose to pursue a different one' - reverse coded), capturing long-term goal focus; and (2) Perseverance of Effort (e.g., 'Setbacks don't discourage me; I don't give up easily'), capturing resilience and stamina. Items are evaluated on a 5-point Likert scale. Psychometric validation involves second-order confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) or bifactor modeling to evaluate the general grit factor versus specific facet variance, alongside hierarchical regressions predicting achievement outcomes while controlling for Big Five Conscientiousness.
terms.benchmarks: Psychometric standards: (1) Cronbach's alpha and Composite Reliability (rho_c) for Grit-S typically range between 0.73 and 0.84; (2) Factor loadings in CFA should exceed 0.50 (ideally >= 0.70); (3) Incremental validity: Grit must demonstrate statistically significant Delta R^2 in predicting objective retention, GPA, or sales performance after partialling out Conscientiousness and cognitive ability (Crede et al., 2017 meta-analysis indicates Perseverance of Effort drives the vast majority of predictive validity).
terms.pitfalls: Common methodological traps: (1) Jangle fallacy: Failing to establish discriminant validity between Grit and the Conscientiousness facet of industriousness (latent correlation often exceeds r = 0.80); (2) Aggregating Consistency of Interest and Perseverance of Effort into a single composite score when Perseverance accounts for nearly all criterion variance while Consistency exhibits weak or inconsistent criterion relations; and (3) Relying exclusively on self-report questionnaires vulnerable to social desirability and reference-group effects.
terms.apa_reference: Duckworth, A. L., Peterson, C., Matthews, M. D., & Kelly, D. R. (2007). Grit: Perseverance and passion for long-term goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 92(6), 1087–1101. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.92.6.1087

terms.vietnamese: Tư duy phát triển và tư duy cố định
vietnamese_variants: Thuyết ngầm định về trí tuệ
Mô hình tư duy Carol Dweck
terms.core_definition: The Growth Mindset vs. Fixed Mindset framework, originated by Carol Dweck (1999, 2006) as Implicit Theories of Intelligence, conceptualizes the fundamental lay beliefs individuals hold regarding the malleability of human capabilities. A Fixed Mindset (entity theory) posits that human attributes, intelligence, and creative talents are static, immutable traits that individuals either possess or lack. Conversely, a Growth Mindset (incremental theory) views human competence as dynamic qualities that can be cultivated and developed through effort, strategic adaptation, deliberate practice, and feedback.
terms.seminal_citation: Dweck, C. S. (1999). Self-theories: Their role in motivation, personality, and development. Psychology Press.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Growth Mindset vs. Fixed Mindset (Carol Dweck) according to Dweck (2006).
terms.operational_mechanism: Mindsets are measured using Dweck's Implicit Theories of Intelligence Scale (typically 3 to 8 Likert items, such as 'You have a certain amount of intelligence, and you can't really do much to change it'). High scores on entity statements indicate a fixed mindset, whereas disagreement or agreement with incremental statements indicates a growth mindset. In experimental designs, mindsets are manipulated via randomized brief socio-cognitive interventions (e.g., reading scientific articles on neuroplasticity versus control texts) to examine causal mediation chains: Mindset -> Goal Orientation (Learning vs. Performance) -> Attributional Style (Effort vs. Ability) -> Academic/Work Resilience.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Mindsets are measured using Dweck's Implicit Theories of Intelligence Scale (typically 3 to 8 Likert items, such as 'You have a certain amount of intelligence, and you can't really do much to change it'). High scores on entity statements indicate a fixed mindset, whereas disagreement or agreement with incremental statements indicates a growth mindset. In experimental designs, mindsets are manipulated via randomized brief socio-cognitive interventions (e.g., reading scientific articles on neuroplasticity versus control texts) to examine causal mediation chains: Mindset -> Goal Orientation (Learning vs. Performance) -> Attributional Style (Effort vs. Ability) -> Academic/Work Resilience.
terms.benchmarks: Measurement and intervention standards: (1) Scale reliability: Alpha >= 0.82; (2) In meta-analyses (Sisk et al., 2018; Yeager et al., 2019 in Nature), the average correlation between mindset and academic achievement is small (r approx 0.10), but targeted interventions yield meaningful effect sizes (d = 0.20 to 0.35) specifically among socioeconomically disadvantaged students and academically struggling populations.
terms.pitfalls: Common research pitfalls: (1) False mindset: Misrepresenting a growth mindset as merely praising effort rather than praising effective learning strategies and outcomes; (2) Overstating intervention effect sizes without pre-registering randomized controlled trials; and (3) Treating mindset as a rigid binary personality dichotomy rather than a context-dependent, domain-specific belief system (e.g., holding a growth mindset for math but a fixed mindset for leadership).
terms.apa_reference: Dweck, C. S. (1999). Self-theories: Their role in motivation, personality, and development. Psychology Press.

terms.vietnamese: Phương pháp lý thuyết nền tảng (Grounded Theory)
vietnamese_variants: Lý thuyết phát sinh từ thực địa
Nghiên cứu quy nạp Grounded Theory
terms.core_definition: Grounded Theory (GT) is a qualitative research methodology developed by Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss (1967) designed to construct substantive or formal theories inductively from systematic empirical data rather than testing deductive hypotheses derived from extant literature. Operating through simultaneous data collection and analysis, theoretical sampling, the constant comparative method, and theoretical saturation, Grounded Theory aims to generate conceptually dense explanations of psychosocial or organizational processes grounded directly in the lived experiences of social actors.
terms.seminal_citation: Glaser, B. G., & Strauss, A. L. (1967). The discovery of grounded theory: Strategies for qualitative research. Aldine Publishing Company.
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of GT according to Yêu cầu quy trình so sánh liên tục (Constant Comparative Method), lấy mẫu lý thuyết (Theoretical Sampling) và dừng lại khi đạt điểm bão hòa lý thuyết (Theoretical Saturation)..
terms.benchmarks: Evaluation criteria for Q1 publications: (1) Theoretical Saturation: Clear evidence that continued sampling yields no new conceptual properties or dimensional variations for the core category; (2) Theoretical Traceability: Complete audit trail linking raw field codes to the core category; (3) Paradigmatic consistency: Explicitly stating whether the study adheres to Glaserian emergent GT, Straussian coding paradigm, or Charmaz's constructivist GT.
terms.operational_mechanism: Core procedural stages across GT traditions (Glaserian classical, Straussian procedural, and Charmazian constructivist): (1) Theoretical Sampling: Selecting subsequent cases and participants based on emerging theoretical concepts rather than statistical representativeness; (2) Constant Comparative Method: Continuously comparing incidents with incidents, concepts with incidents, and concepts with concepts; (3) Three-phase coding: Initial/open coding (line-by-line fracture of data), focused/axial coding (linking categories with subcategories around causal conditions, context, strategies, and consequences), and theoretical/selective coding (identifying a single core category that integrates the entire theoretical scheme); (4) Memo-writing: Documenting analytical reflections throughout; and (5) Achieving Theoretical Saturation.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Core procedural stages across GT traditions (Glaserian classical, Straussian procedural, and Charmazian constructivist): (1) Theoretical Sampling: Selecting subsequent cases and participants based on emerging theoretical concepts rather than statistical representativeness; (2) Constant Comparative Method: Continuously comparing incidents with incidents, concepts with incidents, and concepts with concepts; (3) Three-phase coding: Initial/open coding (line-by-line fracture of data), focused/axial coding (linking categories with subcategories around causal conditions, context, strategies, and consequences), and theoretical/selective coding (identifying a single core category that integrates the entire theoretical scheme); (4) Memo-writing: Documenting analytical reflections throughout; and (5) Achieving Theoretical Saturation.
terms.pitfalls: Critical reviewer rejection traps: (1) Methodological slurrying—mixing contradictory philosophical tenets of Glaser (objectivist discovery) and Charmaz (constructivist co-creation) without epistemological justification; (2) Confusing basic thematic content analysis with Grounded Theory (GT requires theoretical sampling, constant comparison, and core category theorization, not merely descriptive theme listing); and (3) Conducting an extensive literature review before analysis in classical GT, causing premature theoretical preconception.
terms.apa_reference: Glaser, B. G., & Strauss, A. L. (1967). The discovery of grounded theory: Strategies for qualitative research. Aldine Publishing Company.

terms.vietnamese: Tác giả danh dự (Đứng tên biếu tặng / Khách mời)
terms.core_definition: Guest Authorship (interchangeably termed Honorary Authorship or Gift Authorship) is a pervasive form of academic publication malpractice wherein authorship credit is conferred upon individuals who have not made significant intellectual contributions to the research. Typically granted to department heads, senior laboratory directors, prominent scholars, or institutional benefactors out of deference, intimidation, academic patronage, or the strategic calculation that a recognized name will increase peer review acceptance probability, guest authorship severely violates international publication ethics and undermines academic accountability.
terms.seminal_citation: International Committee of Medical Journal Editors. (2023). Defining the role of authors and contributors (ICMJE Recommendations). ICMJE.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Guest Authorship (Honorary / Gift Authorship) according to ICMJE (2019).
terms.operational_mechanism: Guest authorship violates the foundational four-pillar authorship framework established by the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE): (1) Substantial contributions to conception/design or acquisition/analysis/interpretation of data; (2) Drafting or revising the manuscript critically; (3) Final approval of the version to be published; and (4) Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work. Non-contributing senior scholars who only provided laboratory space, departmental prestige, or general administrative oversight qualify solely for the Acknowledgments section, not the author byline.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Guest authorship violates the foundational four-pillar authorship framework established by the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE): (1) Substantial contributions to conception/design or acquisition/analysis/interpretation of data; (2) Drafting or revising the manuscript critically; (3) Final approval of the version to be published; and (4) Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work. Non-contributing senior scholars who only provided laboratory space, departmental prestige, or general administrative oversight qualify solely for the Acknowledgments section, not the author byline.
terms.benchmarks: Ethical compliance benchmarks: (1) Implementation of CRediT (Contributor Roles Taxonomy) matrices declaring each co-author's exact contribution across 14 discrete categories; (2) Zero-tolerance policies by COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics) and leading publishers (Elsevier, SpringerNature, Wiley); (3) Mandatory signed authorship declaration forms confirming that all authors meet all four ICMJE criteria.
terms.pitfalls: Consequences and risks: (1) Retraction of papers or formal correction notices removing unjustified authors; (2) Institutional ethics investigations for research misconduct; (3) Dilution of meritocratic academic promotion systems; and (4) Co-responsibility liability—guest authors remain legally and ethically accountable for fabricated data or plagiarized text in manuscripts they never reviewed.
terms.apa_reference: International Committee of Medical Journal Editors. (2023). Defining the role of authors and contributors. ICMJE. http://www.icmje.org/recommendations/browse/roles-and-responsibilities/defining-the-role-of-authors-and-contributors.html

terms.vietnamese: Hàm Gumbel Copula
terms.core_definition: The Gumbel Copula (also known as the Gumbel-Hougaard Copula) is an asymmetric Archimedean copula function specifically designed to model non-linear multivariate dependence structures characterized by strong upper tail dependence. Rooted in extreme value theory, the Gumbel copula captures phenomena where extreme positive co-movements (joint booms, simultaneous price surges, joint catastrophic claims) occur with substantially higher probability than joint negative extremes, making it a critical tool in financial risk management, actuarial science, and environmental hydrology.
terms.seminal_citation: Nelsen, R. B. (2006). An introduction to copulas (2nd ed.). Springer.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Gumbel Copula Function according to Gumbel (1960).
terms.operational_mechanism: For bivariate uniform marginal distributions u, v in [0, 1], the Gumbel copula is mathematically defined as: C_{theta}(u, v) = exp( - [ (-ln(u))^{theta} + (-ln(v))^{theta} ]^{1/theta} ), where theta in [1, infinity) is the copula parameter governing the strength of dependence. When theta = 1, the variables are completely independent: C(u, v) = u * v. As theta -> infinity, the copula approaches perfect co-monotonicity (Frechet-Hoeffding upper bound). Kendall's rank correlation tau is directly related to theta via: tau = 1 - 1/theta. The upper tail dependence coefficient is lambda_U = 2 - 2^{1/theta} > 0, while lower tail dependence is zero: lambda_L = 0.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: For bivariate uniform marginal distributions u, v in [0, 1], the Gumbel copula is mathematically defined as: C_{theta}(u, v) = exp( - [ (-ln(u))^{theta} + (-ln(v))^{theta} ]^{1/theta} ), where theta in [1, infinity) is the copula parameter governing the strength of dependence. When theta = 1, the variables are completely independent: C(u, v) = u * v. As theta -> infinity, the copula approaches perfect co-monotonicity (Frechet-Hoeffding upper bound). Kendall's rank correlation tau is directly related to theta via: tau = 1 - 1/theta. The upper tail dependence coefficient is lambda_U = 2 - 2^{1/theta} > 0, while lower tail dependence is zero: lambda_L = 0.
terms.benchmarks: Empirical parameter thresholds: (1) Dependence parameter theta >= 1.0; (2) Moderate dependence: theta approx 1.5 corresponds to Kendall's tau = 0.33 and lambda_U = 0.37; (3) Strong dependence: theta >= 2.0 corresponds to tau >= 0.50 and lambda_U >= 0.59; (4) Model selection: Evaluated against alternative copulas (Clayton, Frank, Student-t) using Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Cramér-von Mises goodness-of-fit tests.
terms.pitfalls: Common econometric errors: (1) Applying the standard Gumbel copula to model joint market crashes or downside financial contagion (which exhibit lower tail dependence; modeling joint crashes requires the Rotated/Survival Gumbel Copula or Clayton Copula); (2) Imposing the Gumbel copula without formally testing for asymmetric tail dependence; and (3) Violating the parameter restriction theta >= 1.0, leading to degenerate mathematical formulations.
terms.apa_reference: Nelsen, R. B. (2006). An introduction to copulas (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-28678-0

terms.vietnamese: Thang đo Guttman (Phân tích đồ thị tích lũy)
vietnamese_variants: Thang đo đơn hướng tất định
terms.core_definition: Thang đo Guttman (Guttman Scaling / Scalogram Analysis / Cumulative Scaling, do nhà xã hội học và thống kê học Louis Guttman phát minh năm 1944, 1950) là mô hình đo lường tất định (deterministic measurement model) tiên phong thiết lập nên khái niệm về Tính đơn hướng tuyệt đối (Perfect Unidimensionality) trong khoa học xã hội. Thang đo Guttman bao gồm một chuỗi các mục câu hỏi được sắp xếp theo trật tự thứ bậc tăng dần nghiêm ngặt về cường độ thái độ hoặc mức độ khó khăn. Cốt lõi của thang đo Guttman là Quy tắc Tích lũy Tất định (Cumulative Property): một người trả lời đồng ý (hoặc làm đúng) một câu hỏi ở một bậc cường độ nào đó thì bắt buộc phải đồng ý (hoặc làm đúng) với tất cả các câu hỏi ở các bậc thấp hơn trước đó. Do đó, chỉ cần biết duy nhất Tổng điểm số (Total Score) của một cá nhân, ta có thể tái tạo lại chính xác 100% chuỗi phản hồi cụ thể của người đó đối với từng câu hỏi mà không hề có sự mơ hồ.
terms.seminal_citation: Guttman, L. (1944). A basis for scaling qualitative data. American Sociological Review, 9(2), 139-150.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Guttman Scaling according to Guttman (1944).
terms.short_definition: Kỹ thuật thang đo tích lũy đơn hướng tất định trong đó việc đồng ý với một mục có độ khó cao ngụ ý việc đồng ý với tất cả các mục có độ khó thấp hơn.
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Thiết kế chuỗi phát biểu thứ bậc tích lũy: Xây dựng các câu hỏi nhị phân có cường độ tăng dần rõ rệt (ví dụ về khoảng cách xã hội Bogardus: 'Chấp nhận người nhập cư làm cư dân cùng quốc gia' → 'Cùng thành phố' → 'Cùng khu phố' → 'Làm bạn bè' → 'Kết hôn').
2. Xây dựng Ma trận Scalogram: Lập bảng nhị phân với các hàng là người trả lời (sắp xếp theo tổng điểm từ cao xuống thấp) và các cột là các câu hỏi (sắp xếp từ dễ/phổ biến đến khó/cực đoan từ trái qua phải).
3. Đếm số lượng lỗi lệch chuẩn (Counting Errors): Nhận diện các phản hồi vi phạm quy tắc tích lũy (ví dụ: người làm đúng câu khó bậc 4 nhưng lại làm sai câu dễ bậc 2).
4. Tính Hệ số Tái tạo (Coefficient of Reproducibility - CR):
 CR = 1 - (Tổng số lỗi (Total Errors))/(Tổng số phản hồi (Total Responses)) = 1 - (e)/(N × K),
 trong đó N là số người, K là số câu hỏi.
5. Tính Hệ số Khả năng Mở rộng (Coefficient of Scalability - CS của Menzel, 1953):
 Hiệu chỉnh CR trước nguy cơ điểm số cao giả tạo do phân phối biên cực đoan.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Hệ số Tái tạo Guttman (CR): Tiêu chuẩn vàng kinh điển đòi hỏi **CR ≥ 0.90** (nghĩa là số phản hồi lỗi không được vượt quá 10% tổng số ô ma trận) thì tập hợp câu hỏi mới được chính thức công nhận là một Thang đo Guttman hợp lệ.
2. Hệ số Khả năng Mở rộng Menzel (CS): Đòi hỏi **CS ≥ 0.60** để khẳng định thang đo thực sự có tính tích lũy vượt trội chứ không phải do sự chênh lệch ngẫu nhiên của các câu hỏi cực đoan.
3. Điểm số tối thiểu: Thang đo tích lũy Guttman thường yêu cầu tối thiểu từ 4 đến 6 mục câu hỏi có khoảng cách cường độ phân bổ đều đặn.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Bản chất tất định quá cứng nhắc (Deterministic Rigidity): Trong hành vi thực tế của con người, sự phân tâm ngẫu nhiên, mệt mỏi hoặc hiểu nhầm ngữ nghĩa luôn tạo ra các lỗi vi phạm tích lũy.
