terms.operational_mechanism: The ICER is calculated as the ratio of the difference in mean total costs to the difference in mean clinical consequences between two alternative strategies: ICER = (Cost_B - Cost_A) / (Effect_B - Effect_A) = Delta C / Delta E. The clinical effect Delta E is commonly expressed in natural units (e.g., life-years gained, LYG) or standardized utility metrics—Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALYs) or Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs). Uncertainty is quantified through non-parametric bootstrapping, Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curves (CEAC), and probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) plotted on the Cost-Effectiveness Plane across four quadrants.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: The ICER is calculated as the ratio of the difference in mean total costs to the difference in mean clinical consequences between two alternative strategies: ICER = (Cost_B - Cost_A) / (Effect_B - Effect_A) = Delta C / Delta E. The clinical effect Delta E is commonly expressed in natural units (e.g., life-years gained, LYG) or standardized utility metrics—Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALYs) or Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs). Uncertainty is quantified through non-parametric bootstrapping, Cost-Effectiveness Acceptability Curves (CEAC), and probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) plotted on the Cost-Effectiveness Plane across four quadrants.
terms.benchmarks: Willingness-to-Pay (WTP) threshold standards (lambda): (1) An intervention is deemed cost-effective if ICER <= lambda; (2) UK NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) threshold: £20,000 to £30,000 per QALY gained; (3) US informal threshold: $50,000 to $150,000 per QALY; (4) WHO-CHOICE macro benchmark: Highly cost-effective if ICER < 1x national GDP per capita; Cost-effective if 1x to 3x GDP per capita.
terms.pitfalls: Critical health economic traps: (1) Calculating average cost-effectiveness ratios (ACER = C/E) instead of incremental ratios (ICER = Delta C / Delta E), which distorts decision-making; (2) Misinterpreting negative ICERs without checking the cost-effectiveness quadrant (dominant: lower cost, higher effect; dominated: higher cost, lower effect); and (3) Failing to discount future costs and health gains at recommended discount rates (typically 3% to 5% annually).
terms.apa_reference: Drummond, M. F., Sculpher, M. J., Claxton, K., Stoddart, G. L., & Torrance, G. W. (2015). Methods for the economic evaluation of health care programmes (4th ed.). Oxford University Press.

terms.vietnamese: Chỉ số độ phù hợp gia tăng (IFI trong SEM)
terms.core_definition: The Incremental Fit Index (IFI, also designated Delta_2), developed by Kenneth A. Bollen (1989), is an incremental (comparative) goodness-of-fit index in Covariance-Based Structural Equation Modeling (CB-SEM). It assesses the relative improvement in fit of the hypothesized model compared against a baseline null (independence) model in which all observed variables are assumed to be mutually uncorrelated. Bollen formulated the IFI specifically to reduce the severe downward sample size bias characteristic of Bentler and Bonett's Normed Fit Index (NFI) in small and moderate samples.
terms.seminal_citation: Bollen, K. A. (1989). A new incremental fit index for general structural equation models. Sociological Methods & Research, 17(3), 303-316.
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Incremental Fit Index according to Giá trị IFI ≥ 0.90 biểu thị mô hình cấu trúc phù hợp tốt với dữ liệu khảo sát..
terms.benchmarks: Fit evaluation thresholds: (1) IFI >= 0.90 indicates acceptable model fit (classical threshold); (2) IFI >= 0.95 indicates superior/excellent model fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999 standard); (3) Comparative performance: IFI closely mirrors the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), serving as an effective cross-validation metric in CB-SEM reporting batteries.
terms.operational_mechanism: The mathematical formula for IFI is: IFI = (chi_{null}^2 - chi_{model}^2) / (chi_{null}^2 - df_{model}), where chi_{null}^2 and df_{null} are the chi-square statistic and degrees of freedom of the independence baseline model, and chi_{model}^2 and df_{model} correspond to the hypothesized model. Because the denominator adjusts for model degrees of freedom rather than df_{null}, the IFI incorporates a parsimony adjustment, making its expected value largely independent of sample size N. Values typically range between 0 and 1, though values slightly exceeding 1.0 can occasionally occur in over-fitting models.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: The mathematical formula for IFI is: IFI = (chi_{null}^2 - chi_{model}^2) / (chi_{null}^2 - df_{model}), where chi_{null}^2 and df_{null} are the chi-square statistic and degrees of freedom of the independence baseline model, and chi_{model}^2 and df_{model} correspond to the hypothesized model. Because the denominator adjusts for model degrees of freedom rather than df_{null}, the IFI incorporates a parsimony adjustment, making its expected value largely independent of sample size N. Values typically range between 0 and 1, though values slightly exceeding 1.0 can occasionally occur in over-fitting models.
terms.pitfalls: Common reporting errors: (1) Reporting IFI values greater than 1.0 without capping or explanation (values > 1 indicate an overparameterized model); (2) Relying solely on IFI without pairing it with absolute fit indices (RMSEA <= 0.06 and SRMR <= 0.08); and (3) Using IFI in models with small degrees of freedom where baseline chi-square is low.
terms.apa_reference: Bollen, K. A. (1989). A new incremental fit index for general structural equation models. Sociological Methods & Research, 17(3), 303–316. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124189017003004

terms.term: Incremental Validity (Hierarchical R-Squared Contribution - Hunsley & Meyer)
terms.vietnamese: Giá trị gia tăng / Khả năng giải thích phương sai vượt trội
vietnamese_variants: Đóng góp phương sai gia tăng
terms.core_definition: Incremental Validity (Giá trị gia tăng) là mức độ mà một công cụ đo lường mới có khả năng tăng cường độ chính xác dự báo hoặc giải thích thêm được một lượng phương sai có ý nghĩa thống kê của biến tiêu chí (ΔR²), vượt lên trên và độc lập với tất cả các công cụ đo lường và biến kiểm soát đã tồn tại trước đó (Hunsley & Meyer, 2003; Haynes & Lench, 2003). Giá trị gia tăng là 'bài thử nghiệm khắc nghiệt nhất' để chứng minh một thang đo mới thực sự có giá trị thực tiễn chứ không chỉ là sự lặp lại thừa thãi của những thang đo cũ.
terms.seminal_citation: Hunsley, J., & Meyer, G. J. (2003). The incremental validity of psychological testing and assessment: Conceptual, methodological, and statistical issues. Psychological Assessment, 15(4), 446-455; Haynes, S. N., & Lench, H. C. (2003). Incremental validity of new clinical assessment measures. Psychological Assessment, 15(4), 456-466.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Incremental Validity according to Hunsley & Meyer (2003).
terms.operational_mechanism: Quy trình Hồi quy thứ bậc (Hierarchical Multiple Regression): (1) Bước 1 (Model 1): Đưa toàn bộ các biến nhân khẩu học và các thang đo cạnh tranh hiện có (existing predictors) vào mô hình, ghi nhận R²_base; (2) Bước 2 (Model 2): Bổ sung công cụ đo lường mới vào mô hình; (3) Tính toán mức tăng phương sai: ΔR² = R²_model2 - R²_base; (4) Kiểm định F-test đối với ΔR²: F_change = [ΔR² / k] / [(1 - R²_model2) / (N - p - 1)]. Nếu p < 0.05, giá trị gia tăng được xác lập vững chắc.
benchmarks: Mức tăng phương sai có ý nghĩa thực tế: ΔR² ≥ 0.02 - 0.05 (giải thích thêm 2% đến 5% phương sai) thường được coi là đóng góp gia tăng có giá trị thực tiễn cao trong tâm lý học và hành vi tổ chức.
Hệ số hồi quy chuẩn hóa Beta: Biến mới phải có hệ số Beta có ý nghĩa thống kê (p < 0.01) sau khi đã kiểm soát toàn bộ các biến ở Bước 1.
Tỷ số chi phí - lợi ích (Cost-benefit ratio): Sự gia tăng độ chính xác dự báo phải đủ lớn để bù đắp cho thời gian và chi phí thu thập thêm công cụ mới.
pitfalls: Không kiểm soát các công cụ đo lường tiêu chuẩn: Tuyên bố thang đo mới dự báo tốt nhưng ở Bước 1 không hề kiểm soát các thang đo nổi tiếng nhất trong ngành.
Tăng R² nhỏ li ti không có ý nghĩa thực tiễn: Báo cáo ΔR² = 0.002 đạt p < 0.05 thuần túy do cỡ mẫu khổng lồ (N = 10,000) mà không có ý nghĩa thực tiễn.
Đa cộng tuyến nghiêm trọng giữa thang đo mới và thang đo cũ: Thang đo mới có VIF > 5.0 khi đứng cạnh thang đo cũ, làm sai lệch ước lượng hệ số.
terms.apa_reference: Hunsley, J., & Meyer, G. J. (2003). The incremental validity of psychological testing and assessment: Conceptual, methodological, and statistical issues. Psychological Assessment, 15(4), 446-455. https://doi.org/10.1037/1040-3590.15.4.446

terms.vietnamese: Kiểm định t cho hai mẫu độc lập
vietnamese_variants: Kiểm định t hai mẫu độc lập

terms.core_definition: Kiểm định t cho hai mẫu độc lập (Gosset/Student, 1908; Welch, 1947) là phép kiểm định thống kê tham số nền tảng nhất để so sánh giá trị trung bình của một biến định lượng liên tục giữa hai nhóm quan sát độc lập và loại trừ lẫn nhau (ví dụ: nhóm can thiệp vs. nhóm đối chứng; nam vs. nữ).
terms.seminal_citation: Student (1908); Welch (1947); Delacre et al. (2017)
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Independent Samples t-test according to Hair et al. (2018).
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Student's t-test truyền thống: Giả định phương sai hai nhóm bằng nhau (Homoscedasticity): t = (mean_1 - mean_2) / [s_p * √(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)], với s_p là phương sai gộp. 2. Welch's t-test (Satterthwaite approximation): Không đòi hỏi phương sai bằng nhau: t_w = (mean_1 - mean_2) / √(s²_1/n_1 + s²_2/n_2), với bậc tự do hiệu chỉnh Welch-Satterthwaite df_w. 3. Tính khoảng tin cậy 95% cho chênh lệch trung bình.
terms.benchmarks: Giả thuyết H0: mu_1 - mu_2 = 0. Bác bỏ H0 khi p-value < 0.05. Bắt buộc báo cáo Kích thước hiệu ứng Cohen's d (0.2: nhỏ, 0.5: vừa, 0.8: lớn). Chuẩn mực hiện đại (Delacre et al., 2017) khuyến nghị luôn mặc định sử dụng Welch's t-test thay vì Student's t-test vì Welch kiểm soát sai số loại I hoàn hảo trong mọi điều kiện phương sai.
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: Kiểm tra kiểm định Levene trước, nếu p > 0.05 thì dùng Student's t, nếu p < 0.05 mới dùng Welch (Quy trình hai bước - Conditional testing). Các nghiên cứu thống kê mô phỏng đã chứng minh quy trình hai bước này làm sai lệch tỷ lệ lỗi loại I; chuẩn mực quốc tế hiện nay là sử dụng Welch's t-test làm phương pháp mặc định duy nhất.
terms.apa_reference: Delacre, M., Lakens, D., & Leys, C. (2017). Why psychologists should by default use Welch's t-test instead of Student's t-test. International Review of Social Psychology, 30(1), 92–101. https://doi.org/10.5334/irsp.82

vietnamese_variants: So sánh biến độc lập và công cụ

terms.core_definition: Independent Variable vs. Instrumental Variable represents a pivotal structural demarcation in econometrics and causal inference regarding identification under endogeneity. An Independent Variable (X) is a regressor included in the structural equation to explain variation in the dependent variable (Y). If X is exogenous (Cov(X, epsilon) = 0), OLS yields consistent causal estimates. However, if X is endogenous (Cov(X, epsilon) != 0 due to omitted confounders, measurement error, or simultaneity), OLS is biased. An Instrumental Variable (Z) is an external variable that does not appear in the structural equation but serves as an exogenous lever to purge X of its endogeneity.
terms.seminal_citation: Angrist, J. D., Imbens, G. W., & Rubin, D. B. (1996). Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 91(434), 444-455.
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Independent Variable / Instrumental Variable according to Kiểm định F > 10 cho biến công cụ; phân biệt rõ biến độc lập thực nghiệm với biến đồng biến (covariate)..
terms.benchmarks: Diagnostic cutoffs: (1) First-stage F-statistic: F > 10 (Staiger & Stock) or F > 104.7 (Lee et al. 5% t-ratio bias); (2) Overidentifying restrictions test (Sargan-Hansen J test): p > 0.05 when instruments exceed endogenous regressors (failing to reject valid exogeneity); (3) Durbin-Wu-Hausman test: p < 0.05 confirming that IV is required because OLS is indeed inconsistent.
terms.operational_mechanism: An Instrumental Variable Z must satisfy two core structural identification assumptions: (1) Instrument Relevance (First-Stage condition): Z must be strongly correlated with the endogenous regressor X conditional on other covariates: Cov(Z, X) != 0 (empirically tested via first-stage F-statistic, threshold F > 10, or Lee et al., 2022 threshold F > 104.7); (2) Exclusion Restriction (Independence / Exogeneity condition): Z must affect outcome Y ONLY through its effect on X, possessing no direct link to Y and no correlation with the disturbance: Cov(Z, epsilon) = 0. Estimation is typically executed via Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) or GMM.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: An Instrumental Variable Z must satisfy two core structural identification assumptions: (1) Instrument Relevance (First-Stage condition): Z must be strongly correlated with the endogenous regressor X conditional on other covariates: Cov(Z, X) != 0 (empirically tested via first-stage F-statistic, threshold F > 10, or Lee et al., 2022 threshold F > 104.7); (2) Exclusion Restriction (Independence / Exogeneity condition): Z must affect outcome Y ONLY through its effect on X, possessing no direct link to Y and no correlation with the disturbance: Cov(Z, epsilon) = 0. Estimation is typically executed via Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) or GMM.
terms.pitfalls: Critical econometrics errors: (1) Weak instrument bias: When first-stage F < 10, 2SLS estimates are severely biased toward OLS and exhibit invalid standard errors; (2) Violating the exclusion restriction: Using an instrument that has a plausible direct causal channel to Y; and (3) Treating instruments as magical fixes without proving theoretical validity.
terms.apa_reference: Angrist, J. D., Imbens, G. W., & Rubin, D. B. (1996). Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 91(434), 444–455. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1996.10476902

terms.core_definition: Independent Variables (IVs, also termed Predictor, Explanatory, Treatment, or Exogenous Variables) are operational constructs or experimental stimuli manipulated, controlled, or selected by the researcher to determine their relationship to, effect on, or predictive power over one or more Dependent Variables (DVs). In experimental research, the IV represents the intervention whose levels are actively manipulated by the experimenter; in observational and econometric research, the IV represents an explanatory attribute whose statistical variation is hypothesized to drive changes in the outcome.
terms.seminal_citation: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Independent variables according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism: IV operationalization follows structural requirements: (1) Experimental Manipulation: Partitioning participants into distinct treatment arms versus control/placebo groups (e.g., dosage, framing); (2) Observational Scaling: Continuous (ratio/interval scales), categorical (dummy-coded {0, 1}), or ordinal; (3) Identification of Exogeneity: Assessing whether E[epsilon | X] = 0 (strict exogeneity) or whether the IV is subject to confounding; (4) Multicollinearity checking: Assessing tolerance (> 0.20) and Variance Inflation Factor (VIF < 5.0) among multiple independent variables in regression equations.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: IV operationalization follows structural requirements: (1) Experimental Manipulation: Partitioning participants into distinct treatment arms versus control/placebo groups (e.g., dosage, framing); (2) Observational Scaling: Continuous (ratio/interval scales), categorical (dummy-coded {0, 1}), or ordinal; (3) Identification of Exogeneity: Assessing whether E[epsilon | X] = 0 (strict exogeneity) or whether the IV is subject to confounding; (4) Multicollinearity checking: Assessing tolerance (> 0.20) and Variance Inflation Factor (VIF < 5.0) among multiple independent variables in regression equations.
terms.benchmarks: Methodological standards: (1) Construct validity of manipulation: Manipulation checks in experiments verifying that participants perceived the intended treatment levels (p < 0.01); (2) Measurement reliability: Cronbach's alpha >= 0.70 and AVE >= 0.50 for survey-based independent constructs; (3) Exogeneity justification: Detailed theoretical defense ruling out reverse causality and omitted confounders.
terms.pitfalls: Common research pitfalls: (1) Conflating statistical association with causal influence in cross-sectional observational models; (2) Common method variance: Measuring both IV and DV via identical self-report surveys at the same time point; and (3) Inadequate manipulation strength in laboratory experiments resulting in false negative null results.
terms.apa_reference: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.

terms.core_definition: Chỉ số trung gian bị điều tiết (Index of Moderated Mediation - Hayes, 2015) là kiểm định thống kê chính thức duy nhất kiểm tra xem hiệu ứng gián tiếp có thực sự là một hàm tuyến tính biến thiên theo biến điều tiết W hay không. Về mặt giải tích, chỉ số này chính là đạo hàm bậc nhất của tác động gián tiếp có điều kiện theo biến điều tiết W (d(omega) / dW).
terms.seminal_citation: Hayes (2015)
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #1278
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Index of Moderated Mediation according to Hayes (2015).
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Trong mô hình điều tiết tuyến tính đơn giản: Index = a_3 · b (với a_3 là hệ số tương tác X × W lên M, và b là hệ số từ M lên Y). 2. Ước lượng khoảng tin cậy phi đối xứng hiệu chỉnh chệch BCa Bootstrap (tối thiểu 5.000 đến 10.000 mẫu lặp) cho đại lượng tích số a_3 · b. 3. Không thể dùng kiểm định phân phối chuẩn thông thường (như Sobel hay Wald test) do tích số a_3 · b có phân phối phi chuẩn nghiêm trọng.
terms.benchmarks: Tiêu chuẩn vàng bắt buộc: Hiện tượng Trung gian bị điều tiết được khẳng định tồn tại có ý nghĩa thống kê khi và chỉ khi Khoảng tin cậy BCa Bootstrap 95% của Index of Moderated Mediation KHÔNG chứa giá trị 0 (ví dụ [0.034, 0.185]).
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: Báo cáo kết quả kiểm định điều tiết trên từng nhánh riêng biệt (a_3 có ý nghĩa VÀ b có ý nghĩa) rồi suy diễn kết luận mà không báo cáo Index of Moderated Mediation; các tạp chí quản trị hàng đầu (AMJ, JOM) sẽ yêu cầu bổ sung bảng chỉ số này.
terms.apa_reference: Hayes, A. F. (2015). An index and test of linear moderated mediation. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 50(1), 1–22. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2014.962683

terms.term: Index of Moderated Mediation Testing Protocol

terms.core_definition: Giao thức kiểm định chỉ số trung gian bị điều tiết Hayes (2015) là quy chuẩn thực hành phương pháp luận thay thế hoàn toàn cho các phương pháp phân mảnh cũ kỹ trước năm 2015 (như phương pháp kiểm định phân nhóm nhỏ Subgroup analysis hay kiểm định từng phần của Baron-Kenny). Giao thức cung cấp quy trình lượng hóa và báo cáo tác động gián tiếp có điều kiện một cách khoa học và chặt chẽ nhất.
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #1277; LaTeX thô; lộ tên file nội bộ
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Index of Moderated Mediation (Hayes 2015) according to Hayes (2022); Hayes (2022).
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Thiết lập mô hình hồi quy đa biến tích hợp trên macro PROCESS (Model 7, 8, 14, 21, 58, 59). 2. Trích xuất giá trị ước lượng điểm của Index. 3. Tạo 5.000 mẫu Bootstrap có hoàn lại để tạo phân phối mẫu thực nghiệm. 4. Xác định giới hạn dưới (Bootstrap Lower Level Confidence Interval - BootLLCI) và giới hạn trên (BootULCI). 5. Báo cáo bảng ma trận tác động gián tiếp kèm kết luận kiểm định Index.
terms.benchmarks: Áp dụng bắt buộc trong mọi bài báo nghiên cứu hành vi tổ chức, quản trị nhân lực và marketing xuất bản trên các tạp chí quốc tế Q1. Đạt chuẩn khi báo cáo đầy đủ: Ước lượng điểm, Sai số chuẩn Bootstrap (BootSE), BootLLCI và BootULCI.
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: Chia biến điều tiết liên tục W thành hai nhóm 'Cao' và 'Thấp' bằng phép chia đôi trung vị (Median Split) rồi chạy phân tích đa nhóm. Phép chia đôi trung vị làm vứt bỏ phương sai dữ liệu thực tế, giảm mạnh sức mạnh thống kê và bị coi là thực hành phương pháp luận lỗi thời.
terms.apa_reference: Hayes, A. F. (2015). An index and test of linear moderated mediation. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 50(1), 1–22. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2014.962683

terms.core_definition: Indication of Research Process (Methodological Transparency) is an overarching standard of scientific rigor requiring researchers to document, disclose, and substantiate every operational, analytical, and interpretive decision made throughout the research lifecycle. Across qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods paradigms, an explicit indication of the research process provides an exhaustive audit trail that enables independent scholars to reconstruct, evaluate, verify, and replicate the findings, guarding against confirmation bias, selective reporting, and opaque data practices.
terms.seminal_citation: Aguinis, H., Ramani, R. S., & Alabduljader, N. (2018). What you see is what you get? Enhancing methodological transparency in management research. Academy of Management Annals, 12(1), 83-110.
terms.expert_notes: Rác Markdown/bảng; mảnh trích
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Indication of Research Process according to Flick et al. (2004).
terms.operational_mechanism: Operationalizing process indication encompasses: (1) Sampling and Access Audit: Documenting response rates, attrition, participant recruitment protocols, and inclusion/exclusion criteria; (2) Data Preparation Audit: Transparent disclosure of outlier handling, data trimming, missing data imputation routines, and codebooks; (3) Qualitative Audit Trail: Maintaining raw transcripts, reflexive field memos, codebook evolution matrices, and member checking logs; (4) Quantitative Open Scripts: Providing push-button replication code (R, Python, Stata) deposited in open data archives (e.g., OSF, Dataverse).
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Operationalizing process indication encompasses: (1) Sampling and Access Audit: Documenting response rates, attrition, participant recruitment protocols, and inclusion/exclusion criteria; (2) Data Preparation Audit: Transparent disclosure of outlier handling, data trimming, missing data imputation routines, and codebooks; (3) Qualitative Audit Trail: Maintaining raw transcripts, reflexive field memos, codebook evolution matrices, and member checking logs; (4) Quantitative Open Scripts: Providing push-button replication code (R, Python, Stata) deposited in open data archives (e.g., OSF, Dataverse).
terms.benchmarks: Reporting standards in elite journals: (1) Adherence to disciplinary reporting guidelines: EQUATOR Network checklists (STROBE for observational studies, CONSORT for trials, PRISMA for reviews, COREQ/SRQR for qualitative research); (2) Open Science Framework (OSF) pre-registration badges; (3) Explicit disclosure of all exploratory and post-hoc modifications.
terms.pitfalls: Common methodological deficiencies: (1) The 'black box' method section: Summarizing complex data collection in a single vague paragraph; (2) Omitting data cleaning decisions, which prevents exact numerical replication; and (3) Post-hoc rationalization of methodological deviations.
terms.apa_reference: Aguinis, H., Ramani, R. S., & Alabduljader, N. (2018). What you see is what you get? Enhancing methodological transparency in management research. Academy of Management Annals, 12(1), 83–110. https://doi.org/10.5465/annals.2016.0011

terms.core_definition: Indicator Reliability is a fundamental metric in the evaluation of reflective measurement models in structural equation modeling (both PLS-SEM and CB-SEM). It represents the proportion of an individual manifest indicator's variance that is explained by its underlying latent construct, as opposed to measurement error. In standardized reflective models, indicator reliability is mathematically defined as the square of the indicator's standardized outer loading (loading^2), indicating whether the observed item functions as a dependable measure of the latent variable.
terms.seminal_citation: Hair, J. F., Hult, G. T. M., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2022). A primer on partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) (3rd ed.). SAGE Publications.
terms.expert_notes: LaTeX thô; lộ tên file nội bộ
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Indicator reliability according to Henseler et al. (2015); Henseler et al. (2015).
terms.operational_mechanism: Evaluation proceeds through sequential examination: (1) Standardized Outer Loadings (lambda_i): Obtained from the reflective measurement model; (2) Squaring the loading: Compute Indicator Reliability = lambda_i^2; (3) Item retention decisions: Items with loadings >= 0.708 (where 0.708^2 = 0.50) extract at least 50% of the indicator's variance and must be retained; items with loadings between 0.40 and 0.70 are considered for removal only if deletion increases Composite Reliability or Average Variance Extracted (AVE); items with loadings < 0.40 are permanently removed.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Evaluation proceeds through sequential examination: (1) Standardized Outer Loadings (lambda_i): Obtained from the reflective measurement model; (2) Squaring the loading: Compute Indicator Reliability = lambda_i^2; (3) Item retention decisions: Items with loadings >= 0.708 (where 0.708^2 = 0.50) extract at least 50% of the indicator's variance and must be retained; items with loadings between 0.40 and 0.70 are considered for removal only if deletion increases Composite Reliability or Average Variance Extracted (AVE); items with loadings < 0.40 are permanently removed.
terms.benchmarks: Evaluation thresholds (Hair et al., 2022): (1) Preferred benchmark: Outer loading lambda >= 0.708 (Indicator Reliability >= 0.500); (2) Minimum acceptable exploratory loading: lambda >= 0.60; (3) Elimination rule: Delete items with lambda < 0.40 immediately; (4) Impact on construct-level metrics: All retained indicators must collectively achieve Average Variance Extracted (AVE) >= 0.50.
terms.pitfalls: Common research mistakes: (1) Retaining items with extremely low loadings (lambda < 0.50) without realizing they depress the construct's AVE below 0.50; (2) Mechanically deleting items with loadings between 0.60 and 0.70 that are theoretically indispensable to content validity; and (3) Applying reflective indicator reliability rules to formative indicators (formative indicators are evaluated via outer weights and VIF, not outer loadings).
terms.apa_reference: Hair, J. F., Hult, G. T. M., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2022). A primer on partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) (3rd ed.). SAGE Publications.

terms.core_definition: An Indirect Mechanism Variable (interchangeably termed an Intervening Variable, Mediating Variable, or Causal Intermediate) is an endogenous operational construct that lies on the causal trajectory between an independent predictor variable (X) and a dependent outcome variable (Y). Rooted in Baron and Kenny's (1986) framework and modernized by Preacher and Hayes (2008), the indirect mechanism variable explains HOW or WHY a given predictor exerts an effect on the outcome, absorbing and transmitting the focal causal influence through indirect paths.
terms.seminal_citation: Preacher, K. J., & Hayes, A. F. (2008). Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects in multiple mediator models. Behavior Research Methods, 40(3), 879-891.
terms.expert_notes: Đã được biên tập và chuẩn hóa định nghĩa học thuật theo giáo trình kinh điển.
terms.core_definition_en: Rigorous scholarly definition of Indirect mechanism variable according to established research methodology literature.
terms.operational_mechanism: In structural and mediation models: (1) Path a represents the direct effect of predictor X on mediator M; (2) Path b represents the effect of mediator M on outcome Y controlling for X; (3) Indirect Effect is the product of paths: a * b; (4) Direct Effect is path c'; (5) Total Effect: c = c' + (a * b). Modern statistical inference tests the indirect effect a * b using non-parametric bootstrapping (typically 5,000 to 10,000 resamples) to generate bias-corrected confidence intervals, abandoning the underpowered Sobel test.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: In structural and mediation models: (1) Path a represents the direct effect of predictor X on mediator M; (2) Path b represents the effect of mediator M on outcome Y controlling for X; (3) Indirect Effect is the product of paths: a * b; (4) Direct Effect is path c'; (5) Total Effect: c = c' + (a * b). Modern statistical inference tests the indirect effect a * b using non-parametric bootstrapping (typically 5,000 to 10,000 resamples) to generate bias-corrected confidence intervals, abandoning the underpowered Sobel test.
terms.benchmarks: Mediation appraisal criteria: (1) Statistical significance: The 95% bootstrap confidence interval of the indirect effect (a * b) must not include zero; (2) Mediation classification (Zhao, Lynch, & Chen, 2010): (a) Complementary mediation: Both a*b and c' are significant and in the same direction; (b) Competitive mediation: a*b and c' are significant but in opposite directions; (c) Indirect-only (full) mediation: a*b is significant while c' is non-significant; (3) Variance Accounted For: VAF = (a * b) / c (VAF > 80% full mediation, 20% to 80% partial mediation).
terms.pitfalls: Critical methodological traps: (1) Relying on the outdated Baron & Kenny causal steps approach (which requires a significant total effect c, overlooking competitive mediation where c can be zero); (2) Inferring mediation from cross-sectional data without addressing reverse causality (M -> X or Y -> M); and (3) Violating the no-omitted-confounder assumption between M and Y.
terms.apa_reference: Preacher, K. J., & Hayes, A. F. (2008). Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects in multiple mediator models. Behavior Research Methods, 40(3), 879–891. https://doi.org/10.3758/BRM.40.3.879

terms.vietnamese: Dữ liệu cấp độ cá thể từng người tham gia
vietnamese_variants: Dữ liệu thô cấp bệnh nhân/cá thể
terms.core_definition: Dữ liệu cấp độ cá thể (Individual Participant Data - IPD - Stewart & Parmar, 1993; Riley et al., 2010) là tập hợp dữ liệu thô chi tiết ở cấp độ vi mô của từng cá nhân tham gia từ tất cả các nghiên cứu gốc độc lập, được nhóm tác giả tổng quan hệ thống thu thập lại trực tiếp từ các tác giả chính để tiến hành phân tích tổng hợp.
terms.seminal_citation: Stewart & Parmar (1993); Riley et al. (2010)
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Individual Participant Data according to Loại bỏ hoàn toàn thiên lệch sinh thái (Ecological fallacy) và cho phép phân tích tương tác điều tiết ở cấp độ cá thể chính xác 100%..
terms.benchmarks: Được công nhận là 'Tiêu chuẩn Vàng' (Gold Standard) cao nhất của y học thực chứng và kinh tế lượng thực nghiệm tổng hợp. Được báo cáo theo hướng dẫn mở rộng PRISMA-IPD.
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Khác biệt với Dữ liệu Tổng hợp (Aggregate Data - AD: chỉ trích xuất các con số trung bình và sai số từ bài báo đã xuất bản). 2. Ưu điểm vượt trội: (A) Làm sạch và chuẩn hóa lại các biến số theo cùng một định nghĩa thống nhất; (B) Xử lý dữ liệu khuyết thiếu nhất quán; (C) Phân tích chính xác tương tác ở cấp độ cá thể (Individual-level treatment-covariate interactions) mà không mắc bẫy Ngụy biện sinh thái (Ecological Fallacy).
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: Khó khăn cực lớn về tính khả thi hậu cần và chia sẻ dữ liệu; việc không thể thu thập được IPD từ 100% các nghiên cứu có thể tạo ra Thiên lệch sẵn có của dữ liệu (Data availability bias); bắt buộc phải so sánh đặc trưng của các nghiên cứu cung cấp được IPD với các nghiên cứu không cung cấp.
terms.apa_reference: Riley, R. D., Lambert, P. C., & Abo-Zaid, G. (2010). Meta-analysis of individual participant data: Rationale, conduct, and reporting. BMJ, 340, c221. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.c221

terms.vietnamese: Giao thức phân tích gộp dữ liệu cấp cá thể IPD
vietnamese_variants: Phân tích gộp một giai đoạn và hai giai đoạn
terms.core_definition: Giao thức phân tích gộp dữ liệu cấp cá thể (IPD Meta-Analysis Protocol - Debray et al., 2015) quy định quy chuẩn mô hình hóa thống kê dữ liệu đa cấp gộp từ nhiều thử nghiệm hoặc nghiên cứu đoàn hệ, phân chia thành hai phương pháp tiếp cận chính: Phương pháp Một giai đoạn (One-stage approach) và Phương pháp Hai giai đoạn (Two-stage approach).
terms.seminal_citation: Debray et al. (2015); Stewart & Clarke (1995)
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis (IPD) according to Riley et al. (2010).
terms.operational_mechanism: 1. Phương pháp Hai giai đoạn (Two-stage): Bước 1 phân tích riêng biệt dữ liệu IPD của từng nghiên cứu bằng mô hình hồi quy vi mô thích hợp; Bước 2 tổng hợp các kích thước hiệu ứng thu được bằng phân tích gộp truyền thống. 2. Phương pháp Một giai đoạn (One-stage): Gộp toàn bộ dữ liệu thô vào một tập dữ liệu đa cấp khổng lồ duy nhất và ước lượng bằng Mô hình Tuyến tính Hỗn hợp Đa cấp (Multilevel Mixed-Effects Model) với hệ số chặn hoặc hệ số góc ngẫu nhiên theo từng nghiên cứu. 3. Bóc tách hiệu ứng nội nghiên cứu (within-trial) và hiệu ứng giữa các nghiên cứu (across-trials).
terms.benchmarks: Phương pháp Một giai đoạn được ưu tiên tuyệt đối khi mô hình hóa các biến số thay đổi theo thời gian, phân tích sống sót phức tạp hoặc kiểm định tương tác điều tiết phi tuyến tính.
terms.pitfalls: Bẫy phản biện: Chạy mô hình gộp một giai đoạn như một hồi quy OLS gộp đơn giản (Pooled regression) mà không kiểm soát cấu trúc phân cụm theo nghiên cứu (Clustering by trial). Sai sót này vi phạm nghiêm trọng tính độc lập của quan sát và làm bóp méo sai số chuẩn.
terms.apa_reference: Debray, T. P., Moons, K. G., Abo-Zaid, G. M., Koffijberg, H., & Riley, R. D. (2015). Individual participant data in systematic reviews: A guide to individual participant data meta-analysis. In Evidence-based medical monitoring: From principles to practice (pp. 95–118).

terms.term: Inductive Category Development (Mayring Qualitative Content Analysis)
terms.vietnamese: Xây dựng danh mục phân tích quy nạp (Theo Philipp Mayring)
vietnamese_variants: Phát triển mã quy nạp Mayring
Phân tích nội dung định tính quy nạp
terms.core_definition: Inductive Category Development is a systematic, rule-guided qualitative text analysis procedure formulated by German methodologist Philipp Mayring (2000, 2014) in Qualitative Content Analysis (QCA). Distinct from purely open-ended grounded theory coding, Mayring's approach establishes explicit a priori selection criteria and levels of abstraction before inductively deriving analytical categories directly from raw text. This procedure bridges qualitative interpretive flexibility with quantitative procedural rigor, inter-coder reliability, and transparent rule-bound traceability.
terms.seminal_citation: Mayring, P. (2000). Qualitative content analysis. Forum Qualitative Sozialforschung / Forum: Qualitative Social Research, 1(2), Article 20.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Inductive category development according to Flick et al. (2004).
terms.operational_mechanism: Mayring's step-by-step inductive category model proceeds through seven distinct phases: (1) Formulating the research question and theoretical goal; (2) Determining the selection criterion and definition of the category domain; (3) Formulating the target level of abstraction; (4) Step-by-step textual examination: Line-by-line reading to reduce raw text into first-level paraphrases; (5) Category formation: Grouping identical or conceptually similar paraphrases into new categories or subsuming them under existing ones; (6) Formative check of categories: Reviewing and revising category definitions after analyzing approximately 10% to 50% of the material; (7) Final summative coding and computation of inter-coder agreement.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Mayring's step-by-step inductive category model proceeds through seven distinct phases: (1) Formulating the research question and theoretical goal; (2) Determining the selection criterion and definition of the category domain; (3) Formulating the target level of abstraction; (4) Step-by-step textual examination: Line-by-line reading to reduce raw text into first-level paraphrases; (5) Category formation: Grouping identical or conceptually similar paraphrases into new categories or subsuming them under existing ones; (6) Formative check of categories: Reviewing and revising category definitions after analyzing approximately 10% to 50% of the material; (7) Final summative coding and computation of inter-coder agreement.
terms.benchmarks: Methodological rigor standards: (1) Detailed Coding Agenda containing: Category label, clear definition, anchor examples (verbatim exemplar quotes), and explicit coding/exclusion rules; (2) Inter-coder reliability: Double-coding by independent raters achieving Cohen's kappa >= 0.75 or Krippendorff's alpha >= 0.80; (3) Audit trail documenting category merges and splits.
terms.pitfalls: Common research errors: (1) Shifting the level of abstraction erratically across different categories (mixing broad macro-themes with micro-details); (2) Failing to conduct the formative check halfway through the text, leading to code drift; and (3) Omitting anchor examples in the codebook.
terms.apa_reference: Mayring, P. (2000). Qualitative content analysis. Forum Qualitative Sozialforschung / Forum: Qualitative Social Research, 1(2), Article 20. https://doi.org/10.17169/fqs-1.2.1089

terms.vietnamese: Suy luận quy nạp (Logic quy nạp trong khoa học)
vietnamese_variants: Lập luận quy nạp từ thực nghiệm
terms.core_definition: Inductive Reasoning is a foundational mode of logical inference in which general propositions, empirical generalizations, or theoretical principles are derived from the observation of specific instances or empirical cases. Moving from the particular to the general, inductive reasoning is fundamentally 'ampliative'—the conclusion contains more empirical content than the premises. While induction is the engine of exploratory discovery and qualitative theory-building, it is logically probabilistic rather than truth-preserving: true empirical premises can never guarantee the absolute truth of an inductive conclusion (the classical Problem of Induction; David Hume, Karl Popper).
terms.seminal_citation: Hume, D. (1748). An enquiry concerning human understanding. A. Millar.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Inductive Reasoning according to Francis Bacon; Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism: Inductive workflow in empirical inquiry: (1) Observation: Gathering rich, contextualized empirical observations without imposing rigid a priori hypotheses; (2) Pattern recognition: Identifying recurring empirical regularities, linguistic themes, or behavioural covariations across cases; (3) Substantive theorizing: Synthesizing observed patterns into nascent theoretical categories and propositions; (4) Inductive generalization: Formulating a broader theoretical framework subject to subsequent deductive testing. In qualitative research, induction is operationalized through constant comparative coding and grounded theory.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Inductive workflow in empirical inquiry: (1) Observation: Gathering rich, contextualized empirical observations without imposing rigid a priori hypotheses; (2) Pattern recognition: Identifying recurring empirical regularities, linguistic themes, or behavioural covariations across cases; (3) Substantive theorizing: Synthesizing observed patterns into nascent theoretical categories and propositions; (4) Inductive generalization: Formulating a broader theoretical framework subject to subsequent deductive testing. In qualitative research, induction is operationalized through constant comparative coding and grounded theory.
terms.benchmarks: Epistemic criteria in inductive science: (1) Sample richness and theoretical saturation: Observations must be sufficiently deep and diverse to capture variations across the phenomenon; (2) Epistemic modesty: Acknowledging that inductive generalizations represent probabilistic hypotheses rather than definitive universal laws; (3) Negative case analysis: Actively searching for disconfirming instances.
terms.pitfalls: Critical philosophical and empirical traps: (1) The Black Swan fallacy: Believing that observing 1,000 white swans proves the law that 'all swans are white' (a single negative case refutes the universal generalization); (2) Naive inductivism—assuming observation can occur without any prior theoretical or cognitive frame (observation is always theory-laden); and (3) Claiming deductive certainty for inductive qualitative findings.
terms.apa_reference: Hume, D. (1748). An enquiry concerning human understanding. A. Millar.

terms.vietnamese: Mô hình giải thích quy nạp - thống kê (Carl Hempel)
vietnamese_variants: Mô hình giải thích thống kê I-S
Mô hình quy nạp thống kê
terms.core_definition: The Inductive-Statistical (I-S) Model is a foundational account of scientific explanation formulated by Carl G. Hempel (1965) within his broader 'Covering Law' framework. Complementing the Deductive-Nomological (D-N) model (which explains events deductively using deterministic universal laws), the I-S model explains individual events subsuming them under statistical or probabilistic laws. An I-S explanation shows that given certain initial antecedent conditions and a statistical law asserting a high probability of the outcome, the occurrence of the event was to be expected with high inductive probability.
terms.seminal_citation: Hempel, C. G. (1965). Aspects of scientific explanation and other essays in the philosophy of science. Free Press.
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #1290; rác Markdown/bảng; mảnh trích
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Inductive-Statistical (I-S) Model according to Hunt (2015).
terms.operational_mechanism: An I-S explanation is structured as an inductive argument: Explanans comprises (1) Statistical Law L: p(G | F) = r, where the probability of property G occurring given condition F is close to 1.0 (r approx 1); (2) Antecedent Fact C: Case a possesses property F (Fa); (3) Double horizontal line: Signifies inductive inference with probability r; Explanandum E: Case a possesses property G (Ga). To maintain logical coherence, Hempel imposed the 'Requirement of Maximal Specificity' (RMS), requiring that the statistical law must take into account all relevant available information regarding the reference class to prevent the problem of explanatory ambiguity.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: An I-S explanation is structured as an inductive argument: Explanans comprises (1) Statistical Law L: p(G | F) = r, where the probability of property G occurring given condition F is close to 1.0 (r approx 1); (2) Antecedent Fact C: Case a possesses property F (Fa); (3) Double horizontal line: Signifies inductive inference with probability r; Explanandum E: Case a possesses property G (Ga). To maintain logical coherence, Hempel imposed the 'Requirement of Maximal Specificity' (RMS), requiring that the statistical law must take into account all relevant available information regarding the reference class to prevent the problem of explanatory ambiguity.
terms.benchmarks: Epistemic appraisal criteria: (1) High inductive probability: r must be substantially greater than 0.5 (approximating 1.0); (2) Maximal specificity: Demonstrating that no narrower reference class exists with a significantly different probability; (3) Distinguished from statistical relevance models (Salmon's S-R model) which allow low-probability explanations.
terms.pitfalls: Common philosophical pitfalls: (1) Explanatory ambiguity: Contradictory inductive conclusions can be derived with equal probability if different reference classes are chosen; (2) Inability to explain rare or low-probability events (e.g., explaining why a patient contracted a rare disease that occurs in only 1% of exposed individuals); and (3) Conflating statistical correlation with authentic causal mechanisms.
terms.apa_reference: Hempel, C. G. (1965). Aspects of scientific explanation and other essays in the philosophy of science. Free Press.

terms.vietnamese: Mô hình quy nạp thống kê trong giải thích khoa học
vietnamese_variants: Giải thích khoa học quy nạp thống kê
terms.core_definition: The Inductive-Statistical Model (IS Model) is the probabilistic variant of the covering law theory of scientific explanation in philosophy of science (Hempel, 1962, 1965). Designed to extend scientific explanation into non-deterministic disciplines such as quantum mechanics, biology, psychology, economics, and sociology, the IS model conceptualizes an explanation as an inductive argument where the explanans provides strong inductive support—rather than deductive certainty—for the explanandum event, grounded in robust statistical regularities.
terms.seminal_citation: Hempel, C. G. (1962). Deductive-nomological vs. statistical explanation. In H. Feigl & G. Maxwell (Eds.), Scientific explanation, space, and time (pp. 122-169). University of Minnesota Press.
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #1289
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Inductive-Statistical Model (IS Model) according to Hempel (1965).
terms.operational_mechanism: The model operates through three core components: (1) Statistical generalization: Asserting that a certain percentage of entities sharing condition C exhibit outcome E; (2) Particular instantiation: Proving the focal entity meets condition C; (3) Probabilistic subsumption: Concluding the entity will exhibit E with probability p. In empirical social sciences, the IS model underpins probabilistic regression modeling and survival analysis, where covariates provide probabilistic inductive explanations for behavioral outcomes.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: The model operates through three core components: (1) Statistical generalization: Asserting that a certain percentage of entities sharing condition C exhibit outcome E; (2) Particular instantiation: Proving the focal entity meets condition C; (3) Probabilistic subsumption: Concluding the entity will exhibit E with probability p. In empirical social sciences, the IS model underpins probabilistic regression modeling and survival analysis, where covariates provide probabilistic inductive explanations for behavioral outcomes.
terms.benchmarks: Criteria for explanatory adequacy: (1) Robust empirical grounding: Statistical laws must be backed by replicated large-sample empirical studies (p < 0.001); (2) Inductive strength: The conditional probability must be sufficiently high to justify expectation; (3) Resilience against Simpson's Paradox across disaggregated subgroups.
terms.pitfalls: Common research errors: (1) Believing high statistical correlation alone constitutes a complete scientific explanation without identifying the underlying generative causal mechanism; (2) Violating the requirement of total evidence by omitting known confounders; and (3) Misinterpreting probabilistic statements as deterministic rules.
terms.apa_reference: Hempel, C. G. (1962). Deductive-nomological vs. statistical explanation. In H. Feigl & G. Maxwell (Eds.), Scientific explanation, space, and time (pp. 122–169). University of Minnesota Press.

terms.vietnamese: Phản hồi từ người cung cấp thông tin (Kiểm tra chéo với đối tượng nghiên cứu)
vietnamese_variants: Kỹ thuật kiểm tra thành viên member checking
Lấy ý kiến phản hồi người tham gia
terms.core_definition: Informant Feedback (widely known as Member Checking, Respondent Validation, or Member Validation) is a premier methodological strategy in qualitative inquiry formulated by Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba (1985) to establish credibility (the qualitative analogue to internal validity). It involves returning preliminary findings, interview transcripts, synthesized analytical summaries, or emerging theoretical models to research participants (informants) for review, critique, verification, and commentary, determining whether the researcher's reconstructions accurately reflect their lived experiences.
terms.seminal_citation: Lincoln, Y. S., & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic inquiry. SAGE Publications.
terms.expert_notes: Đã được biên tập và chuẩn hóa định nghĩa học thuật theo giáo trình kinh điển.
terms.core_definition_en: Rigorous scholarly definition of Informant feedback according to established research methodology literature.
terms.operational_mechanism: Member checking is operationalized across three procedural levels: (1) Transcript Checking: Returning raw audio transcripts to participants to correct factual errors and verify quotation permissions; (2) Synthesized Member Checking: Providing participants with executive summaries of emerging themes and category frameworks; (3) Theoretical Member Checking: Sharing the draft conceptual model or process diagram to evaluate whether participants recognize their organizational reality in the theoretical abstraction. All participant corrections, affirmations, and disagreements are logged in a structured Member Checking Audit Table.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Member checking is operationalized across three procedural levels: (1) Transcript Checking: Returning raw audio transcripts to participants to correct factual errors and verify quotation permissions; (2) Synthesized Member Checking: Providing participants with executive summaries of emerging themes and category frameworks; (3) Theoretical Member Checking: Sharing the draft conceptual model or process diagram to evaluate whether participants recognize their organizational reality in the theoretical abstraction. All participant corrections, affirmations, and disagreements are logged in a structured Member Checking Audit Table.
terms.benchmarks: Credibility benchmarks (Lincoln & Guba; Morse): (1) Explicit documentation: Reporting the exact proportion of participants who reviewed materials (e.g., '18 of 22 interviewees provided formal feedback'); (2) Transparent audit trail: Detailing specific modifications made to the analysis based on informant critique; (3) Handling divergent feedback: Documenting how disagreements between participants were analyzed without suppressing dissenting voices.
terms.pitfalls: Common qualitative pitfalls: (1) Treating member checking as a simplistic positivist 'truth test' (participants may change their views over time or reject unflattering truths about their organizational behavior); (2) Dumping lengthy 80-page draft chapters onto participants, resulting in superficial acquiescence; and (3) Violating participant confidentiality by revealing comments made by other organizational members during group feedback sessions.
terms.apa_reference: Lincoln, Y. S., & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic inquiry. SAGE Publications. https://doi.org/10.1016/0147-1767(85)90062-8

terms.vietnamese: Sự dư thừa thông tin (Ngưỡng bão hòa Lincoln & Guba)
terms.core_definition: Informational Redundancy is the operational criterion for terminating qualitative data collection introduced by Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba (1985) in 'Naturalistic Inquiry'. Serving as the naturalistic counterpart to Glaser and Strauss's theoretical saturation, informational redundancy occurs when the researcher discovers that newly sampled participants or observational events yield no substantially new information, perspectives, or contextual insights, but merely repeat, corroborate, and reinforce previously gathered data.
terms.seminal_citation: Lincoln, Y. S., & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic inquiry. SAGE Publications.
terms.expert_notes: Đã được biên tập và chuẩn hóa định nghĩa học thuật theo giáo trình kinh điển.
terms.core_definition_en: Rigorous scholarly definition of Informational redundancy according to established research methodology literature.
terms.operational_mechanism: Operationalizing informational redundancy involves: (1) Concurrent sampling and analysis: Analyzing data immediately after each interview or fieldwork encounter; (2) Saturation tracking grid: Creating a cumulative matrix where newly collected transcripts are cross-checked against established conceptual codes; (3) Redundancy threshold: When 3 to 5 consecutive comprehensive interviews generate zero new conceptual codes or unique situational properties, informational redundancy is declared; (4) Stopping data collection based on empirical saturation rather than arbitrary pre-determined sample size quotas.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Operationalizing informational redundancy involves: (1) Concurrent sampling and analysis: Analyzing data immediately after each interview or fieldwork encounter; (2) Saturation tracking grid: Creating a cumulative matrix where newly collected transcripts are cross-checked against established conceptual codes; (3) Redundancy threshold: When 3 to 5 consecutive comprehensive interviews generate zero new conceptual codes or unique situational properties, informational redundancy is declared; (4) Stopping data collection based on empirical saturation rather than arbitrary pre-determined sample size quotas.
terms.benchmarks: Evaluation standards in top-tier qualitative publishing (Guest et al., 2006; Hennink & Kaiser, 2022): (1) Code saturation typically occurs within 9 to 12 in-depth interviews in homogeneous study populations; (2) Meaning saturation (understanding the full nuance and boundaries of codes) requires 16 to 24 interviews; (3) Manuscript reporting must document the trajectory of saturation (e.g., 'No new codes emerged after interview 14; 4 additional interviews were conducted to confirm redundancy').
terms.pitfalls: Common reviewer critique traps: (1) Claiming 'data saturation was achieved' without providing a saturation graph, code emergence curve, or comparative matrix; (2) Conflating sample size with informational richness (10 richly probed interviews often provide greater redundancy than 40 superficial surveys); and (3) Halting data collection prematurely after only seeing repetition in a single narrow demographic subgroup.
terms.apa_reference: Lincoln, Y. S., & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic inquiry. SAGE Publications. https://doi.org/10.1016/0147-1767(85)90062-8

terms.vietnamese: Sự đồng thuận có hiểu biết (Đạo đức nghiên cứu và Báo cáo Belmont)
vietnamese_variants: Sự đồng ý tham gia nghiên cứu
Đồng thuận tự nguyện có nhận thức
terms.core_definition: Informed Consent is the cornerstone ethical doctrine and legal mandate governing all research involving human participants, formalized in the Nuremberg Code (1947), Declaration of Helsinki (1964), and the Belmont Report (1979). Rooted in the ethical principle of Respect for Persons (Autonomy), informed consent ensures that individuals enter research voluntarily, with adequate comprehension of the study's purpose, experimental procedures, potential risks, anticipated benefits, alternative options, and with the explicit right to withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of entitled benefits.
terms.seminal_citation: National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research. (1979). The Belmont Report: Ethical principles and guidelines for the protection of human subjects of research. U.S. Government Printing Office.
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #1296
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Informed Consent according to Nuremberg Code; Belmont Report.
terms.operational_mechanism: Informed consent requires the simultaneous satisfaction of three core elements: (1) Information: Full disclosure of research aims, sponsorship, risks (physical, psychological, social, legal), data privacy safeguards, and conflict of interest; (2) Comprehension: Delivering information in clear, non-technical language tailored to the participant's educational and cultural background (typically 8th-grade reading level); (3) Voluntariness: Total absence of coercion, excessive financial inducement, or undue influence from authority figures. Documented via formal signed consent, audio-recorded oral consent, or electronic click-through consent.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Informed consent requires the simultaneous satisfaction of three core elements: (1) Information: Full disclosure of research aims, sponsorship, risks (physical, psychological, social, legal), data privacy safeguards, and conflict of interest; (2) Comprehension: Delivering information in clear, non-technical language tailored to the participant's educational and cultural background (typically 8th-grade reading level); (3) Voluntariness: Total absence of coercion, excessive financial inducement, or undue influence from authority figures. Documented via formal signed consent, audio-recorded oral consent, or electronic click-through consent.
terms.benchmarks: Institutional Review Board (IRB) compliance benchmarks: (1) Explicit declaration of right to withdraw without repercussion; (2) Special protections and assent protocols for vulnerable populations (minors, prisoners, cognitively impaired, pregnant women); (3) De-identification and data storage protocols specified in compliance with GDPR, HIPAA, and institutional ethics guidelines.
terms.pitfalls: Critical ethical violations: (1) Coercive recruitment: Offering excessive financial compensation to impoverished participants that impairs their rational assessment of physical risks (undue inducement); (2) Concealing research risks or commercial conflicts of interest; (3) Using dense, legalistic jargon that participants cannot comprehend; and (4) Conducting covert research without prior IRB waiver of consent.
terms.apa_reference: National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research. (1979). The Belmont Report: Ethical principles and guidelines for the protection of human subjects of research. U.S. Government Printing Office.

terms.vietnamese: Tài liệu đồng thuận có hiểu biết (Mẫu phiếu và quy trình chấp thuận)
vietnamese_variants: Phiếu chấp thuận tham gia nghiên cứu
terms.core_definition: Informed Consent Documentation refers to the formal written instruments, consent forms, participant information sheets, and assent agreements approved by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or Research Ethics Committee (REC). Functioning as a legal and ethical record, these documents operationalize human subject protections by providing potential participants with an unambiguous, written account of the research parameters before they make a voluntary decision to participate.
terms.seminal_citation: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. (2018). Federal policy for the protection of human subjects ('Common Rule'). 45 CFR 46.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Informed consent forms according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism: A standard IRB-compliant consent form must incorporate ten mandatory structural sections: (1) Title and Principal Investigator contact information; (2) Statement that the study involves research and expected duration; (3) Purpose of the research; (4) Detailed description of procedures to be followed; (5) Foreseeable risks or discomforts; (6) Reasonably expected benefits to participant or society; (7) Appropriate alternative procedures or treatments; (8) Confidentiality and data security provisions; (9) Compensation and injury treatment policies; and (10) Explicit contact information for both the researcher and the independent institutional ethics board.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: A standard IRB-compliant consent form must incorporate ten mandatory structural sections: (1) Title and Principal Investigator contact information; (2) Statement that the study involves research and expected duration; (3) Purpose of the research; (4) Detailed description of procedures to be followed; (5) Foreseeable risks or discomforts; (6) Reasonably expected benefits to participant or society; (7) Appropriate alternative procedures or treatments; (8) Confidentiality and data security provisions; (9) Compensation and injury treatment policies; and (10) Explicit contact information for both the researcher and the independent institutional ethics board.
terms.benchmarks: Documentation standards: (1) Readability score: Flesch-Kincaid reading grade level <= 8.0; (2) Secure archiving: Signed consent forms must be stored securely (locked cabinet or encrypted server) for a minimum of 3 to 7 years post-study completion as mandated by federal regulations; (3) Assent forms: Required for children aged 7 to 17 alongside formal parental permission.
terms.pitfalls: Common compliance errors: (1) Modifying study procedures or questionnaires without submitting a formal protocol amendment to the IRB; (2) Storing signed consent forms containing participant names in the same folder as raw de-identified survey data, destroying anonymity; and (3) Presenting consent forms as legal liability waivers relieving the institution of negligence.
terms.apa_reference: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. (2018). Federal policy for the protection of human subjects ('Common Rule'). Code of Federal Regulations, Title 45, Part 46.

terms.vietnamese: Quy trình thực thi đồng thuận có hiểu biết
vietnamese_variants: Quy trình lấy ý kiến đồng thuận
Tiến trình đồng thuận liên tục
terms.core_definition: The Informed Consent Process emphasizes that informed consent is an ongoing, dynamic educational dialogue and ethical relationship between researcher and participant, rather than a single, transactional event of signing a form. Particularly in longitudinal studies, clinical trials, and ethnographic fieldwork, the consent process requires continuous reaffirmation, clear communication of newly emergent risks or findings, and active monitoring to ensure participant autonomy is respected throughout the entire research trajectory.
terms.seminal_citation: Beauchamp, T. L., & Childress, J. F. (2019). Principles of biomedical ethics (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Informed Consent Process according to Faden & Beauchamp (1986).
terms.operational_mechanism: The dynamic process encompasses four operational phases: (1) Pre-recruitment dialogue: Introducing the study and providing ample time for participants to consult family or physicians; (2) Enrollment: Clarifying questions and securing initial written consent; (3) Process Consent (Ongoing Consent): Reaffirming consent at each subsequent data collection wave, especially when sensitive personal events occur in longitudinal panels; (4) Post-study debriefing: Providing full disclosure in studies involving approved deception, offering psychological counseling support, and sharing synthesized findings.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: The dynamic process encompasses four operational phases: (1) Pre-recruitment dialogue: Introducing the study and providing ample time for participants to consult family or physicians; (2) Enrollment: Clarifying questions and securing initial written consent; (3) Process Consent (Ongoing Consent): Reaffirming consent at each subsequent data collection wave, especially when sensitive personal events occur in longitudinal panels; (4) Post-study debriefing: Providing full disclosure in studies involving approved deception, offering psychological counseling support, and sharing synthesized findings.
terms.benchmarks: Process rigor indicators: (1) Re-consent protocols: Mandatory re-consenting when study protocols, drug formulations, or risk profiles are updated; (2) Comprehension verification: Using 'teach-back' questions to ensure participants with cognitive or language barriers genuinely understand procedures; (3) Explicit documentation of oral check-ins in qualitative field notes.
terms.pitfalls: Common ethical failures: (1) Treating consent as a 'one-and-done' legal checkbox, ignoring participant discomfort during traumatic qualitative interviews; (2) Inadequate debriefing after experimental deception studies; and (3) Failing to re-consent adolescent participants when they turn 18 and attain adult legal status in longitudinal cohort studies.
terms.apa_reference: Beauchamp, T. L., & Childress, J. F. (2019). Principles of biomedical ethics (8th ed.). Oxford University Press.

terms.core_definition: Inside-Outside Legitimation is a premier mixed methods validity type formulated by Anthony J. Onwuegbuzie and R. Burke Johnson (2006) in their seminal mixed methods legitimation typology. It evaluates the extent to which a mixed methods researcher accurately captures, balances, and synthesizes both the 'insider' (emic, subjective, participant-lived viewpoint) and the 'outsider' (etic, objective, researcher-theoretical lens). A study achieving high inside-outside legitimation presents a nuanced integration where participant meanings are authentically respected while being rigorously analyzed through objective scientific frameworks.
terms.seminal_citation: Onwuegbuzie, A. J., & Johnson, R. B. (2006). The validity issue in mixed research. Research in the Schools, 13(1), 48-63.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Inside-Outside Legitimation according to Onwuegbuzie & Johnson (2006).
terms.operational_mechanism: Achieving inside-outside legitimation requires structured methodological integration: (1) Emic Immersion: Collecting rich qualitative data (interviews, fieldnotes) that preserves participant voice, cultural idioms, and subjective meanings; (2) Etic Discipline: Implementing rigorous quantitative measurement, validated psychometric scales, and standardized econometric models; (3) Dialectical Synthesis: Using joint displays to directly compare emic participant narratives against etic statistical parameters, identifying convergence, dissonance, or expansion; (4) Peer debriefing and member checking to verify emic fidelity.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: Achieving inside-outside legitimation requires structured methodological integration: (1) Emic Immersion: Collecting rich qualitative data (interviews, fieldnotes) that preserves participant voice, cultural idioms, and subjective meanings; (2) Etic Discipline: Implementing rigorous quantitative measurement, validated psychometric scales, and standardized econometric models; (3) Dialectical Synthesis: Using joint displays to directly compare emic participant narratives against etic statistical parameters, identifying convergence, dissonance, or expansion; (4) Peer debriefing and member checking to verify emic fidelity.
terms.benchmarks: Legitimation benchmarks (Onwuegbuzie & Johnson): (1) Balanced presentation in findings: Equal analytical fidelity to qualitative narrative voices and quantitative statistical indices; (2) Reflexivity audit: Transparent disclosure of researcher positionality and cultural distance from participants; (3) Absence of interpretive imperialism (forcing emic qualitative findings into rigid etic survey categories).
terms.pitfalls: Common mixed methods traps: (1) Etic imperialism: Subordinating qualitative participant narratives into mere decorative quotes to substantiate pre-existing quantitative hypotheses; (2) Emic romanticism: Uncritically reporting participant claims without subjecting them to etic statistical verification; and (3) Failing to address discrepancies when emic experiences contradict etic statistical trends.
terms.apa_reference: Onwuegbuzie, A. J., & Johnson, R. B. (2006). The validity issue in mixed research. Research in the Schools, 13(1), 48–63.

terms.vietnamese: Dân tộc học thể chế (Dorothy Smith)
vietnamese_variants: Phương pháp dân tộc học thể chế
Xã hội học vì con người Dorothy Smith
terms.core_definition: Institutional Ethnography (IE) is an alternative sociological and qualitative research methodology founded by feminist sociologist Dorothy E. Smith (1987, 2005). Conceived as a 'sociology for people' rather than a 'sociology about people', IE begins from the actual, everyday lived experiences and standpoint of marginalized or frontline individuals (e.g., nurses, single mothers, social workers) to explore and map how their local everyday activities are coordinated, mediated, and ruled by translocal institutional relations, bureaucratic discourses, and standardized texts.
terms.seminal_citation: Smith, D. E. (2005). Institutional ethnography: A sociology for people. AltaMira Press.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Institutional Ethnography (Dorothy Smith) according to Smith (2005).
terms.operational_mechanism: IE proceeds through a distinct reflexive research trajectory: (1) Identifying the Standpoint: Anchoring the research in the embodied experience of specific frontline workers or service users; (2) Everyday Work Analysis: Examining what people actually do (treating 'work' broadly as any intentional activity requiring effort, time, and skill); (3) Textual Analysis: Investigating the 'ruling relations'—how bureaucratic forms, standardized clinical rubrics, electronic medical records, and policy documents coordinate local work with translocal corporate or state power; (4) Institutional Mapping: Mapping how local problems are structurally produced by institutional mandates.
terms.operational_mechanism_en: IE proceeds through a distinct reflexive research trajectory: (1) Identifying the Standpoint: Anchoring the research in the embodied experience of specific frontline workers or service users; (2) Everyday Work Analysis: Examining what people actually do (treating 'work' broadly as any intentional activity requiring effort, time, and skill); (3) Textual Analysis: Investigating the 'ruling relations'—how bureaucratic forms, standardized clinical rubrics, electronic medical records, and policy documents coordinate local work with translocal corporate or state power; (4) Institutional Mapping: Mapping how local problems are structurally produced by institutional mandates.
terms.benchmarks: Rigor criteria in institutional ethnography: (1) Preservation of the standpoint: The analysis must continuously serve as an exploratory resource for the individuals studied, rather than converting them into institutional objects of study; (2) Text-work-text sequences: Explicit empirical tracing of how texts enter and transform frontline work practices; (3) Translocal mapping: Demonstrating the organizational links connecting local sites to distant policymaking apparatuses.
terms.pitfalls: Common research misapplications: (1) Treating IE as conventional organizational ethnography (IE does not study an organization as a bounded container; it investigates translocal ruling relations that cut across institutions); (2) Converting participant accounts into abstract theoretical jargon, violating the core commitment to everyday language; and (3) Ignoring the active agency of institutional texts.
terms.apa_reference: Smith, D. E. (2005). Institutional ethnography: A sociology for people. AltaMira Press.
