When persistent empirical Anomalies accumulate that resist resolution within the reigning paradigm, the discipline enters a period of Crisis, which culminates in Revolutionary Science—the non-cumulative, paradigm-shifting transformation wherein the scientific community abandons the old paradigm in favor of an incommensurable new disciplinary matrix.
terms.seminal_citation: Kuhn, T. S. (1962). The structure of scientific revolutions. University of Chicago Press.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Normal Science vs. Revolutionary Science according to Kuhn (1962).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. The Kuhnian Evolutionary Cycle:
   - Phase 1 (Pre-Paradigmatic Stage): Disorganized, competing schools of thought with no consensus on foundational facts.
   - Phase 2 (Normal Science): Emergence of a dominant paradigm; scientists engage in 'puzzle-solving', articulating and extending theoretical predictions without challenging foundational axioms.
   - Phase 3 (Anomaly & Crisis): Persistent empirical anomalies accumulate that contradict core paradigm predictions and resist ad-hoc patching.
   - Phase 4 (Revolutionary Science): Disciplinary crisis prompts radical theoretical exploration; competing paradigms emerge.
   - Phase 5 (Paradigm Shift / New Normal Science): The community converts to a new paradigm (e.g., Newtonian physics -> Einsteinian relativity; behaviorism -> cognitive psychology); the cycle restarts.
2. Thesis Defense Implication: Grounding a dissertation means establishing whether the proposed contribution is an articulation of Normal Science (solving a puzzle within an established theory) or a Revolutionary challenge questioning foundational axioms.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Incommensurability Thesis: Competing paradigms cannot be directly compared via a single neutral observation language because their concepts, vocabularies, and standards of evidence are fundamentally different.
2. Puzzle-Solving Rigor: In normal science, failure to solve a puzzle reflects upon the competence of the researcher, not the validity of the paradigm.
3. Theory Selection Criteria (Kuhn, 1977): Five standard values for evaluating rival paradigms: Accuracy, Consistency, Scope, Simplicity, and Fruitfulness.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Claiming a 'Paradigm Shift' for Trivial Studies: Labeling minor empirical variations or modest survey papers as a 'revolutionary paradigm shift', inviting severe reviewer cynicism.
2. Relativistic Misinterpretation: Assuming Kuhn meant science is purely arbitrary mob psychology; Kuhn defended science as a rational, socially organized enterprise governed by shared scientific values.
3. Paradigm Incommensurability Dogmatism: Using incommensurability as an excuse to avoid empirical debate with rival theoretical perspectives.
terms.apa_reference: Kuhn, T. S. (1962). The structure of scientific revolutions. University of Chicago Press. (4th ed., 2012, University of Chicago Press).

terms.vietnamese: Lý thuyết quá trình chuẩn hóa (NPT - Carl May & Tracy Finch)
vietnamese_variants: Lý thuyết bình thường hóa quy trình
terms.core_definition: Normalisation Process Theory (NPT), developed by sociologists Carl May, Tracy Finch, and colleagues (2007, 2009), is an influential middle-range implementation science framework that explains how novel complex interventions, healthcare technologies, or organizational working practices become routinely embedded, integrated, and sustained ('normalized') into everyday organizational workflows—or conversely, why they fail to be sustained. Unlike psychological theories focused on individual user acceptance (e.g., TAM, UTAUT), NPT focuses on collective social action and operational work.
terms.seminal_citation: May, C., & Finch, T. (2009). Implementing, embedding, and integrating practices: An outline of Normalization Process Theory. Sociology, 43(3), 535-554.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Normalisation Process Theory (NPT) according to May & Finch (2009).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Four Core Generative Mechanisms of Normalization:
   - Coherence (Sensemaking Work): How actors understand, differentiate, and conceptualize the purpose and value of the new practice.
   - Cognitive Participation (Relational Work): How actors build commitment, buy-in, and collective community around the new practice to enroll users.
   - Collective Action (Operational Work): The actual day-to-day work, training, allocation of resources, and operational restructuring required to execute the intervention.
   - Reflexive Monitoring (Appraisal Work): How actors informally and formally appraise, assess, and adapt the intervention based on experiential feedback.
2. Methodological Application: Used in qualitative process evaluations alongside clinical trials, longitudinal ethnographic case studies, and mixed-methods implementation studies using the validated NoMAD survey instrument (Finch et al., 2018).
terms.benchmarks:
1. Multi-Dimensional Coding: Qualitative coding must analyze all four NPT domains and their 16 sub-constructs to map the entire normalization trajectory.
2. Processual Immersion: Requires longitudinal data collection capturing organizational shifts across pre-implementation, rollout, and post-implementation maintenance.
3. Policy Output: Generates targeted diagnostic matrices pinpointing operational bottlenecks (e.g., high Coherence but zero Collective Action due to workload overload).
terms.pitfalls:
1. Treating NPT as an Individual Attitude Checklist: Reducing NPT to individual psychological motivation rather than analyzing collective institutional and collaborative work.
2. Static Cross-Sectional Snapshots: Evaluating normalization through a single one-time survey, ignoring that normalization is an evolving process requiring months or years.
3. Force-Fitting Data Mechanistically: Forcing rich qualitative data mechanically into NPT sub-constructs without attending to emergent contextual themes.
terms.apa_reference: May, C., & Finch, T. (2009). Implementing, embedding, and integrating practices: An outline of Normalization Process Theory. Sociology, 43(3), 535-554. https://doi.org/10.1177/0038038509103208

terms.vietnamese: Đánh giá chất lượng nghiên cứu theo thang Newcastle-Ottawa (NOS)
vietnamese_variants: Quy trình thẩm định nguy cơ sai lệch NOS
Tiêu chuẩn đánh giá nghiên cứu quan sát NOS
terms.core_definition: Quy trình Đánh giá chất lượng nghiên cứu theo thang Newcastle-Ottawa (NOS Quality Assessment Protocol, do Wells et al., 2000 khởi xướng) là quy chuẩn thao tác kỹ thuật bắt buộc khi thực hiện các phân tích tổng quan hệ thống tuân thủ hướng dẫn PRISMA đối với các nghiên cứu quan sát. Trong khi các nghiên cứu can thiệp ngẫu nhiên (RCT) được đánh giá bằng công cụ RoB 2 của Cochrane, các nghiên cứu quan sát vốn tiềm ẩn nguy cơ sai lệch lựa chọn (Selection Bias), sai lệch thông tin (Information Bias) và nhiễu (Confounding) nghiêm trọng. Thang NOS đóng vai trò như một bộ lọc phương pháp luận để lượng hóa nguy cơ sai lệch của từng bài báo thành phần, cung cấp cơ sở cho việc trọng số hóa nghiên cứu hoặc thực hiện phân tích độ nhạy (Sensitivity Analysis) trong mô hình phân tích gộp.
terms.seminal_citation: Wells, G. A., Shea, B., O'Connell, D., Peterson, J., Welch, V., Losos, M., & Tugwell, P. (2000). The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for assessing the quality of nonrandomised studies in meta-analyses. Ottawa Hospital Research Institute.
terms.expert_notes: LaTeX thô; nguồn ghi ngưỡng
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of NOS according to Hệ thống xếp hạng sao (tối đa 9 sao) qua 3 nhóm tiêu chí: Lựa chọn nhóm nghiên cứu (4 sao), Tính so sánh được (2 sao), và Đo lường kết quả/phơi nhiễm (3 sao). Nghiên cứu ≥ 7 sao được xếp loại chất lượng cao..
terms.short_definition: Quy trình hệ thống đánh giá nguy cơ sai lệch trong nghiên cứu quan sát phi ngẫu nhiên phục vụ phân tích gộp theo thang điểm sao Newcastle-Ottawa.
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Xây dựng Sổ tay Quy chuẩn Tiêu chí (Customized Coding Protocol):
 Trước khi chấm bài, nhóm nghiên cứu phải xác định cụ thể trong đề cương:
 - Biến gây nhiễu quan trọng nhất (Most important factor) bắt buộc phải kiểm soát là gì (ví dụ: tuổi, giai đoạn bệnh, thu nhập).
 - Thời gian theo dõi tối thiểu được coi là 'đủ dài' là bao nhiêu tháng/năm.
 - Ngưỡng tỷ lệ mất dấu theo dõi tối đa được chấp nhận là bao nhiêu phần trăm.
2. Đánh giá chéo độc lập và tính chỉ số Cohen's κ: Đo lường mức độ đồng thuận giữa hai nhà nghiên cứu trước khi bước vào phiên đối thoại dung hòa.
3. Xây dựng Bảng tổng hợp Nguy cơ sai lệch (Risk of Bias Summary Table): Thể hiện rõ số sao đạt được ở từng hạng mục chi tiết của từng nghiên cứu thay vì chỉ ghi điểm số tổng.
4. Thực hiện Phân tích dưới nhóm (Subgroup Analysis by Study Quality): Tách biệt nhóm nghiên cứu chất lượng cao (≥ 7 sao) và chất lượng thấp (< 7 sao) để kiểm định tính ổn định của kích thước hiệu ứng tổng thể (Pooled Effect Size).
5. Kiểm tra hiện tượng Xuất bản sai lệch (Publication Bias / Meta-regression): Đưa điểm số chất lượng NOS vào phương trình Meta-regression để đánh giá xem chất lượng nghiên cứu có phải là nguồn gốc gây ra tính không đồng nhất (Heterogeneity) hay không.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Ngưỡng phân định chất lượng chuẩn:
 - Nghiên cứu đạt ≥ 7 sao được phân loại vào nhóm Nguy cơ sai lệch thấp (Low Risk of Bias).
 - Nghiên cứu đạt 5 - 6 sao: Nguy cơ sai lệch trung bình (Moderate Risk).
 - Nghiên cứu < 5 sao: Nguy cơ sai lệch cao (High Risk of Bias).
2. Độ tin cậy thẩm định (Inter-rater Agreement): Hệ số Cohen's κ hoặc Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) giữa hai thẩm định viên phải đạt ≥ 0.70.
3. Bắt buộc minh bạch: Toàn bộ bảng chấm sao chi tiết cho từng bài báo bắt buộc phải được đính kèm trong phần Phụ lục trực tuyến (Supplementary Materials) khi nộp cho các tạp chí y sinh và khoa học xã hội Q1.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Áp dụng quy chuẩn tùy tiện mà không định nghĩa biến nhiễu trước (Post-hoc criteria tampering): Quyết định biến nhiễu nào quan trọng sau khi đã đọc bài báo sẽ tạo ra sự thiên vị có chủ đích của thẩm định viên nhằm tăng số sao cho các nghiên cứu ủng hộ giả thuyết của mình.
2. Tự động loại bỏ các nghiên cứu điểm thấp khỏi phân tích gộp: Không nên loại bỏ ngay lập tức các bài báo có số sao thấp; giải pháp khoa học nhất là đưa tất cả vào mô hình chính và chạy phân tích độ nhạy loại trừ dần để chứng minh tính vững chắc của kết quả.
3. Đánh đồng công cụ NOS cho nghiên cứu cắt ngang (Cross-sectional studies): Thang NOS gốc chỉ thiết kế cho nghiên cứu đoàn hệ và bệnh-chứng. Nếu áp dụng cho nghiên cứu cắt ngang, phải dùng phiên bản chuyển đổi của Hertog et al. hoặc công cụ JBI (Joanna Briggs Institute).
terms.apa_reference: Wells, G. A., Shea, B., O'Connell, D., Peterson, J., Welch, V., Losos, M., & Tugwell, P. (2000). The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for assessing the quality of nonrandomised studies in meta-analyses. Ottawa Hospital Research Institute.

terms.vietnamese: Lý thuyết cú hích (Kiến trúc lựa chọn)
vietnamese_variants: Kiến trúc lựa chọn hành vi
Chủ nghĩa gia trưởng tự do Thaler-Sunstein
terms.core_definition: Lý thuyết cú hích (Nudge Theory) và Kiến trúc lựa chọn (Choice Architecture, do nhà kinh tế học đoạt giải Nobel Richard H. Thaler và giáo sư luật Cass R. Sunstein hệ thống hóa năm 2008) là trường phái can thiệp chính sách dựa trên triết lý 'Chủ nghĩa gia trưởng tự do' (Libertarian Paternalism). Kiến trúc lựa chọn là cách thức mà các quyết định được tổ chức, đóng khung và trình bày trước mắt người ra quyết định. Thaler và Sunstein định nghĩa một 'Cú hích' (Nudge) là bất kỳ khía cạnh nào của kiến trúc lựa chọn làm thay đổi hành vi của con người theo một cách có thể dự báo được, mà không cấm đoán bất kỳ sự lựa chọn nào và không làm biến đổi đáng kể các khuyến khích kinh tế cốt lõi (như tiền phạt, thuế hay trợ cấp lớn). Cú hích tận dụng các thiên kiến nhận thức có sẵn của Hệ thống 1 (tư duy nhanh, trực giác, lười biếng theo Daniel Kahneman) để dẫn dắt cá nhân tự nguyện đưa ra các quyết định tốt hơn cho sức khỏe, tài chính và xã hội (ví dụ: mặc định tự động đăng ký tiết kiệm hưu trí, đặt trái cây ở vị trí ngang tầm mắt trong căng tin).
terms.seminal_citation: Thaler, R. H., & Sunstein, C. R. (2008). Nudge: Improving decisions about health, wealth, and happiness. Yale University Press.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Nudge Theory & Choice Architecture according to Thaler & Sunstein (2008).
terms.short_definition: Khung can thiệp hành vi tinh tế làm thay đổi hành vi của con người theo hướng có lợi có thể dự đoán được mà không cấm đoán bất kỳ phương án nào hay thay đổi đáng kể động cơ kinh tế.
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Khảo sát chuỗi hành trình quyết định và rào cản hành vi: Nhận diện các điểm nghẽn nhận thức, độ trễ trì hoãn (Procrastination) và thiên kiến duy trì hiện trạng (Status Quo Bias).
2. Áp dụng khung công cụ kiến trúc lựa chọn EAST (Easy, Attractive, Social, Timely) của Behavioral Insights Team (BIT):
 - Thiết lập mặc định thông minh (Default Options): Đổi từ cơ chế Chủ động tham gia (Opt-in) sang Tự động tham gia nhưng có quyền từ chối (Opt-out) - đây là cú hích có sức mạnh thay đổi hành vi lớn nhất.
 - Giảm thiểu ma sát nhận thức (Sludge Reduction): Cắt bỏ các thủ tục giấy tờ phiền hà, đơn giản hóa biểu mẫu đăng ký.
 - Định chuẩn xã hội (Social Norms Feedback): Cung cấp thông tin so sánh hành vi của cá nhân với số đông xung quanh (ví dụ: '90% cư dân trong khu vực đã đóng thuế đúng hạn').
 - Tăng tính nổi bật và phản hồi tức thì (Salience & Timely Prompts): Gửi tin nhắn nhắc nhở đúng thời điểm hành động xuất hiện.
3. Thiết kế thử nghiệm ngẫu nhiên có đối chứng (Randomized Controlled Trial - RCT): Phân bổ ngẫu nhiên người dân vào nhóm tiếp nhận kiến trúc lựa chọn cũ và nhóm tiếp nhận Cú hích mới để đo lường tác động chính sách thuần túy.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Tác động của Mặc định (Default Effect): Trong các chính sách hiến tạng hoặc quỹ hưu trí 401(k), việc chuyển từ Opt-in sang Opt-out làm tăng tỷ lệ tham gia từ mức 30 - 40% vọt lên trên 85 - 90% ngay lập tức mà không tốn chi phí hành chính.
2. Hiệu quả chi phí (Cost-Effectiveness): Một can thiệp Cú hích thông qua tin nhắn nhắc nhở chi phí vài xu có thể mang lại hiệu quả tương đương một gói tài trợ tài chính hàng triệu USD.
3. Tiêu chí Đạo đức Cú hích (Nudge Transparency): Can thiệp phải công khai, minh bạch, dễ dàng thoát ra (Opt-out với chi phí bằng 0), và phục vụ lợi ích tối thượng của chính người được tác động.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Biến tướng thành 'Bẫy hành vi độc hại' (Dark Patterns / Sludge): Khi kiến trúc lựa chọn bị doanh nghiệp lợi dụng để trục lợi (ví dụ: cài cắm mặc định mua bảo hiểm phụ trội khi mua vé máy bay, hoặc tạo ra các ma sát cực đoan để người dùng không thể hủy dịch vụ), nó biến thành 'Sludge' và bị xã hội lên án dữ dội.
2. Giảm dần hiệu lực theo thời gian (Decay of Nudge Effects): Nhiều cú hích (như tin nhắn nhắc nhở hoặc đèn cảnh báo) chỉ tạo ra thay đổi hành vi trong ngắn hạn; người dân sẽ nhanh chóng bị 'lờn' (Habituation) và quay trở về thói quen cũ nếu không có sự củng cố thói quen lâu dài.
3. Thay thế cho các cải cách cơ cấu căn bản (Nudge as an Excuse): Sử dụng Cú hích tâm lý như một biện pháp vá víu rẻ tiền để né tránh việc thực thi các cải cách thể chế lớn, đầu tư hạ tầng hoặc điều chỉnh thuế thực chất đối với các vấn đề vĩ mô nghiêm trọng.
terms.apa_reference: Thaler, R. H., & Sunstein, C. R. (2008). Nudge: Improving decisions about health, wealth, and happiness. Yale University Press.

terms.vietnamese: Giả thuyết không (H0)
vietnamese_variants: Giả định không có sai biệt
terms.core_definition: The Null Hypothesis (denoted $H_0$), introduced conceptually by Ronald A. Fisher (1935) and formalized by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson (1933), is the default, baseline statistical proposition stating that there is no true effect, no parameter difference, no treatment impact, or no association between variables in the population ($H_0: \theta = 0$). Serving as the mathematical anchor of frequentist statistical inference, $H_0$ is assumed tentatively to be true for the purpose of deriving the theoretical sampling distribution of a test statistic, which allows researchers to quantify the probability ($p$-value) of observing data as extreme as or more extreme than the empirical sample.
terms.seminal_citation: Fisher, R. A. (1935). The design of experiments. Oliver & Boyd.
terms.expert_notes: LaTeX thô
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Null hypothesis according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Mathematical Anatomy: Formulated as an exact point constraint on parameter space: H0: theta = theta_0 (e.g., mu_1 - mu_2 = 0; beta = 0; rho = 0).
2. Derivation of Sampling Distribution: Under the assumption that H0 is true, the standardized test statistic (t, z, F, chi^2) follows a known probability density function.
3. The P-Value: Defined strictly as the conditional probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as contradictory to H0 as the one observed, assuming H0 is true: p = P(T >= t_obs | H0).
4. The Dual Decision Framework:
   - Reject H0: If p < alpha (concluding data are incompatible with the null model at pre-set Type I error risk).
   - Fail to Reject H0: If p >= alpha (retaining H0; does NOT prove H0 is true).
5. Asymmetry of Proof: In frequentist logic, one can reject H0, but one can NEVER 'prove' or 'accept' H0.
terms.benchmarks:
1. The 'Fail to Reject' Standard: A non-significant p-value (p >= 0.05) indicates absence of evidence, NOT evidence of absence.
2. Power & Sample Size: To make claims of practical equivalence or non-effect, researchers must conduct Formal Equivalence Testing (TOST: Two One-Sided Tests) rather than merely pointing to non-significant null tests.
3. Point Null Reality: In large empirical datasets, the strict point null (beta = 0.0000000) is almost always literally false (Meehl, 1967; Cohen, 1994).
terms.pitfalls:
1. Claiming to 'Prove' the Null Hypothesis: Concluding that 'there is no difference between groups' because p = 0.12; failure to reject H0 may simply reflect low statistical power or noisy measurement.
2. Conflating H0 with the Research Hypothesis: Mistaking the statistical strawman H0 for the researcher's actual theoretical prediction.
3. The Nil-Hypothesis Ritual: Testing trivial, uninformative point null hypotheses that have zero scientific relevance instead of evaluating substantive effect sizes and confidence intervals.
terms.apa_reference: Fisher, R. A. (1935). The design of experiments. Oliver & Boyd. (See also: Neyman, J., & Pearson, E. S., 1933, On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses, Philosophical Transactions).

terms.vietnamese: Kiểm định ý nghĩa giả thuyết không (NHST)
vietnamese_variants: Phép thử ý nghĩa giả định không
terms.core_definition: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) is the ubiquitous, hybrid statistical decision framework that dominates empirical quantitative research across behavioral, economic, and medical sciences. Combining Ronald A. Fisher's inductive p-value significance testing with Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson's deductive decision-theoretic hypothesis testing (Type I error alpha and Type II error beta), NHST evaluates whether sample data deviate sufficiently from a point null hypothesis ($H_0$) to warrant rejecting $H_0$ at an arbitrary threshold ($p < 0.05$). Despite its universal adoption, NHST has faced severe epistemological critiques (Cohen, 1994; Gigerenzer, 2004) for fostering dichotomous thinking and driving the contemporary replication crisis.
terms.seminal_citation: Cohen, J. (1994). The earth is round (p < .05). American Psychologist, 49(12), 997-1003.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) according to Fisher (1925), Neyman & Pearson (1933).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. The Incoherent Hybrid Fusion:
   - Fisherian Component: Set up null hypothesis H0; compute test statistic; calculate exact p-value as continuous measure of evidence against H0; no alternative hypothesis.
   - Neyman-Pearson Component: Pre-specify two competing hypotheses (H0 and H1); set alpha (Type I error rate) and beta (Type II error rate) based on cost-benefit trade-offs; accept inductive decision rule.
   - Modern NHST Synthesis: A mechanical hybrid where researchers set alpha = 0.05, specify a vague directional H1, compute p, and make a binary claim of 'scientific truth' if p < 0.05.
2. American Statistical Association (ASA) 6 Principles (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016):
   - (1) P-values can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model.
   - (2) P-values do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true.
   - (3) Scientific conclusions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a threshold.
   - (4) Proper inference requires full reporting and transparency.
   - (5) A p-value does not measure effect size or importance.
   - (6) By itself, a p-value does not provide a good measure of evidence regarding a model.
3. Modern Reform Alternatives: Mandatory reporting of Effect Sizes (Cohen's d, partial eta^2), 95% Confidence Intervals, and Bayesian Bayes Factors (BF_10).
terms.benchmarks:
1. Effect Size Reporting: P-values must NEVER be reported without accompanying standardized/unstandardized effect sizes and confidence intervals.
2. Pre-Registration: Pre-registering hypotheses and sample sizes prevents p-hacking and exploratory HARKing.
3. Exact P-Value Reporting: Report exact values (e.g., p = 0.024) rather than inequalities (p < 0.05), except for p < 0.001.
terms.pitfalls:
1. The Inverse Probability Fallacy: Misinterpreting p < 0.05 as meaning 'there is a 95% probability that the research hypothesis is true'; p is strictly P(Data | H0), not P(H0 | Data).
2. Dichotomous Cliff Fallacy: Treating p = 0.049 as a 'proven scientific breakthrough' while dismissing p = 0.051 as 'no effect whatsoever'.
3. Confusing Significance with Practical Importance: Reporting a highly significant p-value (p < 0.0001) in a massive dataset (N = 1,000,000) for a completely trivial effect size.
terms.apa_reference: Cohen, J. (1994). The earth is round (p < .05). American Psychologist, 49(12), 997-1003. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.49.12.997

terms.vietnamese: Số người cần gây hại (Number Needed to Harm - NNH)
vietnamese_variants: Số bệnh nhân cần điều trị để gây 1 biến cố có hại
terms.core_definition: The Number Needed to Harm (NNH) is an essential epidemiological and clinical trial metric that quantifies the number of patients or individuals who must be exposed to an experimental intervention or risk factor over a specified time period for one additional person to experience an adverse event or harmful outcome. As the direct safety counterpart to the Number Needed to Treat (NNT), NNH is computed as the reciprocal of the Absolute Risk Increase (ARI): $\text{NNH} = \frac{1}{\text{ARI}}$. In evidence-based policy and healthcare, higher NNH values reflect safer, less toxic interventions.
terms.seminal_citation: Laupacis, A., Sackett, D. L., & Roberts, R. S. (1988). An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment. The New England Journal of Medicine, 318(26), 1728-1733.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Number Needed to Harm (NNH) according to Altman (1998).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. 2x2 Risk Contingency Formulation:
   - Experimental Event Rate for Harm (EER_harm): Adverse events in treated group / Total treated = a / (a + b).
   - Control Event Rate for Harm (CER_harm): Adverse events in control group / Total control = c / (c + d).
2. Absolute Risk Increase (ARI): ARI = EER_harm - CER_harm.
3. NNH Calculation: NNH = 1 / ARI = 1 / (EER_harm - CER_harm). Typically rounded UP to the nearest whole integer.
4. Confidence Interval Calculation: Calculate 95% CI for ARI; invert boundaries to obtain the 95% confidence interval for NNH.
5. Clinical Utility: Balances against NNT to compute the Likelihood of Being Helped or Harmed (LHH = (1/NNT) / (1/NNH)).
terms.benchmarks:
1. Interpretation Heuristic: The larger the NNH, the safer the treatment (e.g., NNH = 1,000 means 1 in 1,000 patients experiences harm; NNH = 5 indicates an extremely toxic treatment).
2. Time Period Specification: NNH is mathematically meaningless without specifying the exact duration of exposure (e.g., NNH = 50 over 1 year vs. over 10 years).
3. Risk-Benefit Balance: An effective drug requires NNT << NNH (e.g., NNT = 10 for cure, NNH = 5,000 for severe adverse reaction).
terms.pitfalls:
1. Omitting the Exposure Timeframe: Reporting NNH = 25 without stating whether the trial lasted 2 weeks or 5 years.
2. Inverting Confidence Intervals Across Zero: When the ARI confidence interval includes zero (non-significant difference), the reciprocal NNH confidence interval spans discontinuous infinity, requiring careful reporting.
3. Comparing NNH Across Unequal Harm Severities: Comparing an NNH for a mild headache (NNH = 10) directly with an NNH for fatal myocardial infarction (NNH = 500).
terms.apa_reference: Laupacis, A., Sackett, D. L., & Roberts, R. S. (1988). An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment. The New England Journal of Medicine, 318(26), 1728-1733. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM198806303182605

terms.vietnamese: Số người cần điều trị (Number Needed to Treat - NNT)
vietnamese_variants: Số bệnh nhân cần can thiệp để đạt 1 kết quả tốt
terms.core_definition: The Number Needed to Treat (NNT), introduced by Andreas Laupacis, David L. Sackett, and Robin S. Roberts (1988), is a standardized clinical epidemiology effect size metric that represents the average number of patients who must receive a specific treatment or intervention over a defined time period in order to achieve one additional positive outcome (or prevent one additional adverse event) compared to a control comparator. Calculated as the reciprocal of the Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR): $\text{NNT} = \frac{1}{\text{ARR}}$, NNT translates abstract statistical probabilities into concrete, clinically intuitive numbers for evidence-based decision-making.
terms.seminal_citation: Laupacis, A., Sackett, D. L., & Roberts, R. S. (1988). An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment. The New England Journal of Medicine, 318(26), 1728-1733.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Number Needed to Treat (NNT) according to Laupacis et al. (1988).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. 2x2 Trial Contingency Table:
   - Control Event Rate (CER): Bad events in control / Total control = c / (c + d).
   - Experimental Event Rate (EER): Bad events in treated / Total treated = a / (a + b).
2. Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR): ARR = CER - EER.
3. NNT Calculation: NNT = 1 / ARR = 1 / (CER - EER). By convention, NNT is rounded UP to the nearest integer.
4. Conversion from Relative Risk: NNT = 1 / [ CER * (1 - RR) ], where RR = EER / CER.
5. Baseline Risk Dependency: NNT is highly sensitive to the patient population's baseline risk (CER); as baseline risk drops, NNT escalates dramatically even when Relative Risk Reduction (RRR) remains constant.
terms.benchmarks:
1. The Perfect Standard: The theoretical ideal is NNT = 1 (every treated patient benefits, no control patient benefits).
2. Clinical Acceptability Benchmarks:
   - Acute interventions (e.g., antibiotics for acute bacterial infection): NNT = 2 to 5.
   - Preventative prophylactic drugs (e.g., statins to prevent heart attack over 5 years): NNT = 30 to 100 is standard and clinically acceptable.
3. Time-to-Event NNT: In survival analysis, compute NNT at time t: NNT(t) = 1 / [ S_T(t) - S_C(t) ].
terms.pitfalls:
1. Confusing NNT with Relative Risk Reduction: Misinterpreting a drug advertised as 'reducing heart attacks by 50%' (RRR); if baseline risk is 2%, ARR is 1%, and NNT = 100 (99 patients experience zero benefit).
2. Omitting the Follow-Up Time Interval: Reporting an NNT = 20 without stating whether this benefit is achieved over 30 days or over 10 years.
3. Extrapolating Across Different Risk Groups: Applying an NNT derived from high-risk hospital patients directly to low-risk community populations.
terms.apa_reference: Laupacis, A., Sackett, D. L., & Roberts, R. S. (1988). An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment. The New England Journal of Medicine, 318(26), 1728-1733. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM198806303182605

terms.vietnamese: Quy tắc Nuremberg về đạo đức nghiên cứu y sinh
terms.core_definition: The Nuremberg Code (1947) is the landmark foundational charter of modern biomedical and human research ethics, formulated as part of the judicial verdict by the American military tribunal during the Doctors' Trial at Nuremberg prosecuting Nazi physicians for crimes against humanity. Comprising ten non-negotiable ethical directives, the Nuremberg Code established for the first time in human history that the voluntary, informed, and competent consent of the human subject is absolutely essential, legally inviolable, and cannot be subordinated to scientific advancement, state interests, or military utility.
terms.seminal_citation: Trials of War Criminals before the Nuremberg Military Tribunals under Control Council Law No. 10. (1949). The Nuremberg Code (Vol. 2, pp. 181-182). U.S. Government Printing Office.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Nuremberg Code according to Trials of War Criminals (1947).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Ten Foundational Directives:
   - (1) Voluntary Informed Consent: Subject must have legal capacity, be free from coercion or deceit, and possess enlightened understanding.
   - (2) Fruitful Results for Society: Experiment must yield unprocurable results beneficial to society, not random or unnecessary.
   - (3) Anticipatory Animal Experimentation: Study must be designed based on prior animal trials and natural disease knowledge.
   - (4) Avoidance of Unnecessary Suffering: Physical and mental suffering and injury must be minimized.
   - (5) Prohibition of Experiments Involving Death/Disability: No trial permitted where death or disabling injury is a known a priori risk (except where physician serves as subject).
   - (6) Proportionality of Risk: Degree of risk must never exceed humanitarian importance of the problem.
   - (7) Adequate Protection and Facilities: Complete physical protection against remote injury.
   - (8) Scientific Qualification of Investigators: Conducted only by scientifically qualified personnel.
   - (9) Liberty to Withdraw: Subject has the absolute right to terminate participation at any moment.
   - (10) Investigator Duty to Terminate: Investigator must halt trial if continuation is likely to result in injury or death.
2. Modern Legal & Institutional Integration: Direct progenitor of the Declaration of Helsinki (1964), Belmont Report (1979), and modern Institutional Review Boards (IRBs).
terms.benchmarks:
1. Inviolability of Consent: Coercion, deception, or taking advantage of vulnerable populations automatically violates Directive 1.
2. IRB Compliance: All modern human research proposals must trace their ethical protections to Nuremberg principles.
3. Absolute Right to Exit: Consent forms must explicitly inform participants of their right to withdraw at any time without penalty.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Passive Historical Relegation: Viewing the Nuremberg Code as a relic of WWII rather than active legal doctrine cited in modern clinical and algorithmic surveillance ethics.
2. Coercive Institutional Pressures: Enrolling medical students, military recruits, or employees into research where subtle career penalties make consent involuntary.
3. Misleading Consent Protocols: Hiding known experimental risks inside 30-page complex legalistic consent forms that participants cannot comprehend.
terms.apa_reference: Trials of War Criminals before the Nuremberg Military Tribunals under Control Council Law No. 10. (1949). The Nuremberg Code (Vol. 2, pp. 181-182). U.S. Government Printing Office.

terms.vietnamese: Thông diễn học khách quan (Khung phương pháp Ulrich Oevermann)
vietnamese_variants: Phương pháp thông diễn khách quan
Giải thích học khách quan Oevermann
terms.core_definition: Objective Hermeneutics (Objektive Hermeneutik) is an interpretive, reconstructive qualitative research methodology formulated by German sociologist Ulrich Oevermann and colleagues (1979, 1986). Rejecting subjective phenomenology (which focuses on actors' conscious internal intentions), objective hermeneutics posits that communicative and social actions are structured by objective latent meaning structures (Sinnstrukturen) governed by universal linguistic and cultural rules. By subjecting verbatim textual transcripts to sequential, micro-sociological interpretation, it reconstructs the generative grammar of social reality independent of participants' subjective rationalizations.
terms.seminal_citation: Oevermann, U., Allert, T., Konau, E., & Krambeck, J. (1979). Die Methodologie einer "objektiven Hermeneutik" [The methodology of an "objective hermeneutics"]. In H. G. Soeffner (Ed.), Interpretative Verfahren in den Sozial- und Textwissenschaften (pp. 352-434). J.B. Metzler.
terms.expert_notes: Đã chuẩn hóa từ bảng trích xuất sang định dạng từ điển chuẩn.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Objective hermeneutics (Oevermann) according to Flick et al. (2004).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Core Theoretical Assumptions:
   - Text Autonomy: The text possesses an objective structure of meaning that exists independently of the author's conscious motives.
   - Fallibility of Subjective Accounts: What actors claim they intended is merely a subjective rationalization; true social structures are embedded in the objective linguistic rules of interaction.
2. Five Methodological Procedural Rules (Oevermann):
   - Literal Character: Every punctuation mark, pause, and hesitation is analyzed without paraphrasing.
   - Sequentiality: The text is analyzed line-by-line in chronological order; analysts cannot read ahead.
   - Extensiveness: Exhaustive exploration of possible meanings for each utterance.
   - Generation of Thought Experiments (Gedankenexperimente): Formulate alternative hypothetical social contexts that could have produced the utterance to delineate what was ruled out.
   - Context Economy: Internal textual evidence takes priority over external background knowledge.
3. The Case Structure (Fallstruktur): Progresses from micro-sequences to reconstruct the singular, universal latent structure of the case.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Group Hermeneutic Interpretation: Analysis must be conducted in an interpretive research group (Interpretationsgruppe) to prevent individual researcher idiosyncrasies.
2. Sequential Purity: Utterances must be interpreted before revealing the subsequent conversational turn.
3. Reconstructive Validity: The reconstructed case structure must successfully explain subsequent unanalyzed segments of the transcript.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Reading Ahead Trap: Peeking at subsequent turns in the transcript, which destroys the authentic prospective discovery of latent structural alternatives.
2. Psychologizing Interpretations: Imputing psychological neuroses to speakers rather than analyzing the objective sociological rules of communication.
3. Imposing External Theory: Forcing Marxist, Bourdieusian, or psychoanalytic concepts onto the text before completing objective micro-sequential reconstruction.
terms.apa_reference: Oevermann, U., Allert, T., Konau, E., & Krambeck, J. (1979). Die Methodologie einer "objektiven Hermeneutik". In H. G. Soeffner (Ed.), Interpretative Verfahren in den Sozial- und Textwissenschaften (pp. 352-434). J.B. Metzler. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-476-03108-2_17

terms.vietnamese: Quy trình giải thích học khách quan phân tích văn bản
vietnamese_variants: Quy trình phân tích văn bản Oevermann
Thực hành thông diễn khách quan
terms.core_definition: Objective Hermeneutics (Textual Analysis Protocol) encompasses the granular, sequential operational procedures developed by Ulrich Oevermann for the rigorous scientific decoding of textual artifacts (e.g., family therapy dialogues, legal judgments, psychiatric intake interviews, political speeches). Grounded in the dialectic between universal rule-systems (social codes, grammar) and the idiosyncratic selection of options by historical actors, this protocol uncovers the deep latent case structure through intensive counterfactual scenario generation.
terms.seminal_citation: Oevermann, U. (1986). Kontroversen über sinnverstehende Soziologie [Controversies concerning interpretive sociology]. In S. Aufenanger & M. Lenssen (Eds.), Handlung und Sinnstruktur (pp. 19-83). Kindt Verlag.
terms.expert_notes: Trùng #1787; rác Markdown/bảng; mảnh trích; bị cắt cụt
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Objective Hermeneutics (Ulrich Oevermann) according to Flick et al. (2004).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Text Selection and Segmentation: Divide raw verbatim transcripts into sequential interactional turns and micro-utterances.
2. Stepwise Analytical Protocol:
   - Step 1 (Explication of Context-Free Meaning): Analyze what the literal statement means in the general natural language, independently of the specific speaker.
   - Step 2 (Hypothetical Context Generation): Brainstorm all realistic social scenarios in which this specific statement would be meaningful.
   - Step 3 (Context Comparison): Compare hypothetical scenarios against the actual empirical context of the case, identifying what specific social options the actor chosen versus rejected.
   - Step 4 (Sequential Prognosis): Formulate predictions regarding what the conversational partner will say in the immediately following turn based on the reconstructed latent structure.
   - Step 5 (Empirical Verification): Reveal the actual next turn; verify or modify the hypothesized latent structure.
3. Reconstruction of the Core Paradox: Identify the foundational existential or institutional dilemma that defines the case.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Group Deliberation Standard: Must be verified within an independent research seminar group with diverse interpretative perspectives.
2. Falsifiable Prognosis: The analyst's predictions about subsequent turns must be tested against the empirical record.
3. Structural Rigor: Reconstructs deep latent meaning that cannot be captured by surface manifest content coding.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Superficial Paraphrasing: Summarizing what the speaker said rather than analyzing the objective structural possibilities of the interaction.
2. Solitary Hermeneutic Analysis: Conducting objective hermeneutics in isolation without a peer interpretation group, which allows individual researcher bias to dominate.
3. Over-Interpreting Grammatical Slips: Elevating minor typographical transcription errors into profound psycho-social crises.
terms.apa_reference: Oevermann, U. (1986). Kontroversen über sinnverstehende Soziologie. In S. Aufenanger & M. Lenssen (Eds.), Handlung und Sinnstruktur (pp. 19-83). Kindt Verlag.

terms.vietnamese: Chủ nghĩa khách quan (Lập trường bản thể và nhận thức luận)
terms.core_definition: Objectivism is an epistemological and ontological philosophical stance positing that social reality exists independent of human consciousness, cognition, or subjective interpretation, and that this external reality possesses an objective, discoverable structure of universal laws and causal mechanisms. In research methodology (Crotty, 1998; Bryman, 2016), an objectivist stance underpins the positivist and post-positivist research traditions, dictating that the researcher must remain a detached, neutral, value-free observer who measures social entities as external, objective social facts (Durkheim) using standardized quantitative instruments.
terms.seminal_citation: Crotty, M. (1998). The foundations of social research: Meaning and perspective in the research process. SAGE Publications.
terms.expert_notes: Đã được biên tập và chuẩn hóa định nghĩa học thuật theo giáo trình kinh điển.
terms.core_definition_en: Rigorous scholarly definition of Objectivism according to established research methodology literature.
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Ontological Component (Realism): Social entities (e.g., organizations, cultures, market structures) exist as external physical and social objects outside the minds of individual actors.
2. Epistemological Component (Objectivist Knowing): Meaning resides intrinsically within the object waiting to be discovered; valid knowledge is obtained when the researcher directly captures this reality without subjective contamination.
3. Methodological Implementation:
   - Detached measurement: Survey questionnaires, experimental trials, standardized psychometric tests, sensor tracking.
   - Quantitative formalization: Deductive hypothesis testing, econometric modeling, structural equations.
   - Elimination of Researcher Reflexivity: Systematic procedures to eliminate experimenter bias, demand characteristics, and subjective intuition.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Value Neutrality Standard: Research design and data analysis must be entirely decoupled from researcher political, ethical, or personal ideology.
2. Replicability Criterion: Independent researchers following the identical protocol must obtain mathematically identical results.
3. Contrast with Constructionism: Constructionism asserts meaning is socially constructed by actors; Objectivism asserts meaning exists objectively in reality.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Conflating Epistemological Objectivism with Ayn Rand's Philosophy: Mistaking general scientific objectivism for Ayn Rand's specific political-ethical ideology.
2. Naive Positivist Blindness: Assuming that the researcher's own cultural background, language, and measurement choices have zero subjective influence on the data collection process.
3. Inappropriate Application to Intersubjective Realities: Treating purely socially constructed phenomena (e.g., money, national identity, gender roles) as if they were immutable physical objects like rocks or atoms.
terms.apa_reference: Crotty, M. (1998). The foundations of social research: Meaning and perspective in the research process. SAGE Publications. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003115700

terms.vietnamese: Biên bản quan sát nghiên cứu (Observation Protocol)
vietnamese_variants: Biểu mẫu quan sát có cấu trúc
terms.core_definition: An Observation Protocol is a standardized qualitative or mixed-methods field instrument designed by the researcher to systematically record, organize, and structure observational data collected during empirical fieldwork (Creswell, 2014; Spradley, 1980). Typically structured as a two-column field template, an observation protocol formally separates Descriptive Notes (objective, low-inference chronologies of physical settings, participant actions, verbatim speech, and interactions) from Reflective Notes (the researcher's subjective impressions, emotional reactions, emergent theoretical hunches, and methodological memos).
terms.seminal_citation: Spradley, J. P. (1980). Participant observation. Holt, Rinehart and Winston.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Observation protocol according to Creswell & Creswell (2023).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Structural Header Information: Record date, time, physical setting, specific location, participant demographics, researcher role (Complete Participant, Participant-as-Observer, Observer-as-Participant, or Complete Observer), and purpose of observation.
2. The Two-Column Format (Creswell Template):
   - Left Column (Descriptive Notes): Objective, sensory recording of what is seen and heard; physical layout sketch; chronological log of events; low-inference verbatim dialogue.
   - Right Column (Reflective Notes): Theoretical memos, personal feelings, emerging thematic codes, reflections on researcher bias, and methodological adjustments.
3. Spradley's Nine Observational Dimensions: Systematically sample across: Space, Actor, Activity, Object, Act, Event, Time, Goal, and Feeling.
4. Post-Fieldwork Expansion: Within 24 hours of observation, expand abbreviated shorthand field jottings into thick, rich descriptive narrative field texts.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Descriptive-Reflective Separation: Absolute visual separation between factual observation and interpretive reflection to prevent high-inference contamination.
2. Timing Benchmark: Field jottings must be expanded into formal transcripts within 24 hours to preserve episodic memory fidelity.
3. Reflexive Transparency: Explicit documentation of how the researcher's physical presence altered participant behaviors (Hawthorne effect monitoring).
terms.pitfalls:
1. Premature Subjective Evaluation: Filling descriptive notes with evaluative judgments (e.g., 'the manager was rude') instead of recording concrete low-inference behavior (e.g., 'the manager slammed the door and did not greet staff').
2. Lack of Temporal Chronology: Recording random disconnected impressions without noting chronological timestamps, obscuring process sequences.
3. The Memory Trap: Postponing note expansion for days, which causes over 50% of concrete field details to be lost.
terms.apa_reference: Spradley, J. P. (1980). Participant observation. Holt, Rinehart and Winston. (See also: Creswell, J. W., 2014, Research Design: Qualitative, Quantitative, and Mixed Methods Approaches, SAGE).

terms.vietnamese: Phương trình điểm quan sát trong lý thuyết đo lường cổ điển
vietnamese_variants: Phương trình điểm số thực CTT
terms.core_definition: The Observed Score Equation is the foundational axiomatic identity of Classical Test Theory (CTT), formalized by Harold Gulliksen (1950) and Lord & Novick (1968): $X = T + E$. It states that an individual's observed, measured test score ($X$) is an exact additive linear combination of two unobservable latent components: their true latent ability or construct level ($T$) and random unsystematic measurement error ($E$). From this identity and three minimalist independence axioms, the entire mathematical architecture of scale reliability, variance decomposition, standard error of measurement (SEM), and attenuation correction is derived.
terms.seminal_citation: Lord, F. M., & Novick, M. R. (1968). Statistical theories of mental test scores. Addison-Wesley.
terms.expert_notes: Đã chuẩn hóa từ bảng trích xuất sang định dạng từ điển chuẩn.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Observed score equation according to DeVellis (2016).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Fundamental Equation: X_i = T_i + E_i.
2. Axiomatic Assumptions:
   - (1) Expected Error is Zero: E[E] = 0 (random error averages out over infinite repeated testing).
   - (2) True Score Definition: T = E[X] (the expected value of observed scores over hypothetical repeated testings).
   - (3) Error Independence from True Score: Corr(T, E) = 0.
   - (4) Uncorrelated Errors across Occasions/Items: Corr(E_1, E_2) = 0.
3. Variance Decomposition: Taking variance of both sides: Var(X) = Var(T) + Var(E) + 2*Cov(T, E) = Var(T) + Var(E).
4. Reliability Coefficient Derivation: r_XX = Var(T) / Var(X) = 1 - [ Var(E) / Var(X) ].
5. Standard Error of Measurement (SEM): SEM = s_X * sqrt(1 - r_XX), used to construct true score confidence intervals: X +/- 1.96 * SEM.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Reliability Boundedness: 0 <= r_XX <= 1.0 (proportion of observed score variance reflecting true score variation).
2. CTT Reliability Cutoffs: r_XX >= 0.70 for research exploratory scales; r_XX >= 0.80 for standard research; r_XX >= 0.90 for clinical or high-stakes admissions decisions.
3. Confidence Interval Construction: Individual true scores are estimated with 95% certainty within X +/- 1.96 * SEM.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Conflating Random Error with Systematic Error: CTT assumes E represents purely random unsystematic noise; systematic error (e.g., social desirability bias) is incorporated into the True score T, causing high reliability for a biased scale.
2. Sample-Dependent Parameters: In CTT, true score variance and reliability are strictly sample-dependent; a scale will appear highly reliable in a heterogeneous sample and unreliable in a homogeneous sample.
3. Assumption of Uniform SEM: CTT assumes the Standard Error of Measurement is uniform across all score levels, ignoring that tests measure with far greater precision in the middle than in the extreme tails (addressed by IRT).
terms.apa_reference: Lord, F. M., & Novick, M. R. (1968). Statistical theories of mental test scores. Addison-Wesley. (See also: Gulliksen, H., 1950, Theory of Mental Tests, John Wiley & Sons).

terms.vietnamese: Thiên kiến do biến bị bỏ sót (Omitted Variable Bias - OVB)
vietnamese_variants: Thiên lệch biến bị bỏ qua
terms.core_definition: Omitted Variable Bias (OVB) is a pervasive form of endogeneity in regression analysis and econometric estimation occurring when a model omits an unobserved or unmeasured variable that is simultaneously correlated with an included explanatory regressor and causally determinative of the dependent outcome. By leaving this confounder in the regression error term, the Gauss-Markov assumption of strict exogeneity ($E[\epsilon | X] = 0$) is violated, rendering Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) slope estimates biased and inconsistent, regardless of how large the sample size grows.
terms.seminal_citation: Greene, W. H. (2003/2018). Econometric analysis (8th ed.). Pearson.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Omitted Variable Bias (OVB) according to Wooldridge (2010).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Omitted Variable Formula: True model is Y = beta_0 + beta_1 X_1 + beta_2 X_2 + u. The researcher omits X_2 and fits: Y = alpha_0 + alpha_1 X_1 + v.
2. Derivation of Bias: The estimated slope alpha_hat_1 converges asymptotically to: plim(alpha_hat_1) = beta_1 + beta_2 * [ Cov(X_1, X_2) / Var(X_1) ] = beta_1 + beta_2 * gamma_1, where gamma_1 is the slope from auxiliary regression of omitted X_2 on included X_1.
3. Direction of Bias (The Sign Rule):
   - Positive Bias (Overestimation): beta_2 and gamma_1 share the same sign (both positive or both negative).
   - Negative Bias (Underestimation): beta_2 and gamma_1 have opposite signs.
4. Methodological Remedies:
   - Instrumental Variables (IV / 2SLS): Exogenous instrument Z uncorrelated with omitted variable.
   - Panel Data Fixed Effects: Controls for all time-invariant unobserved omitted variables.
   - Difference-in-Differences (DID) & Regression Discontinuity (RDD).
   - Sensitivity Bounds: Oster (2019) coefficient stability and R-max bounding.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Two Necessary Conditions for OVB: Omitted variable X_2 must: (a) be a causal determinant of Y (beta_2 != 0), AND (b) be correlated with included regressor X_1 (gamma_1 != 0).
2. Inconsistency: Unlike sampling variance, OVB is an asymptotic inconsistency that does not diminish as N -> infinity.
3. Oster Diagnostic Bound: Oster's delta bound > 1.0 indicates that selection on unobservables would need to be stronger than selection on observables to wipe out the focal effect.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Confusing OVB with Irrelevant Predictor Omission: Omitting a variable that affects Y but is completely uncorrelated with X_1 does NOT cause OVB; it merely inflates residual variance.
2. The Kitchen-Sink Panacea Fallacy: Attempting to solve OVB by adding dozens of arbitrary control variables, which risks controlling for post-treatment variables or colliders (inducing M-bias).
3. Claiming Large Sample Cures OVB: Believing that gathering N = 100,000 cases eliminates omitted variable bias; OVB is an identification failure, not a power issue.
terms.apa_reference: Greene, W. H. (2018). Econometric analysis (8th ed.). Pearson. (See also: Oster, E., 2019, Unobservable selection and coefficient stability: Theory and evidence, Journal of Business & Economic Statistics).

terms.term: Omitted Variable Bias Test (Ramsey RESET & Oster Stability)
terms.vietnamese: Kiểm định biến bị bỏ sót (Kiểm định Ramsey RESET & Oster Stability)
vietnamese_variants: Kiểm định Oster về độ ổn định hệ số
terms.core_definition: An Omitted Variable Bias Test is an econometric diagnostic procedure designed to detect whether a specified regression model suffers from specification error or omitted confounding. Predominantly operationalized via the Ramsey Regression Equation Specification Error Test (RESET; Ramsey, 1969) and modern Oster Coefficient Stability Bounding (Oster, 2019), these tests evaluate whether higher-order non-linear combinations of fitted values capture omitted structural variance or calculate how strong unobserved confounding would have to be to nullify the estimated treatment effect.
terms.seminal_citation: Ramsey, J. B. (1969). Tests for specification errors in classical linear least-squares regression analysis. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 31(2), 350-371.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Omitted Variable Bias Test according to Wooldridge (2010).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Ramsey RESET Test Execution:
   - Step 1: Fit baseline OLS model: Y = X * beta + u; obtain predicted values y_hat.
   - Step 2: Fit auxiliary expanded regression with powers of fitted values: Y = X * beta + gamma_1 * y_hat^2 + gamma_2 * y_hat^3 + ... + v.
   - Step 3: Compute F-test for the joint null hypothesis: H0: gamma_1 = gamma_2 = 0.
   - Step 4: If F is significant (p < 0.05), reject H0; model suffers from omitted variables, non-linearities, or misspecified functional form.
2. Oster Coefficient Stability Bounding (Oster, 2019):
   - Compare coefficient movement (beta_uncontrolled vs. beta_controlled) against movement in R^2 (R_uncontrolled vs. R_controlled) relative to theoretical maximum R_max.
   - Calculate degree of proportionality delta: delta = [ beta_controlled * (R_controlled - R_uncontrolled) ] / [ (beta_uncontrolled - beta_controlled) * (R_max - R_controlled) ].
   - If delta >= 1.0, unobserved confounders would have to be more powerful than all included observables combined to explain away the result.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Ramsey RESET Decision Rule: p > 0.05 indicates no evidence of omitted variables or functional misspecification.
2. Oster Delta Benchmark: delta >= 1.0 (assuming R_max = 1.3 * R_controlled) is the gold standard benchmark in top economics/finance journals (e.g., AER, JFE) to establish robustness against omitted confounders.
3. Diagnostic Sequence: Conduct Ramsey RESET first; if clean, report Oster delta bounds in robustness sections.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Conflating RESET Rejection with Pure Omitted Regressors: A significant Ramsey RESET (p < 0.05) can be triggered by omitted quadratic/polynomial terms or incorrect link functions (e.g., using linear instead of log), not necessarily missing external variables.
2. Relying on Informal Coefficient Staring: Looking informally at coefficient shifts across control tables and declaring them 'stable' without formally calculating Oster's delta bound.
3. Arbitrary R_max Setting in Oster Analysis: Setting theoretical R_max equal to 1.0 for noisy survey data, which creates artificially pessimistic bounds (use Oster's calibrated 1.3*R).
terms.apa_reference: Ramsey, J. B. (1969). Tests for specification errors in classical linear least-squares regression analysis. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 31(2), 350-371. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1969.tb00796.x

terms.vietnamese: Mô hình logistic một tham số (Mô hình Rasch)
terms.core_definition: Mô hình logistic một tham số hay Mô hình Rasch (One-Parameter Logistic Model / Rasch Model, do nhà toán học Đan Mạch Georg Rasch phát minh năm 1960) là đỉnh cao của lý thuyết đo lường hiện đại (Item Response Theory - IRT). Khác với Lý thuyết trắc nghiệm cổ điển (CTT) vốn tính điểm tổng gộp phụ thuộc vào đề thi cụ thể, mô hình Rasch giả định rằng xác suất để một người có năng lực tiềm ẩn θ trả lời đúng một câu hỏi nhị phân có độ khó b_i tuân theo một hàm logistic duy nhất: P(Y_ni = 1|θ_n, b_i) = e^(θ_n - b_i) / [1 + e^(θ_n - b_i)] = 1 / [1 + e^(-(θ_n - b_i))]. Điểm đặc trưng triết học độc nhất vô nhị của mô hình Rasch (gọi là Tính bất biến đo lường cụ thể - Specific Objectivity) là tham số phân biệt của tất cả các câu hỏi được cố định bằng nhau tuyệt đối (a_i = 1 hoặc hằng số), và xác suất đoán mò bằng 0 (c_i = 0). Nhờ đó, việc so sánh độ khó giữa hai câu hỏi hoàn toàn độc lập với mẫu người làm bài, và việc so sánh năng lực giữa hai thí sinh hoàn toàn độc lập với bộ đề thi được chọn.
terms.seminal_citation: Rasch, G. (1960). Probabilistic models for some intelligence and attainment tests. Danmarks Paedagogiske Institut.
terms.expert_notes: Định nghĩa và ngưỡng kiểm định chuẩn hóa từ Cơ sở dữ liệu Viết tắt Học thuật (Acronym Registry).
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of One-Parameter Logistic Model (Rasch Model) according to Kiểm định mức độ vừa vặn của câu hỏi: Infit MNSQ và Outfit MNSQ trong khoảng 0.7 đến 1.3 (Bond & Fox, 2015)..
terms.benchmarks:
1. Infit/Outfit MNSQ trong khoảng 0.7 - 1.3.
2. Điểm số logit từ -3 đến +3.
3. Separation index ≥ 2.0 (Separation reliability ≥ 0.80).
terms.short_definition: Mô hình lý thuyết ứng đáp câu hỏi (IRT) trong đó xác suất trả lời đúng câu hỏi chỉ phụ thuộc vào sự chênh lệch giữa năng lực thí sinh và độ khó của câu hỏi.
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Thu thập ma trận phản hồi nhị phân: Dữ liệu câu trả lời đúng/sai (1/0) của N thí sinh trên K câu hỏi.
2. Ước lượng thông số mô hình:
 - Sử dụng Ước lượng Hợp lý Cực đại Có điều kiện (Conditional Maximum Likelihood - CML) dựa trên điểm tổng làm thống kê đủ (Sufficient Statistic), giúp triệt tiêu hoàn toàn tham số năng lực cá nhân θ khi ước lượng độ khó b_i.
 - Hoặc ước lượng Hợp lý Cực đại Biên (Marginal Maximum Likelihood - MML) tích phân trên phân phối năng lực chuẩn hóa θ ~ N(0, 1).
3. Đánh giá độ chuẩn khớp câu hỏi (Item Fit Analysis):
 Tính toán hai chỉ số phương sai phần dư chuẩn hóa:
 - Infit Mean Square (Infit MNSQ): Nhạy cảm với các phản hồi bất thường gần với mức năng lực của câu hỏi (Inlying patterns).
 - Outfit Mean Square (Outfit MNSQ): Nhạy cảm với các câu trả lời ngẫu nhiên bất thường ở xa mức năng lực (Outlying patterns).
4. Thiết lập Bản đồ Wright (Wright Map / Person-Item Map): Trực quan hóa phân phối năng lực của người thi và độ khó của các câu hỏi trên cùng một thước đo Logit chung.
5. Kiểm tra tính bất biến đo lường (Differential Item Functioning - DIF): Đảm bảo các câu hỏi không thiên vị giới tính, vùng miền hoặc sắc tộc.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Ép dữ liệu vào mô hình Rasch khi các câu hỏi có độ phân biệt quá chênh lệch: Nếu các câu hỏi trong đề thi có khả năng phân loại thí sinh giỏi-kém rất khác nhau, các đường cong đặc trưng (ICC) sẽ cắt nhau. Cố tình ép vào mô hình 1PL sẽ dẫn đến chỉ số Infit/Outfit bị vi phạm hàng loạt; khi đó bắt buộc phải chuyển sang mô hình 2PL.
2. Bỏ qua tác động của yếu tố đoán mò trong câu hỏi trắc nghiệm nhiều lựa chọn: Trong bài thi 4 lựa chọn, xác suất đoán mò may rủi là 25%. Mô hình Rasch thuần túy giả định c=0, do đó sẽ đánh giá sai lệch độ khó của các câu hỏi khó đối với nhóm thí sinh yếu kém.
3. Nhầm lẫn giữa 'Mô hình Rasch' và 'Mô hình 1PL Birnbaum': Mô hình Rasch coi dữ liệu phải phù hợp với mô hình để đạt chuẩn đo lường cơ bản (Fundamental Measurement); trong khi trường phái 1PL coi mô hình là công cụ thống kê xấp xỉ dữ liệu.
terms.apa_reference: Rasch, G. (1960). Probabilistic models for some intelligence and attainment tests. Danmarks Paedagogiske Institut.

terms.vietnamese: Kiểm định t một mẫu (One-Sample t-test)
vietnamese_variants: Kiểm định t một mẫu Student
So sánh trung bình mẫu với giá trị chuẩn
terms.core_definition: The One-Sample t-test, formulated by William Sealy Gosset under the pseudonym 'Student' (1908), is a fundamental parametric statistical hypothesis test used to determine whether the empirical mean of a single continuous sample ($\bar{x}$) drawn from a normally distributed population differs significantly from a known, theoretical, or hypothesized population benchmark ($\mu_0$) when the true population standard deviation ($\sigma$) is unknown and must be estimated from the sample ($s$).
terms.seminal_citation: Student. (1908). The probable error of a mean. Biometrika, 6(1), 1-25.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of One-Sample t-test according to Kirk (2013).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Hypotheses Formulation:
   - Null Hypothesis: H0: mu = mu_0
   - Alternative Hypothesis (Two-tailed): H1: mu != mu_0.
2. Test Statistic Calculation: t = (x_bar - mu_0) / SE(x_bar) = (x_bar - mu_0) / (s / sqrt(n)), where x_bar is sample mean, s is sample standard deviation, and n is sample size.
3. Sampling Distribution: Under H0, the statistic follows Student's t-distribution with degrees of freedom df = n - 1.
4. Decision Rule: Reject H0 if |t| >= t_{crit, alpha/2, df} (or if exact two-tailed p < 0.05).
5. Effect Size (Cohen's d): d = (x_bar - mu_0) / s (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large).
6. Non-parametric Alternative: If normality is severely violated and n is small, deploy the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Normality Assumption: Tested via Shapiro-Wilk or Q-Q plot; robust to modest non-normality when n >= 30 by Central Limit Theorem.
2. 95% Confidence Interval: CI = x_bar +/- t_{crit, 0.05, df} * (s / sqrt(n)); rejecting H0 at alpha = 0.05 is mathematically equivalent to the 95% CI excluding mu_0.
3. Sample Independence: Observations must be mutually independent random draws.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Severe Outlier Sensitivity: A single extreme outlier in a small sample (n < 20) can drastically inflate sample standard deviation s, causing t to collapse and producing a false failure to reject H0.
2. Using z-test with Sample Standard Deviation: Using the standard normal z-distribution instead of Student's t-distribution when sample size is modest (n < 30), producing anti-conservative p-values.
3. Hypothesizing Sample Statistics: Writing hypotheses about sample means (e.g., H0: x_bar = 5) rather than population parameters (H0: mu = 5).
terms.apa_reference: Student. (1908). The probable error of a mean. Biometrika, 6(1), 1-25. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/6.1.1

terms.vietnamese: Phân tích phương sai một yếu tố (One-Way ANOVA)
vietnamese_variants: Phân tích phương sai đơn yếu tố
terms.core_definition: One-Way Analysis of Variance (One-Way ANOVA), developed by Ronald A. Fisher (1925), is an omnibus parametric statistical test used to evaluate whether there are statistically significant differences among the means of three or more independent categorical groups on a single continuous dependent variable ($H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_k$). By partitioning total observed variance into Between-Group Variance (systematic treatment variation) and Within-Group Variance (random sampling error), the ANOVA F-test preserves the nominal experiment-wise Type I error rate ($\\alpha = 0.05$) that would be catastrophically inflated if multiple independent pairwise $t$-tests were conducted.
terms.seminal_citation: Fisher, R. A. (1925). Statistical methods for research workers. Oliver & Boyd.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of One-Way ANOVA according to Fisher (1925).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Partitioning Sum of Squares:
   - Total Sum of Squares (SST): SST = sum_j sum_i (y_{ij} - y_bar_grand)^2; df_T = N - 1.
   - Between-Group Sum of Squares (SSB): SSB = sum_j n_j (y_bar_j - y_bar_grand)^2; df_B = k - 1.
   - Within-Group / Error Sum of Squares (SSW): SSW = sum_j sum_i (y_{ij} - y_bar_j)^2; df_W = N - k.
2. F-Statistic Formulation: F = MSB / MSW = [ SSB / (k - 1) ] / [ SSW / (N - k) ]. Under H0, F follows F(k - 1, N - k).
3. Assumptions & Diagnostic Testing:
   - Normality within groups (Shapiro-Wilk).
   - Homogeneity of Variances (Levene's Test; if p < 0.05, report Welch's ANOVA or Brown-Forsythe F-test).
   - Independence of observations.
4. Post-Hoc Multiple Comparisons: If omnibus F is significant (p < 0.05), locate specific group differences using Tukey's HSD (equal variances) or Games-Howell (unequal variances).
5. Effect Size: Report eta-squared (eta^2 = SSB / SST) or omega-squared (omega^2, less biased in small samples).
terms.benchmarks:
1. Omnibus F Decision Rule: p < 0.05 rejects omnibus H0, demonstrating at least one group mean differs significantly from another.
2. Levene's Violation Protocol: If Levene's test p < 0.05, standard F-test is invalid; Welch's adjusted F-test must be reported.
3. Effect Size Interpretation: eta^2 >= 0.01 (small), >= 0.06 (medium), >= 0.14 (large effect).
terms.pitfalls:
1. Conducting Multiple Pairwise T-Tests Without ANOVA: Running 10 independent t-tests across 5 groups, causing familywise alpha inflation to 1 - (1 - 0.05)^10 = 40.1%.
2. Interpreting Post-Hoc Tests When Omnibus F is Non-Significant: Hunting for significant post-hoc pairwise differences when the omnibus F-test was non-significant (p >= 0.05).
3. Ignoring Heteroscedasticity with Unequal Cell Sizes: Running standard ANOVA when group variances differ widely and group sizes are severely unbalanced, producing massive Type I error inflation.
terms.apa_reference: Fisher, R. A. (1925). Statistical methods for research workers. Oliver & Boyd. (See also: Kirk, R. E., 2013, Experimental Design: Procedures for the Behavioral Sciences, 4th ed., SAGE).

terms.vietnamese: Chủ nghĩa hiện thực bản thể luận (Ontological Realism)
terms.core_definition: Ontological Realism is the foundational philosophical position in the philosophy of science stating that a mind-independent reality exists objectively, structured by real generative entities, properties, and causal mechanisms that operate regardless of whether human beings observe, conceptualize, or measure them (Bhaskar, 1975, 1978; Searle, 1995). Core to Critical Realism (Roy Bhaskar), ontological realism asserts that reality is stratified into three distinct ontological domains: the Empirical (experiences and observations), the Actual (events that happen, whether observed or not), and the Real (the underlying generative structures and causal mechanisms that have the capacity to produce events).
terms.seminal_citation: Bhaskar, R. (1975). A realist theory of science. Leeds Books.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Ontological Realism according to Bhaskar (1975).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. Stratification of Reality (Bhaskar's Tri-Domain Ontology):
   - The Empirical: Experiences, sensory perceptions, and recorded data.
   - The Actual: Events and states of affairs generated by causal powers, whether experienced or unexperienced.
   - The Real: Transfactual structures, generative mechanisms, and inherent causal liabilities that exist and act intransitively.
2. The Epistemic Fallacy Critique: Bhaskar critiques positivism for committing the 'epistemic fallacy'—reducing ontological questions (what exists) to epistemological questions (what can be observed/measured).
3. Retroduction (Abductive Identification): Methodological logic where the researcher observes an empirical event in the Actual domain and works backward to infer what generative mechanism in the Real domain must exist for that event to occur.
4. Causal Explanation Standard: Causal explanation consists not of finding universal empirical regularities (Hempel), but of describing the generative mechanisms producing tendencies in open systems.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Transitive vs. Intransitive Dimension: Intransitive objects of science (physical laws, social structures) exist independently of scientific inquiry; transitive objects (theories, paradigms) are socially constructed human concepts.
2. Open Systems Realism: Acknowledges that social systems are intrinsically open, meaning generative mechanisms operate as tendencies rather than deterministic clockwork regularities.
3. Anti-Reductionism: Rejects both naive positivist empiricism and radical postmodern constructivism.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Committing the Epistemic Fallacy: Asserting that unobservable theoretical constructs (e.g., organizational culture, latent class power) do not exist simply because they cannot be directly seen on a survey instrument.
2. Confusing Ontological Realism with Epistemological Infallibility: Assuming that because reality is real, our scientific theories must be absolutely true; critical realism embraces ontological realism alongside Epistemic Relativism (our knowledge is always socially situated and fallible).
3. Reification of Social Mechanisms: Forgetting that social structures (unlike physical atoms) depend on human activity for their continued reproduction.
terms.apa_reference: Bhaskar, R. (1975). A realist theory of science. Leeds Books. (2nd ed., 2008, Routledge). (See also: Sayer, A., 2000, Realism and Social Science, SAGE).

terms.vietnamese: Bản thể luận (Ontology trong phương pháp nghiên cứu)
terms.core_definition: Ontology is the foundational branch of philosophy and research methodology concerned with the nature of reality, existence, and being. In scientific research design (Guba & Lincoln, 1994; Crotty, 1998; Saunders et al., 2019), a researcher's ontological assumptions address the core question: 'What is the form and nature of reality, and what can be known about it?' Bounded along a spectrum from Realism/Objectivism (reality exists independently as external objective facts) to Relativism/Constructionism (realities are multiple, socially constructed, and dependent on human consciousness), ontology dictates a researcher's Epistemology (how we can know reality) and Methodology (how we study it).
terms.seminal_citation: Guba, E. G., & Lincoln, Y. S. (1994). Competing paradigms in qualitative research. In N. K. Denzin & Y. S. Lincoln (Eds.), Handbook of qualitative research (pp. 105-117). SAGE Publications.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Ontology according to Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. The Methodological Cascade (Saunders' Research Onion):
   - Level 1: Ontology (Nature of reality: Realism, Critical Realism, Relativism, Pragmatism).
   - Level 2: Epistemology (Nature of knowledge: Positivism, Interpretivism, Pragmatism).
   - Level 3: Axiology (Role of values: Value-free, Value-laden, Transformative).
   - Level 4: Methodology (Deductive, Inductive, Abductive; Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed).
   - Level 5: Methods (Surveys, Experiments, Ethnographies, Interviews).
2. Realism vs. Nominalism/Constructionism:
   - Realist Ontology: Assumes an objective reality existing independent of social actors; operationalized via quantitative measurement and statistical hypothesis testing.
   - Constructionist / Relativist Ontology: Assumes reality is created through social interaction, language, and shared subjective meanings; operationalized via phenomenological or ethnographic inquiry.
3. Pragmatic Ontology: Reality is practical, action-oriented, and evaluated by 'what works' in resolving real-world problems.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Paradigmatic Alignment: The research philosophy chapter of a doctoral dissertation must establish absolute logical coherence between ontology, epistemology, and methodology.
2. Explicit Stance Declaration: Researchers must explicitly declare their ontological positioning in research methodology chapters.
3. Defense Scrutiny: Doctoral committees scrutinize whether an author adopted qualitative methods while maintaining an unacknowledged naive positivist realist ontology.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Ontological Incoherence: Declaring a social constructionist ontology (multiple subjective realities) and then writing quantitative survey hypotheses designed to find 'universal objective truth'.
2. The Generic Boilerplate Trap: Copying generic textbook definitions of ontology without explaining how specific ontological assumptions directly govern data collection and interpretation in this thesis.
3. Dismissing Philosophy as Irrelevant: Treating ontological positioning as academic fluff rather than the foundational filter determining what counts as legitimate scientific evidence.
terms.apa_reference: Guba, E. G., & Lincoln, Y. S. (1994). Competing paradigms in qualitative research. In N. K. Denzin & Y. S. Lincoln (Eds.), Handbook of qualitative research (pp. 105-117). SAGE Publications.

terms.term: Open Coding (First-Cycle Analytic Coding - Strauss & Corbin)
terms.vietnamese: Mã hóa mở / Mã hóa sơ cấp phân rã dữ liệu
terms.core_definition: Open Coding (Mã hóa mở) là giai đoạn phân tích phân rã dữ liệu đầu tiên trong Lý thuyết nền theo Strauss & Corbin (1990, 1998). Quá trình này đòi hỏi việc đọc kỹ lưỡng bản gỡ băng, mở dữ liệu ra để khảo sát chi tiết, phân rã các phát ngôn thành các đơn vị ý nghĩa rải rác, so sánh các điểm tương đồng và dị biệt, và gán cho chúng các nhãn khái niệm (conceptual labels). Mã hóa mở giúp giải phóng tư duy của nhà nghiên cứu khỏi những định kiến thông thường, tạo tiền đề để các phạm trù tiềm năng bắt đầu lộ diện.
terms.seminal_citation: Strauss, A., & Corbin, J. (1990). Basics of Qualitative Research: Grounded Theory Procedures and Techniques. SAGE Publications; Saldaña, J. (2021). The Coding Manual for Qualitative Researchers (4th ed.). SAGE Publications.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Open Coding according to Strauss & Corbin (1998).
terms.operational_mechanism: Ba cấp độ kỹ thuật thực hiện mã hóa mở: (1) Phân tích dòng theo dòng (Line-by-line analysis) - tỉ mỉ và chi tiết nhất; (2) Phân tích theo từng câu/đoạn văn (Sentence/Paragraph analysis); (3) Phân tích toàn bộ văn bản (Whole-document analysis). Với mỗi đoạn dữ liệu, nghiên cứu viên liên tục đặt câu hỏi: 'Dữ liệu này đang đề cập đến điều gì?', 'Hiện tượng này đại diện cho cái gì?'. Các mã có tính chất giống nhau sau đó được gom cụm lại thành các Phạm trù ban đầu (Categories), đi kèm với việc xác định các Thuộc tính (Properties) và Chiều kích (Dimensions) cụ thể.
benchmarks: Tính mở hoàn toàn: Không bị ràng buộc bởi bất kỳ danh mục mã có sẵn (no pre-existing codebook).
Mã hóa sát nghĩa dữ liệu (Close-to-data): Các nhãn mã mở phải phản ánh trung thực phát ngôn và ngữ cảnh nguyên bản.
Tạo lập sổ tay mã hóa mở (Open Coding Codebook): Ghi chép định nghĩa chi tiết của từng mã mở để đảm bảo tính nhất quán khi phân tích các bản phỏng vấn tiếp theo.
pitfalls: Mã hóa quá khái quát (macro-coding): Gán một mã khổng lồ cho cả một trang văn bản khiến dữ liệu bị mất hết chi tiết vi mô.
Mã hóa quá vụn vặt (hyper-coding mà không tổng hợp): Sinh ra hàng ngàn mã nhỏ nhặt cho từng từ một nhưng sau đó không có khả năng phân loại và gộp nhóm thành các phạm trù có ý nghĩa.
Đóng khung định kiến quá sớm: Vừa đọc vài dòng đã vội vã dùng các khái niệm học thuật nổi tiếng để gán nhãn thay vì để dữ liệu tự cất lên tiếng nói.
terms.apa_reference: Strauss, A., & Corbin, J. (1990). Basics of qualitative research: Grounded theory procedures and techniques. SAGE Publications, Inc.

terms.vietnamese: Bình duyệt công khai (Open Peer Review)
vietnamese_variants: Open peer review in scholarly publishing
terms.core_definition: Open Peer Review (OPR) is an umbrella term encompassing scholarly publication models that dismantle the traditional secrecy and anonymity of peer review (Ross-Hellauer, 2017). Contrasting with traditional Single-Blind (reviewers know authors) and Double-Blind (both parties anonymized) reviews, Open Peer Review encompasses seven core operational traits: Open Identities (authors and reviewers know each other's names), Open Reports (referee reports and editorial correspondence published alongside the article), Open Participation (the broader academic community can comment on preprints), and Open Interaction (direct dialogue between authors and reviewers).
terms.seminal_citation: Ross-Hellauer, T. (2017). What is open peer review? A systematic review. F1000Research, 6, 588.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Open Peer Review according to Ford (2013).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. The Seven Facets of Open Peer Review (Ross-Hellauer, 2017):
   - Open Identities: Reviewer names disclosed alongside the published manuscript (promotes accountability and civility).
   - Open Reports: Full peer review reports, revisions, and author rebuttal letters assigned DOIs and published as citable scholarly artifacts.
   - Open Participation: Community crowd-review enabled on preprint platforms (e.g., bioRxiv, arXiv, PubPeer).
   - Open Interaction: Direct conversational exchange between authors, reviewers, and handling editors.
   - Open Pre-review Manuscripts: Manuscripts made publicly accessible prior to formal peer review.
   - Open Final-Version Commenting: Post-publication commenting and annotation platforms.
   - Open Platforms: Decoupled peer review services operating independently of specific traditional journals (e.g., Peer Community In).
2. Institutional Implementations: Adopted by major publishing platforms: BMJ, BioMed Central (BMC), Nature Communications, eLife, and F1000Research.
terms.benchmarks:
1. Transparency Standard: Complete, unedited peer review history permanently attached to the article with dedicated DOIs.
2. Civility & Constructiveness: Empirical bibliometric studies establish that open reviewer identities significantly reduce hostile, sarcastic, or unconstructive reviewer comments.
3. Citation Credit: Reviewers can cite their authored peer review reports on ORCID and Web of Science Reviewer Recognition Service.
terms.pitfalls:
1. Retaliation Risk for Junior Scholars: Early-career researchers may feel intimidated from signing critical reviews of papers written by powerful senior academics (mitigated by publishing reports openly while keeping reviewer names optional).
2. Reviewer Reluctance: Potential reviewers declining invitations because they fear public exposure or increased workload.
3. Commercial Publisher Capture: Publishers charging authors open access fees while capitalizing on free open reviewer labor without structural platform reform.
terms.apa_reference: Ross-Hellauer, T. (2017). What is open peer review? A systematic review. F1000Research, 6, 588. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.11369.2

terms.vietnamese: Huy hiệu khoa học mở (Open Science Badges)
vietnamese_variants: Chứng nhận khoa học mở COS
Huy hiệu dữ liệu và tài liệu mở
terms.core_definition: Open Science Badges are standardized visual certification icons developed by the Center for Open Science (COS; Kidwell et al., 2016) and adopted by prestigious international journals to acknowledge, incentivize, and publicly signal researchers who adhere to open scientific practices. Awarded across three distinct methodological behaviors—Open Data, Open Materials, and Preregistered—these badges serve as behavioral nudges that dramatically increase public data archiving, material sharing, and methodological reproducibility without requiring heavy regulatory mandates.
terms.seminal_citation: Kidwell, M. C., Lazarević, L. B., Baranski, E., Hardwicke, T. E., Piechowski, S., Falkenberg, L. S., ... & Nosek, B. A. (2016). Badges to acknowledge open practices: A simple, low-cost, effective method for increasing transparency. PLoS Biology, 14(5), e1002456.
terms.core_definition_en: Academic definition of Open Science Badges according to Kidwell et al. (2016).
terms.operational_mechanism:
1. The Three Primary Badges (Center for Open Science Taxonomy):
   - Open Data Badge: Awarded when digitally-shareable data relied upon in the paper are deposited in an approved, permanent, citable public repository (e.g., OSF, Zenodo, Dryad) with persistent DOIs, comprehensive codebooks, and metadata enabling independent re-analysis.
   - Open Materials Badge: Awarded when experimental stimuli, software scripts, psychometric survey instruments, and detailed protocols are deposited publicly in an unmodifiable format.
